product_title: Full HD 1080p Bullet 3.6mm Security IP Camera 2.4MP ONVIF Tube CCTV 36 IR POE White
review_body:
I too, like another reviewer tool a risk of ordering this camera with only a single review posted at a time. My experience is similar to what bitNile describes. I ended us returning the camera.

Box includes camera, water proof coupling shell for ethernet cable, mounting screws, mini-CD, and instruction leaflet. Instructions do mention camera's default IP (192.168.1.168), and a sticker attached to the camera specifies MAC address and default user name and password (admin/admin).

I plugged in the camera to PoE-injected connection and saw nothing. No lights, no indication of any kind that camera receives power. It may be a good thing that camera doesn't attract attention, but usually indicator lights are on by default and can be later turned off with the software, but not for this camera. After ~15 seconds I've heard faint internal noises, the sign I took for initialization sequence going on.

I knew camera is configured though ActiveX control, so I pointed my IE to 192.168.1.168 and was immediately prompted to install the plug-in. After installing, I was promoted to login. Entering default credentials I was presented at the home screen. Compared to other camera plug-ins this camera comes with pretty descent looking software. It seems to be thought-out and layout is logical, organized in Windows 8 - like tiles. Aside from the changing top right corner tile which I couldn't see the point for, other tiles navigated me to the places I've expected - setup, network, configuration, motion alarm control, etc.

Most of the screen is dedicated to live view, but unfortunately it didn't display anything. I poked around in settings, but couldn't get live view to display. I tried my mobile app (IP Cam Viewer Pro) to connect to RSCP feed, but couldn't connect.

I didn't bother googling for solution - to me, presenting live view through camera native interface in default, out-of-the-box, mode is a basic functionality any camera must be able to do. If it can't other features don't matter. I've packed the camera back into its box and shipped back to Amazon.

product_title: Olympus SH-1 16 MP Digital Camera
review_headline: It's an in between camera, that can be good
review_body: I just got this delivered today, everything works so far, and I've taken 6 pictures and a video of about 30 seconds, which was about as much as I tried the previous camera I had, that I bought from a store and returned right away for taking blurry, grainy pictures. I believe, though I'm not a camera expert, this camera takes pictures that are more than twice as good as that one did, despite only costing me twice as much. (The camera I'm comparing this with was a Nikon Coolpix L32. I did try putting that other camera on a tripod and it still wasn't as good as this camera is hand held. I thought that camera might be defective.)  This camera is heavy enough to help stabilize the images and large enough to grip, without being as heavy or bulky as a full size camera with a zoom lens, and it has sensor-shift image stabilzation, which is on by default but can be switched off. There are better cameras. This one seems to be doing some tricks with image processing that make a computer zoomed view of leaves on a distant tree in the image look like a sort of impressionist painting, although the detail in some of the branches against the sky is good.  Photo: computer cropped to 1067 x 781 giving 104x zoom, from 4608 x 3456 image at 24x zoom.  I found this camera via looking for an Olympus PEN E-P1, because I read those had good controls for manual settings, as far as that goes in mirrorless digital cameras. I didn't get one of those because although those have a larger sensor, a micro four thirds, their sensor is only a CCD, not a BSI-CMOS like this one. (BSI = back side illumination. Light doesn't have to filter through the sensor circuit before being detected. It goes straight into the back side of the sensor. That means better light sensitivity for a given size of sensor.) Higher end cameras than this one, with an APS-C size BSI-CMOS sensor and interchangeable lenses, are the thing to have if you want to take pictures where a computer zoomed view just shows more details, butI was worried about the size of carrying one of those around in a coat pocket, and not being able to afford to drop one. So although I found a great looking offer here at Amazon on a camera like that, refurbished, the price was beyond my plan, and adding a pancake lens, which would have made that camera a coat-pocket-size camera like this one, would have cost about $200, and a pancake lens isn't a zoom lens, so it seemed like a better deal to have a coat-pocket-size camera that does have zoom, for the price of one lens.  (That was my first review of any purchase online. Obviously I haven't used the camera much yet. I was impatient to get writing that story out of the way. Only four stars because I haven't gotten deep into using the camera yet enough to know.)

product_title: Yuneec Q500 + Typhoon Quadcopter with Aluminum Case, Handheld CGO SteadyGrip Gimbal, HD Camera. Extra Battery.  Extra Propellers Included.
review_body:
I already owned a couple DJI Phantom Quadcopters used mostly for real estate photos. They flew well (with one exception I learned the hard way, do not try to descend them too fast), but I never liked how long they took to acquire the necessary number of GPS satellites and the camera data link. Maybe it has something to do with having to use another device to connect to the data link, just know about half the time the Phantom information would get established just fine (battery info, GPS status, etc.) but the camera would not link. So, turn the power off and reboot everything, maybe a couple times, and it would decide to work.
Saw the Yuneec and read some decent reviews. Liked the all-in-one controller and the 16mb, no distortion camera (correcting the DJI pictures is no big deal if you use Lightroom or Photoshop). Yes, the controller does work much better and the Typhoon seems to acquire the GPS satellites much faster, but my love of the Yuneec product ends there. First of all the Typhoon is bigger and heavier, bigger is better because it make it more stable, but heavier is not good. Just for information, I am an ex-military helicopter pilot and have a pretty good understanding of rotary wing aerodynamics. Density altitude is key to the performance of anything that flies and as I found out, almost the hard way, on a 90 degree day here in Georgia, the Typhoon barely can get off the ground. The batteries for the Yuneec are only 200 mah more powerful than the DJI batteries and while the literature says good for up to 25 minutes, I would not trust them beyond about 10 minutes. That brings me to the battery condition displays, the DJI display has a very intuitive color bar, while the Yuneec uses a small battery voltage readout.
The 16mb camera on the Yuneec does not produce pictures with the clarity of the 14mb DJI camera. Not an expert on photography, but using a side by side comparison there is a difference. Another small thing I don't like on the Typhoon is the camera azimuth control. There is a lag in data transmission, which is expected, however, the control is just too sensitive and hard to align the camera for a tight shot.
Anyway, bottom line. Will probably use the Typhoon more when the weather gets cooler, but for right now the DJI is the only thing I feel comfortable with.

review_body: Bought this camera for my 10 year old son for his birthday, specifically for a trip to Hawaii.  After the very first use (in shallow, snorkeling conditions) we opened the chamber to find that the battery and the SD card were dripping water. I took the battery and SD card out, dried them off, left the chamber door open and in front of a vent to dry out the camera.  Once everything was dry, the photos were still in tact and the camera was still usable.  We checked the seal, wiped everything clean, closed and locked the chamber door for a second try.  The second try was better, having less water inside the chamber, however the camera had not been submerged under water as long and the inside was still wet and had to be dried out again.  It did catch a few great photos.

product_title: TRENDnet WiFi Baby Cam
review_headline: Only took me under 15 min. to set up; simple to use
review_body:
It took me less than 15 minutes to get this set up to work with a Samsung Galaxy Tab 4 tablet (which requires downloading the free TRENDnet Cloud app for Android; the app is also available in an Apple IOS version).

It works as expected in daylight, rooms lit with artificial light, dimly lit rooms, and rooms that are very dark.

After unplugging it and leaving it unplugged for hours at a time, plugging it back in and reconnecting to it via the TRENDnet Cloud app is simple and only takes a few seconds. (In my experience, the easiest glitch-free way to reconnect to the camera after it's been unplugged, then plugged back in, is to close the app on your device, then restart the app.)

The camera unit has a microphone and a speaker which you can operate remotely. There is a delay of a second or two (at least on the unit I received a sample of to review) between the time the microphone picks up a sound and the time you hear that sound on your Android or IOS device. The app has a music option that includes the following selections, as they are listed: Brahm's Lullaby, Moonlight Sonata, Nocturne Opus 9, Piano Sonatas No. 11, and Prelude and Fugue No. 1. You can elect to shuffle and/or repeat your selections, and you can also insert an SD card into a slot on the camera unit and select from any audio files you have on there. The sound from the built-in speaker is good enough for sleepy-time lullaby music, and there are volume control buttons on top of the camera.

The video quality is not great but it's about as good as any I've seen on several baby cams I've seen since my grandchildren were born (just about 7 and 5 years ago), and it's certainly more than adequate for monitoring a baby or keeping an eye on your driveway or whatever. It should go without saying that the video and audio quality are not adequate for movie-making, unless one wants to go an indie lo-tech "found footage" kind of route.

It comes with a CD with a guide and instructions on it; I did not have to use it to set up the camera I received. You will need to come up with a user name and password at some point in the setup process, so it might help to think about what those will be before you start. As I recall, the password needs to be at least 8 letters and/or digits long.

The electric cord is 10' long and ends in a two-prong adapter.to use it to set up the camera I received. product_title: Rokinon 85mm t/1.5 Aspherical Lens for Canon with De-Clicked Aperture and Follow Focus Compatibility Fixed Lens
review_body:
This lens is great! It has great low light capability. It is not at it's sharpest wide open, but no lens is. Close down to T/4, or T/ 5.6, or T/8, and you will get very sharp images. The stops are measured in T/Stops, which measure actual light transmitted. F/ stops are a ratio of the aperture to the focal length, and measured at the front side of the aperture...before the light passes through the aperture. T/Stops are a measure of the light transmitted through the aperture, and are measured after the light passes through the aperture....so it is more accurate. This lens does work on Crop Frame cameras, as well as Full Frame cameras. I have it on a Nikon D3300....a DX format Crop Frame camera.

The aperture ring is click-less, and turns smoothly. Focusing is also smooth. The focusing is touchy, as it allows such fine tuning. Focusing by hand is not as easy as is using a geared accessory focusing device, since it is easy to turn past, or stop short of, the best focus point by hand. That, plus the fact that this is a Manual Focus Only, and Manual Exposure Only, lens, means that photographers who have the patience to take some time, and work at achieving the best image, can get great shots. It also means that the typical, in a hurry, snapshooters-who want their cameras to do it all for them,and do it NOW!-will NOT get good images from this lens....as they will not take the time to focus well, adjust the aperture, or such.

This lens is NOT the equal of the multi thousand dollar lenses offered by Zeiss, Canon, Nikon, and other Big Name brands, and it should not be expected to be...since it does not cost like they do. It IS more than good enough for people who can't afford the costly items. In a 'value for dollar spent' way, this is one of the best third party lenses I have seen in a long time. It is well worth the price you will pay for it. I shot a photo of the books in a bookcase, in my dimly lit apartment interior, with the drapes closed, the blinds closed and lowered, the lights off, and only a hint of sunlight filtering in around the blinds fixture, and through the drapes. By using a shutter speed of 1/100th of a second, and adjusting my ISO upwards to 6400, I was able to get an image which looked so bright that it seemed that I had used a flash....when I had not. It was sharp, too, at T/4.

so bright that it looked as if I had used a flash.

product_title: Canon EOS Rebel SL1 Digital SLR with 18-55mm STM Lens (White)
review_body:
I should open this review by saying I don't even consider myself an 'amateur photographer', as that now seems to be read as implying some kind of expertise. I do enjoy taking photos, and since I print a good amount of them I like them to be as high quality as I can make them without breaking the bank. I had a lower end, compact point and shoot along with a better point and shoot for special events or trips. Over time, it became pretty clear that my cell phone would easily match the cheaper point and shoot and so I decided to get an actual DSLR as my sole non-cell camera. I've used Canon for most of my life, and I wanted to stick with that so I started looking into cameras that were good but under $1000. After a few weeks of reading the pros and cons of a variety of models, I went with the SL1. I had seen some very nice images from it, the size was right, and Amazon had a good deal on a bundle with it.

So far, it's been a great experience with this camera. It pretty much nailed the sweet spot I was looking for as far as giving me really good image quality in a fairly compact DSLR. I found the response time on taking images to very speedy, the clarity in both day and night shots is very good, and overall I feel like there's really not much I can't handle with the unit. For my first DSLR, I think I made the right decision is picking this one up. I also tested it using one of the EyeFi memory cards, and it works well with it although the delay in between taking shots is much more noticeable. Even so, it's great to have the option for times where I want to quickly transfer photos to my phone and post them.

product_title: Canon 55-250mm STM
review_headline: No significant difference in image quality vs. telephoto "L" glass for APS-C camera bodies
review_body:
Pixel peepers may disagree, but I would argue that there is no significant difference between the image quality output of this sub-300 dollar lens and a "professional grade" lens priced at or north of 1000 dollars when mounted on an APS-C body with apertures set equivalent.

I think people who own APS-C bodies (Canon Rebels, 70D, 7D, etc) often assume a common fallacy when they begin to covet expensive lenses such as the Canon 70-200 f2.8L IS II: that "professional" glass will consistently yield significantly sharper images. I know I did until I did some testing and found that for the majority of use cases this is simply not true. Most of your pictures will be viewed by others at a resolution and size where the human eye simply cannot objectively discern a difference in sharpness between pictures taken with this lens vs. a professional lens (stopped down to the same aperture and mounted on the same camera body).

So please APS-C camera body owners, do not go down the gear acquisition rabbit hole of buying expensive lenses without truly assessing where the value resides. Understand that what this lens does not provide is the ability to shoot at low apertures. That is the primary gain of mounting a more expensive EF professional lens on your crop body. Low apertures are beneficial for low light situations and subject isolation (fyi. even f5.6 produces really good shallow depth of field at 200+ mm that would satisfy most non-commercial applications which the Canon 55-250mm IS STM can do). But if low light photography and fancy super blurry backgrounds is really your thing, then instead spend those big bucks towards a full frame camera. Your APS-C body with that expensive lens is the wrong combination for that application.

Of course others will praise the build quality/ruggedness and weather sealing as other values of a more expensive, professional lens.... whatever... I feel a lot less nervous taking this cheap lens on rugged adventures, knowing at most I'm out a few hundred bucks vs. thousands in the unlikely event that I damage my gear.

So if you have a legitimate need to shoot 70-200mm at f2.8 or even at f4 then by all means pay the extra thousand bucks for a fancier lens than this one. Please understand that it's not a significant image quality gain, but instead it is actually a gain in versatility. Otherwise know that the Canon 55-250 IS STM lens will give you brilliant, sharp images within its very reasonable aperture limitations at a price that is affordable.rugged adventures, knowing at most I'm out a few hundred bucks vs. thousands in the unlikely event that I damage my gear.

product_title: Datacolor S5X100 Spyder5EXPRESS
review_headline: Works well in finding accurate color and brightness. Easy to setup and use.
review_body:
The Datacolor Spyder5PRO calibrates a monitor to have correct color and brightness. You can create multiple profiles for different types of computer use.The calibration process takes about 10 minutes and is very easy to follow. The device is 3" W x 2.75" H x 1.75" D.
You have to download the software from datacolor's website first. The file was about 70MB and the install was quick and easy. Then plug in the Spyder device (colorimeter) into the USB port of the computer. Then run the software. Everything is explained in easy to follow steps. There is also a quick-start guide available for download in case you need it, at the same area as the software. In order to calibrate properly, your monitor has to be on for at least 30 minutes, you have to turn off auto-brightness, and reset the monitor to factory settings ( this should set the color temp back to 6500K but just check anyway if it is an option on your monitor). Be sure to write down your monitor's settings before running the software. With the PRO version, you can create different profiles that have different calibrations, and load them easily and also turn the calibration off with a single mouse-click (in the Spyder software).
The calibration process requires you to hold the device up to the monitor. The first part is about 5 minutes long, it cycles through several colors, and my arm was getting tired of holding the device. There is a screw hole on the device that lets you mount it to a tripod, but make sure it is touching the monitor for accurate calibration. After the first part, I had to adjust the brightness on my monitor using the monitor's buttons so that it would match the brightness determined by the device. Once set, click continue, and it will cycle through several more colors, and this second part lasts about 7 minutes. My arms were very tired. Be sure to get comfortable and have proper access to your monitor because you have to hold the device to the monitor screen, or mountit on something. Don't press on it hard because you don't want to damage your monitor. Once the calibration was complete, I was happy with the calibration it provided me.
Now the calibration it had determined was very similar to the manual calibration I did myself without using a colorimeter device. So it wasn't that much different from my manual calibration, but since you have to reset the monitor to factory settings, the Spyder calibration difference was big compared to factory settings.
There are three models, the Express, PRO, and Elite. The PRO and Express models look exactly the same, even the label on the top. The only different between the two packages is the identification of the version on the label in the box near the serial number. I'm guessing the serial number is specific to the software version that you download. When you download the software, you have to choose the Express, PRO, or Elite software, whichever is identified by your serial number label. Check the datacolor website for the differences in models.
So, does the Spyder5 colorimeter device work? Yes. It accurately sets color. The PRO and Elite versions will adjust it even further based on the ambient light in the room. Was the color calibration so much better than what I had? No. I normally keep the brightness low on all my electronic devices anyway because of the sensitivity of my eyes to light. I noticed that most of these always lower the brightness to a low-medium or medium level. Similar to how TV's will lower the brightness when you use the Cinematic picture setting. This Spyder5 PRO does exactly what it's supposed to, and that's adjust brightness and color for accurate color representation. If you look at your photos on your calibrated monitor, and then on your friend's or another uncalibrated monitor, you will notice the difference. Some people may tell you that the colors or brightness are off in your photos or videos that you sent them, but the issue may be theirmonitor, or you may have to recalibrate.

review_body:
I bought this lens for my new Canon 70D. I love photography. But I don't do it professionally. So I didn't need the absolute sharpest lens. I mostly wanted to photograph my young son and have a walkabout lens that wouldn't require me to switch between lenses and carry extra gear.

Sometimes my son is right next to me, so 16mm feels right. And sometimes we're at the park, so 100mm is good. Sometimes I take him to a theme park and he's on a ride far away, so 300mm is perfect. Considering the focal length range on this lens, I knew going in I'd be sacrificing on quality a bit.

Right out of the box, I take my Canon 70D with the Tamron 16-300mm to the playground and start shooting my son. From the first picture, I realize there is blur at the focal point when I zoom in on the camera LCD. After many days of playing around with this lens, I begin to realize that at EVERY focal depth... the focal point is soft. From 16 to 300, I don't have a single sharp image. My manual settings are correct. It is NOT camera shake -- my hands are very still. I tested this even with a tripod. I tested it in really good light. I tested it every which way possible to produce what I consider a reasonably sharp image for a lens of this much range.

I did not want to believe the image quality was this bad. I did not want to go through a return process. I even began to question the quality of the 70D. 2 weeks passed and I decided to buy a Canon 18-135mm lens (that would have been part of a kit but I bought just a camera body alone cause I knew I'd be using the Tamron). I knew that it would be an unfair test considering the differences in these 2 lenses, but I wanted to see just how much better the quality would be in the 18-135mm. If it wasn't going to be much of a difference, I would return the Canon lens and stick with the Tamron. I wanted the Tamron to be decent enough to "live with" because the other way around would have me going through the hassle of returning the Tamron lens AND the 70D so that I could re-purchase the 70D with the kit lens to save a little money ($300 worth of savings).

After several days of playing around with the Tamron and Canon lenses, testing them both at good light and low light on tripods and handheld at the same focal depths, same ISOs, same apertures and same shutter speeds, I came to the conclusion that I could not live with the Tamron. The benefits of the extra zoom and comfort of not switching lenses and carrying extra gear was not worth sacrificing that much quality. The kit lens was sharper than I could have imagined... especially at the focal point. Not to mention, the Tamron is so LOUD when autofocusing. It is beyond annoying and distracting when in video mode. It takes away from the entire video. It is constantly hunting for focus and you hear it clicking and churning. The Canon lens was COMPLETELY silent. And the autofocusing was much more accurate.

In conclusion, I returned my Canon 70D and Tamron 16-300mm lens and purchased the Canon 70D with the kit lens Canon 18-135mm IS STM. I also purchased the Canon 55-250mm IS STM in addition and the store sold it to me for 50% off. In the end, I saved $450 and my images are so sharp and I am beyond happy with what I have now!!! Yes, I have to now carry an extra lens and switch lenses. But I just couldn't live with the Tamron's soft images. I'm not a crazy pixel-peeper and I'm not planning to make a profession out of photography, but the Tamron's IQ was unacceptable to me.

product_title: Msun 8gb Hd 720p Sports Dv Video Recorder 808 60fps Cam Fpv Camera Pocket Camcorder Hq30 V2
review_headline: One Year Later: Not bad for cheap-o spy cam.
review_body:
Have had this thing for a year now, but Amazon never sent me a review option, so I'm submitting one now. Reason being, it's a decent device:

It has a minor color issue, but corrects itself under good lighting. Obviously, the quality of the video is not spectacular, and there is of course no motion stability (if you hold it and record, it will get EVERY movement of your hand, making for VERY jerky video), so we're working with just a cheap piece of tiny camera here.

But it has held up and provides what I need. I'm kind to it, careful not to bang it around, and I use it for recording situations with troublesome tenants covertly. It works excellently for that purpose, audio and visual. Not anything I'd use in court, etc (not sure it's legal to in my state to use the footage in court regardless) but it provides a record that has been valuable to present to other third parties such as code inspectors, management, etc, so that the overall environment I'm dealing with is on record for people it would matter to.

So I speak up if a product is decent and serves me well for what I need it for. This is one such product. I did not give it five stars because I believe it is overpriced, and it's pretty clearly from China with instructions/etc that are definitely sub-par. But the little insert provided an email address, and I was able to find decent instructions online to get it up and running (the email was also responded to within a day; there is at least some level of sincere customer service via email).

Anyone who's bought these little gizmos from China knows exactly what I'm talking about; horrendous instructions and zero quality on presentation as far as manuals/guides go. So once the learning curve happens in understanding how to use it and get it on one's puter, it's a decent, cheap, product for what it is.

Instructions btw:
-There are two active buttons near the edge camera hole.
-You hold down the lower button for a couple seconds to get the unit on, and a tiny green light will come on, and stay on, indicating the unit is ready to record (and will shut down after a minute or so if you do NOT record).
-Then, press and hold down the higher button (near the edge where the camera hole is) for several seconds and the same light will flash on and of rapidly, then go *off* completely. At that time, when the light is off, *the camera is recording*.
-To stop, press and hold down that same edge button, and the light will come back on, and recording has stopped.
-Press and hold the other button again to turn the unit off...the light will again flash, and then turn off.
That's how the record function works.

As far as getting it into your puter goes, it's basically plug 'n play. After usb connecting, the trick is to turn the unit ON per above, to get the put er to recognize it. Then you just have to navigate the folder a bit to find the recorded material.

That's it.

A decent, cheap, spy cam. Passes as a car starter/keychain from a distance, but won't fool anyone up close...really cheap/crappy plastic. But good for what I need it for, and has provided many videos for me over the past year (about two dozen and counting).

review_headline: Why Do I Keep Buying Cheap Junk?
review_body:
There are lots of these GoPro accessories on Amazon and elsewhere, and you should shop for a different one. I was looking for one of the floaty handles, and was about to buy another one for about $7. Then I noticed this deal: the handle, plus a telescoping pole, a handlebar mount and another mount for just a few bucks more. I'd been looking for a handlebar mount for my motorcycle anyway, so I bought it.

Right out of the mailer, before I even opened the plastic, I could see a problem. The yellow floaty thing was in two pieces (it's not supposed to be). The end cap, which is supposed to be glued or fused to the main part, was not attached and didn't look like it ever had been. It's not meant to come off, and it doesn't screw back on. In the end, I used PVC cement left over my lawn sprinklers to refasten it. We'll see how that goes.

PROS:
- Handlebar mount seems good, though I haven't tried it.
- The lanyards seem OK.

CONS:
- It was broken.
- Poor materials, quality and workmanship.
- The telescoping pole is worthless, because there's not enough friction between the different segments to keep them from rotating. So the tiny weight of the GoPro is more than enough to cause it to turn. Want your GoPro on the top? Too bad, it will spin around to the bottom.

product_title: Celestron SkyMaster Giant 15x70 Binoculars with Tripod Adapter
review_headline: Great for watching nature, and for sweeping the sky at night to check out open clusters and large nebulae.
review_body:
I somewhat recently sold my telescope, as I wasn't getting much use out of it. The pacific northwest is not exactly a friendly place for sky gazing due to all the rain, and especially at my house where I have a very small slice of open sky due to all the trees. I needed something small, ultra-portable, and with a wide field of view. Enter these.

With 70mm lenses and 15x magnification, they will pull in distant objects very nicely. They're big, but not so huge they're unwieldy. If you have weak hands and wrists, prolonged usage will probably become uncomfortable. Even if you're in great shape and strong, after a while they will still start taking their toll. The nice thing is they come with a tripod mount, so you can thread them onto one and offload all that weight for extended viewing.

They function just like any other binoculars I've owned. They adjust for the width of your eyes, and also have a diopter adjustment so you can use them without glasses. And of course there's an adjustment knob for focus. All of these, especially the focus knob, are butter smooth when you adjust them. They eyecups are comfortable, made of soft rubber. The case is a standard run of the mill pouch with a cover that drapes over the top and fastens with velcro.

The only thing I can ding these on is there is a bit of noticeable chromatic aberration. You'll see it when you're focused on a somewhat close object, like the branch of a tree, against a bright cloudy sky. The pink and green "shadows" indicative of aberration is there, but not distracting, However, at under $70 at the time of this review, I don't think anyone could expect optical performance of much pricier glass.

So yes, I would recommend these for checking out the heavens at night, or for nature during the day. You get a lot of performance for the money.

Detaching is just as fast after pressing the release lock and flipping the lever to release the camera.

product_title: Nikon COOLPIX P900 Digital Camera with 83x Optical Zoom and Built-In Wi-Fi(Black)
review_body: Having just returned from a trip to Colorado where I used this camera extensively in Rocky Mtn National Park, I can state that I absolutely love it. For my purposes, there couldn't have been a better choice. I love to photograph beautiful scenery and wildlife, and this camera worked extremely well. My co-workers were very impressed with the photographs that I took, so much so that two of them are also interested in buying this camera. For action shots, I can't say what it will do, because the most action I saw was a herd of bighorn sheep grazing a mountainside, a moose wading and eating in a shallow lake, deer and elk that were mostly grazing and some baby great horned owls in their nest with heads turning back and forth. I didn't buy it to take action shots. As for the WiFi capability, meh. I didn't buy it for that either and it's a darn good thing, because I couldn't ever get that to work. A lot of people were complaining on the app store about the app not working since they did an update, so maybe that's the problem, and it will hopefully be resolved for those who like to share photos via Facebook. I don't do that anyway. I mainly wanted a camera that had a powerful zoom and this one has it. I wanted one that didn't force me to haul around a case full of lenses, and this one fits that bill as well. It does everything that I need it to do. If it doesn't hold up, or if I find things about it that I don't like, I'll update later. For now, I'm totally pleased.

product_title: THE EDUCATOR ALL NEW EDUCATOR II NIGHT VISION SMALL METAL ELECTRICAL BOX CAMERA/DVR WITH 2 YEAR STANDBY BATTERY, IR ILLUMINATION, BODY HEAT (PIR) MOTION ACTIVATION-OUTDOOR WEATHERPROOF
review_body:
PROS: Stealthy, nice concept.
CONS: Unreliable, hassle to maintain, poorly manufactured.

The idea is great and the unit is fairly stealthy. However, it doesn't work well. You will need to charge the battery pack at about 3 day intervals, maybe more if there is a lot of activity on the camera. With very little activity, the battery will last up to 5 days and no indication is given a charge is needed.

When reconnecting the battery, sometimes (about 40-50% of the time) the SD card does not automatically enter the record mode, even if you have pre-configured it to do so. In such cases, you will never know until you check the SD card, only to find it has no files on it. When this happens, you will need to ensure you have a fresh battery pack, reconnect it, make some movement, disconnect the battery, pull the SD card and check to see if it is recording. All of this is more trouble than it is worth. You could potentially lose data from the time you connect a fresh battery pack until depleted, because you will never know it is recording, and when you check the SD card, there may be no files recorded.

Bottom line, when you need to catch a vandal, you have a 50-50 chance this thing is going to record as advertised. The unit appears to be put together by hand, like a kit project. For 400 bucks it's just not worth it.

review_headline: Worth the extra money for the kit, but still has downfalls.
review_body:
This is a fantastic camera, five stars on the camera, four stars on the kit. It allows you to attach external lenses and accessories, which come with this kit. I will mostly be reviewing the kit that came with this camera. If you want to look up reviews of the HC-v770, Google it. Overall, it is a very good midrange camcorder. I will not be using the light or the tripod. The microphone is pretty decent, it is not top of the line, but it still works well. The memory card is great. It is high capacity and transfers videos at high speeds. The lense cleaning kit does what it is supposed to. When you zoom in while using the telescope and wide angle lenses, they distort the light on objects and makes them seem like they are glowing. Objects that are not in the center of the picture also get distorted. If you don't zoom in far enough, you can see a vignette around the image from the lense. Not just a subtle one either, a very obvious, distracting one. I found that the camcorder's built-in 20x optical zoom works very well (I do not use digital zoom due to losing picture quality). The lense covers are great though! My favorite part about the kit is the case. It looks good and has plenty of room to fit everything in this kit in it if you pack it properly, excluding the tripod, which comes with its own carrying bag.

In conclusion, I like the camcorder, memory card, microphone, lense covers, case, cleaning kit, memory card holder, and screen protectors. I do not like the tripod, light, telescope and wide angle lenses. It was still worth the extra money to me, but if you want this for the tripod, look elsewhere!

On the whole, this is a good deal for a decent camera kit - just let's hope Anart updates their WiFi app again soon. I did have a few crashes... but then, I had crashes with the far more expensive HP WiFi camera app... Hewlett Packard software crashing?

product_title: Olympus 40-150mm F4.0-5.6 R Lens
review_headline: A must buy for everyone with an m4/3 camera.
review_body:
So, what can you expect out of a 40-150mm zoom on a micro 4/3 system, which can be had for $120 or less on a regular basis?

Frankly, more than you might expect.

Let's get the bad over with. This thing is chintzy. It is all plastic. It feels like a toy in hand. No compromises were made in the price of this lens. Every expense was spared. The build of this lens is, at best, as bad as the worst kit lens I have used in the last decade. That isn't to say it feels bad. It doesn't. But you're not going to mistake it for a well built lens once you've actually used one. And you know what? That's fine.

I don't think this lens is great for the normal price. But at the sale price? You can't not buy it, even if you have a nicer setup. Why is that? This thing is absolutely, positively, miniscule. It will fit in many pockets. It barely weighs more than a pancake lens. It isn't any longer when retracted than many little kit lenses, so it can fit in very shallow spaces.

I use an Olympus PEN alongside my big Canon system, and particularly with prime lenses, it can compare very well to my 6D and 24-105L. If I only bring the Pen with me, I never feel bad about it like I did when I used to use a P&S as a secondary lightweight camera. The 40-150 isn't good enough to hold the mantle of "Well, this is damn near as good as my big kit!". It's not even as good as the first generation Canon 55-250mm IS... but it's close enough to that that the size and price make up for everything - it makes the Canon 55-250mm look like a monster in comparison.

If you need some reach on an m4/3 camera, but also desire the smallest possible kit - this lens is a fantastic little compromise in a tiny, inexpensive package. It won't wow you if you're used to shooting bigger lenses, but if you want something that you can take anywhere, aren't too fussy about the results, and, if you can get close enough, will get some genuinely good looking shots. Some people freak out a little bit when you point a "small" telephoto lens - my 70-200 f4L is a relatively compact telephoto lens for a full frame system, and it will literally scare some people away from the camera because they think I am filling the whole picture with a pimple. While a quick look through the lens can quell that fear, this little lens will scare nobody.

In short, this is a fun little lens. Image quality isn't great on an absolute scale, but it's good enough for casual use, and will surprise you from time to time. But it is so tiny and so inexpensive that there's literally nothing like it out there at all with this sort of range. Pick this lens up. Shove it somewhere when you're bringing your camera around, and you might just find a shot with it that you would have never had otherwise.

After all, if the best camera is the one you have with you, shouldn't that apply to lenses too?

product_title: K&F Concept Neutral Density Filter
review_headline: Very Nice ND Filter for 58mm Thread-Size Lenses
review_body:
I have been learning more about photography and as time has permitted I have been improving my skill as an amateur photographer. I have worked with other types of filters, in particular CPL and FL-D filters, but before now I have never worked with ND filters. I have been able to achieve good results with it and so far I am pleased with this filter though I know I have more to learn about it.

A neutral-density filter is used to reduce light reaching the aperture without fiddling too much with the colors. This allows one to get creative with shutter speeds. This particular filter is adjustable and turns on the lens body face, allowing the photographer to increase or decrease the amount of filtering done. At the lowest setting the filter does very little filtering; when turned up to the maximum filtering level very little light gets through and a moire pattern appears so I do not recommend turning up the filter to this level.

To get a feel for how well this filter works I took my camera outside as a big thunderstorm approached and took some pictures of one of the cloud formations. I selected two pictures from that set, one where I did not use the filter and one where I did use it on about 1/4 strength. Although the filter evenly reduced light levels, the color contrast in the filtered image is much more pronounced and obvious.

The most common use for this kind of filter is to reduce the light levels, then take an extended exposure for a scene with motion, such as a waterfall.

This is a very nice filter and I could not be happier with it. It is very easy to use and it really works well.

product_title: Interfit INT337 Strobies Triple Flash Bracket with Bracket and Handle
review_headline: Perfect for Photek Softlighter and other heavy modifiers
review_body: Sometimes I buy a product "blind" because, though there are hundreds of reviews, none of them tells me what I need to know. So I write the review I wish I had seen before deciding to buy. In this case, I needed to know if the bracket is strong enough to work in conjunction with a 60" enclosed parabolic, the Photek Softlighter that's a staple for so many portrait photographers. I had a Lastolite Tri-Flash, and though I normally swear by Lastolite, it cost me three times what this gizmo costs and routinely unhinged itself, dropping speedlights into the umbrella, or, worst of all, not holding the umbrella pole firmly enough and falling apart on location. The hinge that set the angle was way too flimsy too. Anyone that does a lot of mobile studio work knows how embarrassing and tense these kinds of snafus make an otherwise productive shoot.  Now here's a brief aside: Amazon reviews have gotten dumbed-down by the fact that people seem to automatically rate any product they like with five stars and any product they dislike with one star. Just to be clear, I save my five star reviews for products that make me do handstands. Four stars is a great rating in my book.  To answer the question I set up in the first paragraph, this bracket is perfect for the Photek Softlighter, or, I imagine, any large, heavy modifier. It's strong as hell (though not as heavy as other reviews would lead you to think) and has some design features that make me think it was invented for the Softlighter. The bracket that holds the three flashes is a separate piece that mounts and dismounts from the base that hold the umbrella and attaches to the stand. Anyone who's tried to stretch the "sock" of the Softlighter front diffuser baffle around three flashes will see the beauty in this. You can set up your umbrella and diffuser and then reach in and install your lights in one fell swoop, easily maneuvering them through the stocking-cuff opening. Another big benefit is that you can mount all of your lights on the attachment at home or at the studio, transport them to the location, and attach them to the base all at once. There's nothing that inspires less confidence in clients or photo subjects than fiddling with multiple, unreliable mounts on site. The big knob is impossible to miss, so you don't have to grope around in there. The only downside is that you have one more grip knob (for this separate bracket) that you have to make sure is tight; if it's at all loose, your three flashes will wind up in the bottom of your brolly.  Also perfect for the Softlighter is the tilt handle, which you see in the product picture. It protrudes from the sock so you can adjust angles without reaching into the diffuser. It even comes with an angle gauge on the stem so you can robotically follow the hack lighting rule that tells you to set your light source at a 45-degree angle to your subject (or not—the choice is yours). Once you get them buttoned down, all of the grips work solidly enough to hold a fairly cumbersome modifier. It's a huge improvement over every other triple flash bracket I've tried, none of which seem to take into account the fact that if you're mounting three flashes you might be using a modifier and if so, a HEAVY modifier.  Let's face it, stuff is manufactured way to chintzilly these days. This is a nice exception.  So why four and not five stars? The coldshoes, though well machined, are fiddly because they have screw tighteners. I vastly prefer inert, non-tightening coldshoes. So you might want to set these at nearly-tight tolerance for your speedlights and then use the lever or knurled fastener on the flashgun itself to tighten them down the last little bit. Screwing and unscrewing these things all the time will almost surely result in one or two of them not being tight on location. Better to get the last pinch of tightness from the flash mount mechanism itself. One advantage of these coldshoes is that they too are separate pieces that canbe rotated on the bracket, so I imagine that Nikon shooters who don't have radio technology can aim the sensors of the slave flashes at each other by rotating the flash orientations. I have no reason to know if this works, but if it does, bear in mind that Lastolite charges almost an extra hundred bucks for this functionality in their "Joe McNally" signature tri-flash, which I think might be the only version they still manufacture.  The other thing that isn't perfect is the umbrella mount. It's way better than the Lastolite screw tightener, which didn't prevent the umbrella pole from sliding and rotating, but it's still a tricky screw. You have to turn it clockwise beyond where you think it's done tightening to get it to "bite" the umbrella pole properly, after which point the umbrella is secure. I dunno, if I were designing the thing I'd have made this screw longer.  If you think these are small complaints, you're right. It's a terrific bracket, and, like I say, four stars is a great rating.

product_title: Celestron Heavy-Duty Altazimuth Tripod
review_headline: Heavy-doodie tripod for terrestrial viewing in Kansas?
review_body:
This is a strange tripod. I'm not sure who or what it's designed for. Here are the pros and cons:

PROS:

+ It is relatively stable.
+ The feet on the bottom-- while spikes-- are not metal, so they can be used on most surfaces without scratching.
+ The cables and knobs are really great for small and smooth adjustments to horizontal and vertical

CONS:

- As many other reviewers have mentioned, there is very little altitude adjustment available (i.e. this tripod would be useless for astronomy because you can't angle it up barely at all). The tripod is really only good for looking at terrestrial objects that are level with the horizon or slightly above. I bought this tripod for use with a spotting scope at the gun range, so this wasn't a deal-breaker, but be warned if you intend to attempt to use it for astronomy.
- The tripod is of very cheap construction. The legs are uncoated/unpainted matte aluminum, with cheap plastic tension clamps, and what appears to be pressed zinc metal head coated with a thick lacquer of cheap gray paint.
- The tripod is bulky and would not be easy to transport to the gun range or to a any remote location with low light pollution for astronomy use (e.g. up on a hill or out in a field).

Overall, I'm actually really upset that Celestron would sell and market this tripod the way they do. It's really dishonest. They are intentionally selling a very cheap tripod while giving it the appearance of being a quality product. With probably $10 in actual upgrades from the factory, this could be a decent tripod. But they want to create an artificial gap between their low-end cheap tripods and their high-end expensive tripods, so this tripod is artificially expensive. For the price of this tripod, I wasn't expecting a Manfrotto. But I was expecting something better.

I'm going to return this tripod and get a better one for half the price.

product_title: Celestron 21088 Omni XLT 102
review_body:
I purchased this telescope for planetary and lunar viewing. It's not the just light collector for DSOs but managed to capture some of the brighter Messier objects.

For an intermediate telescope the Omni XLT 102 is the perfect balance of power and portability. I live in a major US city so light pollution restricts what I can see in the night sky. But planets turn out amazingly in this scope. I made out the red spot on Jupiter once and you can easily see the Cassini division in Saturn. The focuser is adjustable, allowing for better control. However the focuser is greasy and lacks a fine tune knob.

Chromatic aberration is not too much of an issue. The coating on the lens is ample but is not what you expect on refractors $800+. Jupiter has a distinct blue halo around it and Saturn has some green hue but this does not ruin the viewing experience at all. Seeing the chromatic aberration is more of an observation than a complaint.

The focal length of the scope is phenomenal and really one of the best features. It allows for better magnification especially with planets. I would recommend at least a 2X Barlow and a 10mm eyepiece to really capture planetary detail such as the Cassini division.

The mount is sturdy and not too shaky. Only when you focus does the image shake for a brief moment. I believe you can attach a motor drive on this mount too, so for astrophotography this is a great semi-portable, semi-powerful telescope.

You won't see amazing images that bigger telescopes like 10" Dobs get, but if you're looking for a somewhat portable telescope that's still good enough to make you gasp. This is the baby for you!

PROs:
Sturdy tripod
Solid EQ mount, with option for polar alignment scope
Nice coating on the lens
Not too heavy (For me. I guess, it is larger than most refractors you see)
Easy to set up (less than 5 minutes)
AMAZING FOCAL LENGTH f/9.8
Easily magnify up to 200x

CONs:
Greasy focuser
Tripod legs could extend longer
EQ mount is not very fluid when balancing
Slow motion knobs can be longer200x

product_title: CowboyStudio 500 LED Ultra Bright Portable Video Photography Portrait Light Panel
review_headline: With 500 points of light, there is no way to direct the light
review_body:
While these are not dimmable, I doubt I would dim them down if they were. I have some small led panels (see my review of the Z-96) and mostly, use them full power. The only time I use less than full is if I am getting glare or an area is too hot.

I had a diffuser made for one of these (I have 4 of them) as a test and need to have more made. I really like the light diffused. The barn doors are mainly eye candy. Barn doors work well when the light source is a single point light source. With 500 points of light, there is no way to direct the light, unless you close them down almost completely. Just closing a little just reduces the light. It has 4 banks of lights. I don't think I have ever used them with less than all of the lights turned on. I guess it is because I am always wanting more light then these produce.

I do like the way they mount with the recessed channels on three sides. The mounting device is very solid and I do like the feature that allows you to push the button in on the lever and move it where you want it after you tighten down the swivel.

Price is right and unless you really think you need dimmers or bi-color then I would recommend these. There may be some others available that do not feature worthless barn doors and are perhaps not as heavy. You do need some stout light stands or flex arms to hold these.

Again, they probably look more professional then lights without barn doors, but the doors really don't help you except they do protect the lights when in transit.

product_title: Polaroid ZIP Mobile Printer Parent ASIN
review_headline: Produces Small High Quality Photo Prints Quickly And Easily
review_body:
I'm old enough to remember the old Polaroid cameras and I always loved the fun they brought to events before digital cameras and mobile phones came around. This little printer helps recapture some of that fun by mixing a bit of the old with a bit of the new. With this device you can take a photo with your phone, both Apple and Android devices are supported with an app, and print them instantly to this portable, rechargeable printer.

The main thing for me is the photo quality and this printer does an amazing job that is on par with professionally printed photographs. I love the glossy finish and the brilliance of the colors produced. The only negative thing is that the printer only prints out 2" x 3" pictures which is slightly smaller than a normal business card or credit card.

The "magic" of this device is that it uses ZINK paper which is completely heat activated so there is no need for the printer itself to contain any ink or toner of any sort. The device uses heat to activate the proper color for each individual pixel which is pretty cool. The ZINK paper itself is not cheap but not super-expensive either as a quick search of Amazon found the paper available in various sized packages for anywhere from 29 cents a sheet to 50 cents a sheet. A nice touch is that the backing of the paper can be peeled away making the photos into a nice, heavy-duty sticker.

The printing process itself is quicker than I imagined it would be. It takes about 15 seconds to beam the image from your device to the printer and then about 45 seconds to print it out giving you a total of about a minute for the process from start to finish. The device sounds like a very small laser printer when operating which I suppose makes sense since it is generating a fair amount of heat like a laser printer.

The app itself, I only tested the Apple version, has controls for how long the device waits to power off after the last picture which can be set to 3 minutes, 5 minutes, 10 minutes or to have no auto-shutoff at all and also for whether it should use an auto-exposure setting to try and make the photos look better. The app also tells you how much battery life is left on the printer as well as the current status of the printer, how many pages have been printed on the printer, the device's Mac address as well as which firmware version is running on the device.

The Polaroid app lets you print photos as they are or add a variety of icons, text and designs over the image. One of these items is hiding "secret messages" in the photo which can be anything from a 10 second audio clip to a URL to a text message. This is done by adding a QR code to the bottom right of the image. Unfortunately, Polaroid is missing the boat here as the only way to access these messages is through their app making this part of the fun pretty useless. I would think Polaroid would get much more benefit from allowing all QR code readers access to the information so people could hand out a photo to someone and have their email address or phone number in the QR code. Having to explain first that they have to download the Polaroid app to see the message makes no sense.

The printer is lightweight and compact and I had no problem slipping it into my jeans pocket. There is a sole USB port on the back of the device that is used for charging it. On a full charge the device will print about 25 images before needing to be recharged. It does work while being charged so you could have it attached to a power bank even if out and about and get more than 25 images if needed.

To load the paper you simply slide the top of the unit back and then off and load the paper in the direction indicated on the packaging. The loading process is as quick and easy as it gets.

Pairing the device to my iPhone 6 was quick and easy. One small gripe was that the iPhone did not automatically reconnect to the printer when itcame back online after being off. The unit I tested was an early unit and there have been firmware updates while I've been using it so this is something that might change. Speaking of the firmware updates they are done completely within the app so they were quick and easy and done completely wirelessly.

Overall there is a lot to like about this printer and it has me hoping that there is eventually a larger version to produce larger prints even if it isn't portable. The portability of this one makes it a fun device that you can carry around with you and print out high quality images on the go. A nice melding of new technology with the feel of the classic Polaroid cameras. Highly recommended.

product_title: Fujifilm X-E1 16.3MP Compact System Digital Camera with 2.8-Inch LCD
review_body:
I bought this slightly used. It was near mint. The most important thing is to update the firmware ASAP- this ensures it is compatible the various lenses, improves the operation of auto focus etc.

The pluses: The quality of the images is superior to other APS-C 16mp camera bodies - not quite in the same league as my Nikon D7100 but close. Light weight and modest size. Handling. The controls laid out extremely well though certainly different from most DLSRs. I use it in manual focus mode nearly all the time because if you also assign back button functionality to the AE-L AF-L, you get the best of both worlds plus a really helpful depth of field bar in the view finder. This can be enhanced further by enabling focus peaking.

The minuses: The auto focus is slow and awkward for photographing action - I've tried at dog agility trials and horse races. With anticipation you may get some good photos but it really not very satisfying. When you have bright sun over your right shoulder the EVF can be hard to see - an eyecup accessory (if one existed) might help but this remains a weak point in comparison to DSLRs. If you use DxO optics pro for lens correction, be aware that Fuji's X-tran bodies are NOT supported. Fortunately, Fuji's lenses don't seem to need much correction.

Every camera has compromises. If you don't shoot fast moving subjects or video and can cope with the EVF on bright sunny days you will find the Fuji will do just about any thing a comparably priced DSLR will do.

product_title: Neewer 750II TTL Flash Speedlite with LCD Display for Nikon D7200 D7100 D7000 D5500 D5300 D5200 D5100 D5000 D3300 D3200 D3100 D3000 D700 D600 D500 D90 D80 D70 D60 D50 and Other Nikon DSLR Cameras
review_headline: Simple and easy to use SB-800 Knock-off. Buy it!
review_body:
This flash is EXACTLY what you want if you are only an occasional flash user, but want something that produces better results than the pop of flash on your Nikon DSLR, and you do not choose to tie up several hundred dollars in the admittedly excellent Nikon Speedlights. I ordered my first one with the idea of sending it as a gift to my friend who is a budding photographer and who gets my old Nikon gear when I upgrade from time to time. It arrived today, and I decided to test it out.

I opened up the box and did not even consult the manual. I popped in some fresh batteries and put it on a D7000 I had laying around. I just switched left it as it came out of the box, which is defaulted to TTL. I then took a series of shots with direct flash, and bounce flash. Direct flash looks good, bounce flash looks great. The unit zooms automatically and is accurate, but do remember if it is not zooming to wake up your Nikon if it has been a bit between shots. I repeated the same shots with my Nikon SB-600 and my Nikon SB-800 and they were identical in results to this flash. I then, without ever opening the manual, was easily able to set up remote TTL flash. I just set my D7000 in Commander Mode, set the Neewer flash to S2 mode and was able to fire it off camera with great results, again indistinguishable from my Nikon Speedlights.

This unit is clearly a knock-off of the SB-800 and a very good one, Construction quality is not quite as good, and this unit may not last quite as long, but given that a used SB-800 is $300 and this one is $52 brand new, you'd have to break six of these before you lost money on the deal. As much s I love my Nikon gear, unless you are using your Speedlight daily, just buy one. If you want to play with more than one light, these make great spares. I was so impressed that since this is a gift, I just ordered two more for myself!

review_headline: this camera is a great buy. I primarily use this as a dashcam ...
review_body:
For the money, this camera is a great buy. I primarily use this as a dashcam for the 60 plus miles commuting on LA area freeways, as well as on my boogie board at the beach. The battery life on this is pretty good (up to 2 hrs); the 1080p resolution is clear enough to read a license plate (good when somebody side swiped me and ran off... but not for long!) and video mode allows you to zoom.

Sound wise the audio can be lacking (especially if you plan on recording loud music - mic will get overloaded and will distort), but for average recording, it works fine. Now this camera is no Go Pro (which I do own a Silver), but it still should be considered as a low cost option (versus the Go Pro). And if you do own a Go Pro and don't want to be using it daily (as I do for driving), this is a great 2nd option...

product_title: Instax SP-1
review_headline: Love it! Very happy with my purchase
review_body:
If you already have the Fujifilm Instax Mini 8 Instant Camera, then you know there are certain woes that are recurring. Like when you give the cameras to others to take a picture, they tend to miss the mark and capture way too much negative background space. A waste of film! Or if you happen to snap a pic and your finger is in it - the worst!

Especially when the film can cost a dollar or more for each picture, I really want them to look good. That is what pushed me to buy the Instax Printer. By using the app on my phone (easy download), I can see clearly what the picture will look like before I print it. I can even edit the photo through the app by adding filters, decorations, and messages on the photo. These don't translate to the border though, strictly on the picture portion. If you already have a decorated border because of special film that you bought, I am not sure how nice the extra stuff will look if you add it to your picture.

Now that I have this printer, I am not sure if I will ever use my Instax Mini Camera again because I can't see what the pictures look like before hand. I still want the novelty of printed pictures, especially Polaroid like ones, but it's really nice to be able to edit and tweak the pictures before hand on my phone.

Definitely definitely recommend this printer to people who want to get into the cuteness of the Instax printed pictures.

First let me say that if you have a small, light point and shoot camera you might get away with using this tripod. It's very light weight and if you don't intend to use it often then it might do okay and be worth a few saved bucks. A bridge camera like in the product photo is not a good idea.

I was not at all pleased with it and am in the process of returning it. It might not have been so bad at half the cost, but the $25 that I paid made this way, way overpriced. I would have given this 2 stars for the above mentioned usage, but the price paid for what you get knocked it down to 1 star. (I almost never do 1 star reviews.)

The tripod is extremely cheaply made and much flimsier than it looks in the product photos. The legs themselves seem okay, but where they connect to the head looks and feels like an obvious point of failure. There is some metal at the top joints, but it's as flimsy and cheap as the plastic.

The head is cheap plastic. The turn key to tighten the ball had a small sharp spike on one side that needs filing down or the user will cut a finger at some point. The ball head does not move smoothly, making it difficult to make the small adjustments needed to frame and compose your photo. You have to loosen the turn key quite a lot to get the best movement, but that means that you often lose your framing while tightening it up again.

Worse, the entire head assembly is wobbly, which negates part of the reason you're using a tripod.

I'm kicking myself that I tried to save a few bucks and ordered this instead of the GorillaPod, but the reviews for this one looked so promising.

I have now purchased and received the Joby GP3 GorillaPod with the ball head rated for 6 pounds as a replacement and there is no comparison in the quality of the two tripods. The GorillaPod is lightyears better. Do yourself a favor and spend the extra 20 bucks for that one instead of cutting corners with this flimsy Kea Sigma Delta.

review_headline: Beware of 8,000 ft. Altitude (Sea Level) Limitation - Will Not Start above that Altitude.
review_body:
[[VIDEOID:8909c2c16882336549d98ab22277e0f7]]** Edit: See later post.. It appears Yuneec has fixed this. **

Original Post: I honestly wish I did not have to write this review because I really like this Quad, but it seems many do not know of this limitation. Beware of 8,000 ft. Altitude (Sea Level) Limitation - Will Not Start above that Altitude. So if you want to do mountain photography, Beware.

This needs to be in the marketing material not something you discover in the user guide or reviews/forums upon receipt of the unit. To my knowledge the Q500 is the only manufacturer that has this limitation.

The Q500 checks GPS Altitude (sea level) at start up and if it reads 8000 ft. or above the motors are disabled. A warning message flashes on the ST-10 and the Quad flashes and starts to make a warning noise. I repeat, this will not fly if you try to start it above 8000 ft. - I live in the Denver foothills at 8500 ft. and I now have to return what is otherwise a fantastic Quad because of this. I was able to take it down to 7995 and it starts and flies just fine, it is only at startup that it checks this. Seems to be a firmware limitation only and not a limitation of the Quad. The GUI has no setting for this or a way to disable it. I have worked with Yuneec customer service for a couple of weeks, which is great, but they have no solution as of this writing. I sure hope this changes because it is otherwise a great Quad. I will continue to work with customer service in hope this can be corrected, and if so I will purchase again and change review to 5 stars.

This is for the Q500, but Yuneec tells me the Q500+ has the same limitation.

A big deal for those of us who enjoy mountain photography. Video included taken from takeoff at 7995 to demonstrate how great this quad behaves in a stiff wind at altitude.

I bought my Nikon Coolpix P80 about 6 years ago. After a few months I bought two of these “replacement” batteries so I could extend photo-shoots without worrying about running out of battery. After about 3 years the “replacement” batteries had difficulty recharging. One of them started to swell when in the charger, suggesting it might explode. So I replaced them with two more “replacements”. And now here I am, 3 years later, buying yet two more of these “replacements”.

Meanwhile, the original Nikon OEM battery is going strong after 6+ years. It still recharges flawlessly and I can take 150 pictures on a single charge (depending on use of flash and zoom).

Given the big price difference between these “replacements” and the Nikon OEM battery these batteries clearly are a value choice. Just don’t expect them to last a long time.

product_title: Lowepro Flipside AW DSLR Camera Backpack
review_body:
I've mistakenly received both the 400 and 500 editions so I've decided to write a comparative review and cross-post it before sending the 500 back. The reason I'm sending the 500 back and keeping the 400 is because it is huge. If you regularly carry a high-end 300/400/500 lens, this could be a good thing. For me, it was a size at which it was going to attract way more attention than I wanted walking down the street. Both of the backpacks look well-built, real solid firm material, comfortable back and strap. Both suffer from a similar defect- no space was allotted in the "safer" portion of the backpack for a computer. It would have been nice if they had made the sleeve large enough to fit something like a MacBook Air/Surface/iPad. This probably could have been done without increasing the size of the packs but just by making the internal pocket bigger. As it is, the only place to carry those items is either floating in the back or in the large outer section. In the camera section, there are many, many lens pockets- about four more than I need (I'm not carrying a dozen 50 mm f/1.4's) but it's nice to have options.

Using the 400 will be a little tight for what I need: two full-frame bodies, three of the smaller sized (5-6 inch) telephotos, a 35 and 50mm prime, a mini-flash, and two tele-converters. I think it will work, though, it will just be like working a jigsaw puzzles. Wearing it, the smaller 400 definitely feels more comfortable on the back- and that much equipment is already starting to get heavy.

Both look great to me but it just depends on your needs. My dream version would be 5-10% larger than the 400, but I think I can make the 400 work. Amazon has raised the price from $96 to $140 in the two days since I bought mine so I'm glad I got it when I did, though I must confess that $96 was less than I was expecting to pay for something like this.

review_headline: This set of bags was a good value, and should keep their contents relatively safe
review_body:
I was looking for a way to carry my lenses and camera in a standard shoulder bag or back pack, without buying a camera insert, or switching to a dedicated camera bag. This set of bags was a good value, and should keep their contents relatively safe.

The construction is good, with decent stitching, and fairly thick neoprene, they should hold up well over time.

I' have the following in my set of bags:

The smallest bag: A Fuji XF 35mm lens, with lens hood, absolutely perfect fit all around.

The next smallest: A Pentax SMC Takumar 135mm f/3.5, perfect length, but a little roomy around the sides

The medium bag: A Pentax SMC Takumar 55mm f/1.8 and a Minolta MD 50mm f/1.7, stack on top of each other. Fits pretty good, but roomy around the sides

The largest bag: A Fujifilm X-Pro1 with accessory grip, no lens, the fit is actually pretty excellent. The X-Pro1 with XF 35mm wouldn't fit, but possibly the 18mm or 27mm would.

Overall, I'm pretty happy with these bags. I would have liked to see more sizing options, like being able to order all Small or all Medium bags, but that's a minor complaint. A great value, I may order another set in the future.

review_headline: Does not even last as long as the Canon BP-820 that came with my camera
review_body: I have not a clue why this battery is so much bigger than the original Canon BP-820 battery that came with my new camera.  This bulky battery doesn't last anywhere close as long as the smaller Canon battery.  I ran this Wasabi battery down shortly after I received it, then charged it overnight in my G30 camera.  I started recording  our church services the next morning at 11:05am in 24Mbps AVCHD mode to card A & 4Mbps MP4 mode to card B.  I stopped recording at 12:41pm when the service ended.  The countdown timer on the camera said I still had 117 minutes left before the battery should be dead.  I immediately took the camera outside for the Easter egg hunt and the camera auto shut off 7 minutes and 55 seconds into the recording.  The battery didn't last anywhere close to the advertised time of 4+ hours.  Thankfully I was also recording with two other cameras so I didn't miss anything.  Update:  I just tested the second battery recording to both slot A & slot B simultaneously.  It lasted 111 minutes before it died, and it was charged using the wall charger.  Definitely not as long as expected.  I have now tested the original Canon BP-820 battery under the same conditions.  The Canon lasted 179 minutes.  Looks like the Canon battery will be my primary battery and the Wasabi batteries will be my backup batteries.

product_title: PolarPro PowerPole
review_headline: Really nice product for the most part, certainly something to have when videoing events or just gofing around.
review_body:
I was pretty excited when I got this product, it is a bit of a game changer for being able to video for longer periods of time and the go-pro style mount does have a lot of adapters out for it so that pretty much anything can be attached to the end of the pole without issue. It would have been nice if it would have included a normal 1/4 20 thread mount for a standard camera mount as it would help diversify this device.

It's a pretty straight forward "selfie" pole but turn the camera around and you can use it at events to get the "birds eye" view of the crowds and happenings. The pole itself is pretty heavy though as it does have a fairly good sized battery in it but is also made of out a rather sturdy aluminum as well which does add a decent amount of weight as it's not the normal thin walled junk. So this will not be for your weakling friends that couldn't handle holding 5lbs for 30 minutes at a time. Granted the lever action of the pole being out stretched will increase the felt weight.

It does have 2 usb ports at the top to plug in multiple devices but I don't have enough devices for that just yet. I do record at a lot of motorcycle stunt shows that go on for extended periods of time so the added battery life is really nice to have for that, I don't have to sit there and swap batteries nearly as much.

I do think they could have lightened this product up some more and still had a good quality system but the main issue that I have is that for the price of the product it really should have included 1-2 adapters for attaching a more varied amount of devices. Granted it is marketed as go-pro specific but adding diversity is important, especially with the large amount of other action cameras on the market now, especially the sony model that has image stabilization, that's a huge leap over other cameras on the market.

Other than that the pole does work well, has good extension and is well built but maybe a little over built for the common user, this is more of a rugged device likely meant to take a few spills and most will not need this much of a device but I do not reduce the rating due to that. I lower the rating due to lack of versatility out of the box and the usb port access at the mount end is rather annoying with the bands that were put up there, they really are a pain to move out of the way to plug in the camera. review_body: This was my second camera from Cannon and although they have pretty great customer service, I will be trying a different camera brand next time I purchase. It happened with my first Cannon and I sent it in and they repaired it under warranty no problem, but then it happened again outside of warranty so I waited a while and replaced it with this. Of course by now the warranty is expired so when I sent it in for an estimation the repairs were going to cost $150. I could get a brand new camera for that price so I now have a useless camera with a jammed lens sitting in my night stand. I had it for 2 1/2 years and got to use it maybe 6 months total. When I looked into Canon deeper I found that their cameras are notorious for lens jamming which is why I decided to not purchase a camera from them again.

review_headline: The Yongnuo YN 560 III is an awesome flash that has a lot of power and is easy to use!
review_body:
The Yongnuo YN 560 III is an awesome flash that has a lot of power and is easy to use. It will also work with the Yongnuo 560 TX transmitter and the transmitter will connect the YN 560 III electronically and wireless as well. With the YN 560 TX or YN 560 IV, the YN 560 III's power and zoom can be controlled from the camera. The YN 560 III flash has to be initialized by the YN 560 TX or the YN 560 IV flash to be used, but that is easy and takes a few seconds to do that.

product_title: Sony Alpha a6000 Mirrorless Digital Camera with 16-50mm Power Zoom Lens
review_headline: A6000 rocks.  I rarely use my Nikon DSLR anymore
review_body:
I've been seriously shooting since 08 (my daughter's birth). I've had a few Nikon DSLRs and a number of quality lenses. I was skeptical of mirror-less cameras until I had a chance to shoot my friends AR7. I did some research and decided on the A6000 because I think it delivers the best bang for the buck. I got mine on black Friday weekend in 2014 for about $500 (body only). I decided to get the sony 20mm 2.8 pancake lens for a compact walk-around lens, and a sigma 60mm 2.8 for portraits (my favorite lens with AF on this camera). I also bought a Nikon to E mount adapter so I can use all my nikon glass.

My large expensive DSLR body is now collecting dust. The A6000 takes great shots. I especially like using my nikon primes in manual focus mode (focus peaking with magnifier make it super easy). I'm shooting more with this camera because its smaller/lighter (easy to carry around) and I'm enjoying manual focus on older/vintage (dirt cheap) nikkor lens. Nikkor lens (with ext app control) I use on this camera: 105mm f/2.5 Ai-S, 50mm f1.8, 28mm f1.8 and 70-300mm F4.

The sensor is pretty good. I can get great shots at ISO 3200 in most situations... sometimes at 6400. The auto focus is amazing... just works. I consistently get amazing shots equal to or sometimes better than APS-C based DSLRs. I love the tilt screen, wifi connectivity to my phone and all the button configurability on this camera. I highly recommend this camera. one thing... buy a backup battery for full day operation.
