review_headline: 1 YEAR of professional use Review - The Long Term - Not for Heavy Duty Photographers
review_body:
Owned the Tamron SP 24-70 SP for EF Mount since June 2013 and by the time of this review (Dic 2014), the lens its literally falling apart.

I bought this lens instead of the Canon 24-70 2.8 mk1 `cause got better optics, and I didn't go for the Canon Mk2 because it's too expensive. But now I regret not buying the Canon Mk2 or the F4. Canon It's just better in some other key areas.

Don't get me wrong, this lens its great! But it can't handle the heavy use at Work.

Optics:
The optics are superior that the Canon Mk1, and far better than most of the Zoom out there. It's great indeed. Colors are better render in the Canon Side although. The only problem it's to get it to focus right and avoiding some AF random issues.

AF / Focus:
If there is one word that could describe this perfectly its \\"Problematic\\".

It's a shame that this beautiful glass can't shine `cause its Autofocus Issues. From the beginning my copy didn't focus correctly, some AF microajustments made in both sides of the lens (Wide and Tele) using Datacolor Spyder Lens Cal, and got it to focus right, but the lens have other issues with the AF motor outside Back/Front Focusing.

I call it \\"The Doubt\\".

It's some kind of Delay in the AF that happens time to time. The AF appears to get the things in focus, but suddenly doubts and doesn't let you take the shot. It's super annoying! And that isn't the whole story. If you get the shot, sometimes the inner elements keep moving and you end up with a blurred image. (Even at 1/200 and you standing Still taking pictures of a rock).

This kind of problems counters the excellent image quality and takes out the Professional Grade title of this lens.

Build Quality:
I own in the past Tamron SP 17-55 2.8 non VR, and the build quality was horrible. Switch to the Canon 17-55 2.8 after all the grip areas fall out of the lens. I hoped that the new looks of the Tamron SP 24-70 2.8 VR wasn't like that.

The feel of the lens its pretty impressive, and its weather sealed. Looks improved over other Tamron lenses in the past and better than the old Sigmas. Unfortunately it shares the same rubber grip and the same problems of previous Tamron lenses. All rubber in the lens falls apart over 1-2 years.

Its not meant to last forever, not even 5 years.

Recommendations:
This lens its for casual photographers, serious amateurs and travelers. Has some serious punch pack in it, great IQ, weather sealing, VR; and look cool. If you don't mind dealing with the AF Issues and missing a few shots, GO FOR IT! Its a great lens.

But if you are into the business, working in photography (weddings, journalism, or anything heavy duty), save more money and go for the Canon 24-70 F2.8 or F4 IS. Tamron SP 24-70 isn't reliable, and can't take the pressure of work over time. You will be selling it for half-price half-broken in 1 year just to go for the Canon version.

3 Stars Only.

product_title: Uniden High Definition Outdoor Wi-Fi Camera
review_headline: Great starter surveillance camera overall, great value
review_body:
Great starter surveillance camera overall. Great value at around $80 as of 01/10/15. No need to invest much time - to setup and learn how to use. No need for dvr, nvr etc., extra cabling, opening ports, changing router settings. If you want very easy to setup and use camera with basic (but enough) functionality give it a try. The video stream is VGA 640x480, so stay away if you need a crisper video. I have three appcams23s, the first one I bought 4 months ago and the last month I got two more. I tried other IP cams: Lorex, Samsung SNH-E6440BN($230), Foscam 9805W($140). I researched Axis, Swann, Dahua, Hikvision, Trivision, Sharx, Vivotek, Bosch, Dropcam, Amaryllo, Ycam, Blueiris and more.

Pros:
+ Very reliable (based on 4+ months of outdoor use on WiFi connection)
+ Well built (metal) and compact size (Foscam 9805W in comparison is huge, 5 to 6 times bigger)
+ Built-in mic and micro SD card slot (up to 32GB)
+ Easy to setup and to install outdoor
+ Can use in LAN no internet required
+ Motion activated and manual - rec options
+ Snapshots can be saved at you phone
+ Push notifications
+ Email alerts (didn't test it)
+ Companion iOS/android apps - crash and freeze sometimes, but overall work great and have very efficient and easy to use interface. Unlike the Foscam and Samsung techwin apps. BTW others' apps have crash\freeze problems too.

Cons:
- VGA resolution (biggest drawback, but it's hard to find inexpensive WiFi IP 720p or better cam with built-in mic that works well)
- Narrow viewing angle lens, should be at least 70°
- Can't backup to cloud (for example ammarylo let's you do free google drive back up. Wow!, get this dropcam)
- No web browser viewing (I never missed this, because of the low resolution anyway, iPad viewing worked great)
- Can't store video to phone
- No sound activated recording
- No continuous recording
- No motion zone selection
- Can't pull video out of micro SD card remotely. You may have to use ladder, go up, pull the microsd card and put in PC. But this can be a good thing as well.
- Recorded video viewed from the apps appear to be choppy at times and there is a sound problem at sometimes

review_headline: Lytro Illum - let it stimulate your imagination!!
review_body: My photographic training began years ago, using a hand held light meter and a 4x5 film camera on a 20 pound tripod. Exposures were made based on the expected gamma outcome in the negative, the contrast of the scene and the development manipulation that would be needed to make a straight print on # 2 print paper in the darkroom.    The film was processed knowing the shooting conditions that had existed during the exposures and the ability to manipulate the processing to get the desired result with both black and white and color processes. I was exited about having control and being able to get the results that I wanted.    Things have changed - now everything seems to be digital.    I discovered the Lytro Illum camera and it's support team. In September I received the camera that I pre-ordered. With the ability to refocus and change the depth of field after the capturing of an image, the 3D capability and the broad range of macro capability - I am excited again.    I'm adjusting my way of taking pictures to using the active histogram and \\"lytro mode\\" for setting up the image recording and just using the actual screen image to frame what I want to be included in the scene.    My expectation is that the Lytro team will continue to enhance the desktop application. Thus, enabling me to produce the interesting results that I get now and enticing me to continue exploring the range of capabilities that I can develop. The Illum challenges my imagination in new ways of producing meaningful photographic images. Tutorials on Youtube for this model don't go much beyond unboxing, which any idiot can do, without help. product_title: Panasonic Lumix DMC-TS25 16.1 MP Tough Digital Camera with 8x Intelligent Zoom
review_headline: Don't be fooled by the average review
review_body:
EDIT 5/16/15: This camera just gets worse. Stills suck. Video is horrible. All of it worse than my 3-year old Lumia phone camera. That is seriously bad. Tried shooting panoramas with it during a long trail run today up several mountains. It pretty much ruined them all. They're striped like zebras, because the camera is too stupid to fix the exposure and/or the stitching algorithm is too dumb to compensate for vignetting that sometimes comes at the end of individual frames.

I am very disappointed in this camera. I am a normally user of higher-end gear (Fuji finepix x100, Canon EOS full frame SLRs, etc.) I believe my expectations were right on this camera. I just wanted a small, pocketable camera that could handle being out in the rain on trail runs, and produce *decent* pictures. By decent, I mean better than my cell phone (Lumia 920). I did not expect something as good as, say, a Fuji x20 or anything like that.

This camera performs worse than my cell phone and worse than several much older Canon powershots.

I have tested the images from this camera against those produced by my Lumia 920 and they are inferior in every way. I can hardly believe it. Despite being made with what should be a higher-quality lens and with a much higher pixel count, detail is lacking. They're both noisier and over-smoothed. The photos are mushy, indistinct, and incredibly, the phone does a much better job auto-balancing the light source. That's a 3 year-old phone, with a smaller, less pixel-dense chip, outperforming a much newer camera. That's a camera, with a dedicated photo logic chip underperforming a phone's camera app.

Bad.

I cannot speak to its water, weather, or shock proofness, and I don't know if I'll ever be able too. When it takes photos worse than the phone, why would I ever carry it, except maybe into the pool or into the certain death of the beach? That may be all it's good for, but just expect low image quality.

product_title: Pentax K-3 DSLR Camera
review_headline: going from ME Super to SF10 to K100D to Kr to K3
review_body: I could go for a lengthy review about this camera, but at large I would be repeating a lot of things from previous reviews. But here is my take after working with this camera for about a week now, and I took about 500-600 shots with it in different scenes lights and surroundings.  I have shot Pentax cameras for the last 30+ years, going from ME Super to SF10 to K100D and my most recent was the Kr 2 years ago. I have to say that this K3 is a significant step up from the Kr in the following respect:  Going from 12 to 24 MP, the sharpness is amazing, and the JPEG photos look a lot better than with the Kr  The layout of the buttons and controls is in my eyes a lot more logical on the K3, and the buttons on the camera that control menu items are indeed the ones I use most, AF settings for instance.  The camera is quite a lot heavier than the Kr (especially with the battery grip) but it feels super solid and even rugged. For the first time I bought a sling strap, which I love, just had to get used to have this thing hanging up side down....  AF is fast and quiet, I did see some cases where it had a hard time, but overall I think the AF too is an improvement compared to older models. Also I am impressed with the way the shutter operates so quietly and smoothly, and 8 frames a second!!  I don't miss all the shooting modes from the Kr, it works great in P mode and I even catch myself not using the green Auto mode anymore. I set my 3 user mode (right now) for Continuous, 5 shot bracketing and 3 shot bracketing.  The 2 SD cards are set for JPEG on one and RAW on the other which I find convenient for quick viewing of the jpegs on my laptop when I am on the road, and when I come home I don't have to separate the files.  One reviewer was complaining about how cumbersome it was to turn off the display while shooting. But once you turn it off thru the info button, it is easy to turn on with \\"info\\" for a quick adjustment and off again with \\"menu\\"  All together the K3 is new, but I love what I see so far! The camera has a professional feel to it for sure, and may not be for the beginner. I personally am impressed with the design and the way the controls and menus are set up!  I have added some photos and I worked with the 18 - 135 mm WR lens.

review_headline: Great product and excellent customer support
review_body: Great product and excellent customer support.  I considered other devices that did more or less the same  thing and opted for the Alzo in part due to the flash bracket.  The kit is complete and allows for great versatility in conditions that do not allow the lighting controls of a studio setting.  I found reversing the camera allowed for the following:  1) I am able to naturally hold the camera by the grip thus making it easier to flip the camera  2) When shooting in manual mode I can reach the dials to make adjustments  3) When shooting vertically it's much more comfortable and natural to use my left pointer finger to press the trigger and it greatly prevents camera shake  As indicated, I had some minor issues which were speedily resolved:  1) The screw used to tighten the umbrella malfunctioned (the black rubber \\"thumb\\" knob turned), it was replaced with an all-metal screw  2) The screw to tighten the trigger also malfunctioned (would not hold it tightly), that screw was also replaced.  It goes without saying that the bracket adds weight, there is no getting around that.  I use a D700 with Nikon's MB-D10 battery grip plus the Yongnuo YN-622N TXi together with the YN-622N wireless trigger.  The lens that remains on my camera for now is Nikon's 27-70mm f/2.8 and that hunk of steel does contribute a considerable amount of weight to the setup.  It take a while to get used to the weight in my case.  Considering the other devices on the market and from the experience I've had with this flash bracket I'll buy it again without a doubt.  I highly recommend it. By the way, I forgot to mention that I got next day delivery.

product_title: iVAPO 4-12x Zoom Optical Magnification Micro Telephoto Telescope Camera Lens Tripod for 5 5s (Iphone 5/5s)
review_headline: Good image with real zoom, but tricky...
review_body: This lens has a lot going for it, but so distinct limitations.  I debated between three stars and four, but decided to rate higher because it gets right several things that are very hard to find in an affordable iPhone tele lens.    First of all, it is a true zoom lens, a variable focal lens lens.  4X-12X zoom translates (normally) into a 35mm equivalent of a 200mm-600mm zoom.  I haven't tested it to see if it actually achieves those  specs, but it's unquestionably a long zoom.    The Good:  1) No vignetting that I can see at either end of the zoom range  2) Good color saturation  3) reasonably sharp for an affordable zoom accessory lens.  Sharper than another 8X fixed length tele lens I have, for example.  4) Working focus  5) Tripod mount for the lens (which is considerably heavier than the phone, so it's the object that should be mounted to the support)    That stuff may all sound pretty basic, but it's surprisingly hard to find among any of the lower priced tele accessories, esp. those greater than 2X.    The Not So Good  a) not a very bright lens, which makes it hard to achieve good focus on the phone in low-light situations, and increases the need for tripod or other support.  It does well in daylight, although the long end of the zoom (12X) is going to be hard to hand hold steadily for most people, no matter what  b) Noticeable chromatic aberration (but what do you expect for a cheap lens)  c) soft focus in the corners, esp. when zoomed in  d) Zoom ring is not smooth,  That doesn't mater much when you're shooting stills, but you'll probably notice it if you zoom during video  e) large and heavy.  It's longer than the iPhone 5  f) A little awkward to hold when attached to phone.  The zoom and focus knobs are wide, which leaves few places to hold onto the lens for shooting, and you want to support the weight of the lens rather than just holding the phone (see \\"g\\" below)  g) Image is a little squirrelly to shoot, because of the flexibility of the case.  The casethat slips onto the phone has the screw-thread that mounts the pens to the phone.  It's thin plastic, and it's flexible enough that the image dances around and distorts while you're composing your shot.  If it's bright enough to shoot a fast shutter speed, you probably won't see it on the image, but at slow speeds, this could even cause blur.  You can limit the flexing by holding the lens rather than the phone, but every time you try to use the onscreen controls (focus-spot, exposure) or fire the shutter, the images dances and wiggles as the case flexes.    What that adds up to is a lens that will get far away shots normally unavailable to your iPhone, and shoot them with reasonably good quality (though not as good as you phone alone shoots up close), but it takes some practice, some luck, some patience, and some lugging around of a sizeable accessory.    I am worried that the special case will lose its mounting threads easily and render the system useless.  But that's just my guess.    A nice bonus is that the lens can be used as a field telescope, just held up to your eye.    So, on balance, I think the benefits outweigh the flaws.    The photo attached was taken in bright sunlight at full (12x) zoom on the iPhone 5.

product_title: WB350 Parent
review_body:
I bought this camera to give to my sister and brother in law. In trade they gave me their Nikon D40 because they feel a DSLR is too big to carry around and too much for their photography skill level. Before I gave it to them, I tried it out for a few days. I'd say for less than 150usd you get alot of camera at that price. The 483mm(35mm equiv.)is impressive and good for some light duty wildlife. But even with image stabilization, don't expect to zoom it all the way and get really sharp shots in low light such as heavy overcast. Plan on getting a small tripod. These tiny sensor cameras don't do well at high ISO's. I wouldn't go past ISO 400 or maybe 800 in a pinch. It is kinda slow to focus, but every point and shoot that I've used is like that. Don't expect lightning fast focus like you can get with an SLR. At lower ISO's it would probably make a good 8X10 or possibly 11X14, but I wouldn't go any larger than that. The built in flash won't pop up on it's own in any mode. But all you have to do is push a button when you want it and it comes up. And the flash doesn't have very good range. You could bump up the ISO very high and increase the range-but it doesn't give good image quality at high ISO's. In full auto, the camera decides everything. But you can shoot in P(program)and it will decide shutter and f stop for a properly exposed picture. And will allow you to control other things such as ISO, white balance, and more. I saw no real increase in image quality going from the 10MP setting to 16, so I left it at 10. One great thing is you can send pics to phone or email to email addresses directly. But the files straight out of the camera are too large for emailing or posting on Facebook. Maybe you can save a smaller copy of the pics to send-I don't know didn't try it. One thing I didn't like is there is no seperate battery charger. You have to charge the battery in the camera. So you can't charge one while you're shooting. If you have more than 1 battery and plan a long photo outing the next day, charge all of them in the camera the day before.

To sum this up, I'd say it's a nice little camera for the price. It has limitations, and if you understand them, you'll know you can't get the whole world for less than 150 bucks. It fits in your pocket, has a nice zoom range, and has the wifi. As long as you know it's limitations, you can get some good photos with it. No it won't compete with a DSLR, mirrorless interchangable lens cameras, or high dollar point and shoots. But it doesn't cost much and will fit in your pocket. If you want pro caliber photos, you'll have to get something that you can't pocket.g photo outing the next day, charge all of them in the camera the day before.

review_headline: Good Manual Lens if You want to LEARN
review_body: This is a good lens for the price. It does require a learning curve and definitely requires a tripod to steady the lens. No frills at all. This is a straight forward manual lens. Some adjustments need to be made to allow the f/stop dials to be positioned properly. The T-ring has three set screws that need to be loosened after mounting to the camera and this allows the lens to be rotated to the proper position. Once you have the lens where you want it you can tighten the set screws. Requires a very small standard screwdriver like you would use for eyeglasses. The minimum focus distance is not exaggerated you have to be at least 30+ft from whatever you are trying to photograph. Does not work in low light and will unlikely take any action shots even in good light. With some patience and curiosity I think this lens will be fun to work with. I also bought the Macro Extension and a Wide Angle attachment to dink around with. Other reviews state that the extension will turn this lens into a Microscope? We'll see.

product_title: Manfrotto MK394-H Large Photo-Movie Kit with Aluminum Tripod and Photo-Movie Head with Quick Release
review_body:
I love this tripod!!! It is a bit heavy, but not too heavy, which is very good for stability!

I love how simple and easy the head piece is to use, I chose this tripod specifically for its clean design because I hated having to fiddle with so many knobs on my old tripod --- it wastes a lot of time. This tripod pans beautifully and smoothly straight out the box.

Originally I was worried about the height being too short, but when I pulled it up to its full height and put my Canon 60D DSLR sans-battery pack on top it was just slightly above eye-level (not uncomfortably so). I'm 5"5 for reference. It would've been nice if it could go higher though for those moments that I need to shoot something tall. However the fact that it shrinks down to a pretty small tripod when folded is nice, can fit it into my 23" duffle bag.

I also wish there was a hook to hang a weight bag, but since the tripod is sturdy and heavy enough for indoors and calm outsides, it doesn't matter. I have yet to try it out on a windy, horrible day, so I don't know how it will fair.

product_title: Sony a7 Full-Frame Mirrorless Digital Camera with 28-70mm Lens
review_body:
The Zeiss 55 1.8 is one of the many reasons I decided to give the A7 a try. The lens is about the same size as the Canon 50 1.4 but it's far sharper and is actually usable wide open. The Zeiss 55 + A7 combo weighs the same as the Sigma 50 Art, which is considered one of the sharpest 50 prime on the market. The A7 is now my secondary camera. No, it cannot replace my 6D although I thought I could before I bought the A7. It's absolutely awesome to have two cameras so that I don't have to keep changing lenses. Besides it's very nice that I can take advantage of the Sony's slightly higher dynamic range.

The A7 complements well with my 6D. I'd use my wideangle lenses on the A7 and long lenses on my 6D. The advantage for me as a landscape shooter is that since I often shoot f8-16 with my ultrawide lens I can manual focus with A7 very easily. If I had to use long lens, it's still doable but far less efficient than my 6D. By the way, this is the adapter I have. I find it a great value. http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00J3MFI3K/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o03_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1

I love the tilt screen. It makes composing easier especially for low angle shots.

I love the electronic view finder. When I go back to my 6D, I almost miss the EVF of the A7. It's so nice I could see all information there plus I could review pictures on the viewfinder.

I love the fact that I can customize a lot of buttons.

I can potentially use any lens ever made on the A7. This is a huge deal!! I don't need to be stuck with one brand anymore.

Having mentioned all these pros, the biggest thing that bothers me is ergonomics. Because of its compact size it's hard to hold for a long period of time. When I switch back to the 6D after prolonged use of A7, I feel much more at home. I feel like I can hold the 6D all day without fatigue.

I almost always try to bring both cameras to take advantage of their respective strengths (ergonomics,AF speed, tilt screen, etc) depending on the situation. But if I must bring one camera only, the 6D would still be my first choice.

The image quality of both camera are comparable. I did consider the A7r. But I believe I don't benefit from the extra megapixels. And I doubt the usefulness of omitting the low pass filter. I decided to get the cheaper and more versatile model and use the savings to get the Zeiss 55 1.8. I'm very happy with my decision. Although if I had known Sony would come out with A7ii so soon, I would have held off my purchase for a few more months.

The best mode is center-weighted metering, almost no misfire. For spot and matrix metering, it only fires correctly 1 out of 4 frames. When I tried highlight-weighted metering (only available on D810 and D750), it was lost at all. You can see the flash is firing but not synced with shutters at all. I can even noticed it fires between two continuous shots. That is ridiculous. For a $400 flash, how can it not work for the simplest task? Although my main purpose is to use them remotely, I still need it on camera as commander unit and do some fill flash. This kind of bad performance broke the deal immediately. Return and refund!

Before I pack it for return I also tested it remotely. The optical remote sensor is right in front of SU800. Still missed a lot. Even I set it to manual mode, it has 1 off-synced shot out of 5. For remote TTL, in 7 continuous shots, it missed 4, correctly fired 2, and totally overwhelmed 1. I cannot imagine what will happen if I use it for work, it will be a nightmare.

I guess this flash may work with D4/D4s/Df better, because those famous pros supported by Phottix are using them. But obviously Phottix is not paying enough attention on D810.

product_title: Sony Alpha a6000 Mirrorless Digital Camera with 16-50mm Power Zoom Lens
review_headline: Outstanding for size & price if you're OK with Sony-compatible accessories & don't shoot long videos
review_body:
Owned this camera for 6 months now. Very powerful, rather steep learning curve for a point n shoot user, but this camera, at a price and size comparable to point n shoot cameras, is a completely different beast. I have the 16-50 lens package and a larger (and heavy) 18-200. The camera is amazingly fast and accurate with autofocus, and 11fps burst mode shooting is outstanding for action shots like my kids skiing or working the trampoline. There are excellent, detailed reviews on here that I mostly agree with. Overall, I am very happy with this purchase as a recreational user mostly shooting family and travel pics. It's much smaller & ligher than my previous Olympus DSLR, has superior color reproduction and is lightening fast except for the boot process. It takes a while to learn all the functions this camera has especially if you are not an experienced manual mode DSLR shooter, but it is well worth spending the time to learn all this camera has to offer as there are features like vertical panorama shots that I use much more than I thought I would and which have produced amazing shots. Check out the Gary Fong a6000 intro videos on utoob and his website - I found them quite helpful in learning how to use this feature-rich camera.

The only real challenge I have run into with this camera is that it is a Sony, not a Canon or Nikon. You will have to search harder for accessories that are compatible, especially flash units since the Sony units are very expensive and poorly rated because of overheating issues, etc. Popular lower cost flashes like YongNuo don't currently offer a flash with a shoe compatible with the proprietary Sony "multi interface shoe" (MIS). MIS is not standard ISO even though it looks very close - it has extra pins on the front. Certain manufacturers like Metz and Phottix are releasing good, reasonable cost Sony MIS-compatible units, but your choices will be more limited than Canon or Nikon, and they won't be in the lowest cost tier so make sure you research your options for accessories before you buy a Sony camera.

Overall, this is a fun, fast, high build quality, reasonably priced camera. Highly recommended.

UPDATE - Feb 2015 Had this camera for the better part of a year now. I have grown to like it more over time as I have learned about the many somewhat hidden features like the excellent and amazingly fast eye AF. The one complaint I have echoes many other reviewers: be careful about video. It seems that the camera has a tendency to overheat. I was shooting an indoor video of my daughter performing in a famous New York venue, a once in a lifetime opportunity. The venue was a comfortable temperature, but unfortunately, the camera overheated and shut down right in the middle of my daughter's performance while I was shooting video. I don't know if there's a firmware fix for this or if it's a battery design flaw, but the result was that I had to depend on a friend who was shooting the video with a Sony video camera from the next booth over. If I could give 2 stars, I'd give it an easy 5 for photos and a 3 for video. Keep that in mind when making your purchase.

On the upside, 3rd party manufacturers have been developing for the Sony interface. I'm happily using Phottix Mitros+ flash units which now are available with the Sony Multi-Interface Shoe (MIS) which looks like ISO but has Sony proprietary pins in front that are critical for key functions.you research your options for accessories before you buy a Sony camera. product_title: Logitech Alert 750e Outdoor Master Security Camera System with Night Vision
review_headline: I very much regret this purchase…
review_body:
I've had this system for 2 years now. It has been nothing but trouble. I have three cameras: one indoor, and two outdoor. The indoor camera has not had any problem but the outdoor cameras stop working once it gets below 45f degrees outside (I live near the 45th parallel). Even in warmer weather, the outdoor cameras will stop recording on the memory card and will need to be reset. Then they will stop working again after a few days. Logitech sent a replacement camera for one of them, but I still had the same problems. Customer support has been terrible since they don't know their own products and always assume the cameras just need to be reset.

In addition, the cameras need software updates, but the updates will not work with my firewall. I don't have a special firewall, just standard stuff that came with my ordinary router, but many other people have complained of the same problem. I have not been able to do any updates except the first one.

Resolution is terrible. It claims HD, but it is really only poor resolution expanded to a wider angle. You will not be able to identity a stranger unless the person is right up on the camera. Forget about reading license plates.

Night vision range is great, but resolution is way too bad to make out any details that police will need. The refresh rate is so slow that people and cars in movement are just blurs. Not a single useful image the police can use.

Outdoor mounting is a pain. It has this big transformer box that you must mount to your wall/post in addition to mounting the camera pedestal. The stuff in the transformer box should be in the camera.

I am so very disappointed in this system and wish I spent my money more wisely.

product_title: Sony Alpha a6000 Mirrorless Digital Camera with 16-50mm Power Zoom Lens
review_body:
Tremendous! I got mine during black friday from Sony. So this is not an Amazon verified purchase. Anyway, I'm coming from the Canon 70D, before that, the 60D and lugging a full size dslr around started to feel cumbersome. So I decided to jump into the mirrorless world, and I'm not sure if I will ever turn back. Look I'm not a professional, I think I'll be \\"entry level\\" my whole life. I don't have a keen eye for picture differences, nor am I that picky. I cannot tell the difference in quality between my 70d shots and my Sony shots, so if you're like me, and you can't tell the difference... then why lug around the bigger camera? Simple logic.

I'm either going to sell the 70D, or keep it as a dedicated product photography camera, while the Sony will be my take out camera. One feature I really like is how you don't have to choose between the viewfinder or the screen. As your eye approaches the viewfinder, it automatically senses and switches accordingly. I do wish the Sony had touch screen like the 70D, but I'm sure that's down the line. That's how they milk ya!

In terms of aesthetics, after years and years of all black Canon cameras, I wanted a change! So I went with the silver body with the black grip and I think the black and silver contrast looks awesome. I wanted a black lens, but Sony didn't allow to mix and match, but I realize it looks fine since there is a touch of black because the face of the lens is black. I also purchased and highly recommend the Sony lower body case model# LCSEBC/B. It fits nicely.

Highly recommend the A6000! Go for it!

product_title: PHYLINK Bullet Waterproof Outdoor IP network Camera
review_body:
A very good camera. All steel, weatherproof, and compact. Great price for all the features. The camera can be set up/operated with the Phycam android app or the AnyScene app as follows:. First plug the camera into your network with an ethernet cable and power up, then scan to get the camera UID code, set a password and camera name. Once the camera is recognized on the network, hit the arrow key on the right to go to the menu to Edit Camera, and then Advanced Setting to set it for Wifi operation, Network Setup, Alarm Actions, etc.
At the bottom of the Advanced Setting menu is an "About Device" tab from which you can get the local URL address (192.168.1.68:80) - this allows you to setup the camera from your PC computer Internet web browser, and from a submenu you can format a SD card to save video, set the date/time stamp, time zone, etc .

I am using the Samsung microSDXC UHS-1 64gb card and it works great on the camera.
The instructions could be more detailed (hence minus a star), but the Phylink support online is great with timely responses.

A good buy

product_title: Aeon Labs Aeotec Z-Wave Multi-Sensor
review_body:
So far, so awesome! I got this sensor to pair with a SmartThings hub. So far, three weeks in, and I'm loving it! Some reviewers are saying the sensor readings are off, but it seems pretty sensitive to me. You can always adjust your trigger temps up or down to compensate for callibration being off. The most useful features to me are the motion and luminocity sensors. Whenever my hub is set to away mode, I get a text message if the motion sensor is tripped. The sensitivity knob prevents false alarms, which is nice. I've also got it set so that when the luminocity is low, it turns on the front outside lights. Not only is this great for getting home late, but it is also a mild theft deterent.

The only problem I have is that the optional power supply is just USB... Who has random USB plugs hanging on their walls?? Plus, the cord they provide is only about three feet long and they don't provide an AC adapter. On the plus side, the four AAA batteries look like they'll last a long time and the unit has built-in battery life detection which is reported to the hub. I've had mine running for three weeks now and the bat life still says 100%. If the battery life is as long as they claim, I don't see a reason to dock a star for this.

I want a couple more now... One for outside the front door to let me know when someone is at the door, and one more for the back to cover the back door.

review_headline: Nice system, carry case had defects *UPDATED*
review_body: *UPDATED 12/1/14*  **After posting the following review, I was contacted by a rep requesting my order information. Within a week I had another bag delivered to my door. This bag arrived in good condition and was the only piece I was originally not satisfied with. While I still wonder if the bag will hold up long term, I must say that the customer service is simply outstanding. This is clearly a company that stands behind their product and is willing to do what is necessary to make sure they have a satisfied customer. I truly was not expecting further action from Ravelli but am impressed beyond words at the lengths they went to try and resolve my issue. I have updated the review to 5 stars as I believe that Ravelli will make sure you are fully satisfied with your purchase.**       Let me start by saying I really like this backdrop system. It's far superior to another brand I had purchased a few years ago at close to the same cost and they have responsive customer service.  The reason I am only giving 3 stars is because the carry case is not of the same quality as the stands. I ordered this product and received it as expected. Well packaged and on time. However the carry case had two female clips on one of the straps meant to secure the case. Not a huge deal. I emailed support, they requested order number and images which I sent. After a day or two I called since I hadn't received a response. They looked up my info and expedited a new case out to me with two day shipping. Excellent, I was very pleased with the response and quite satisfied with the service. However, when I received the new case it has a massive tear on the top where the sewing is simply coming apart at the seams (hole is about 4 inches along the seam). Now I have not contacted them again and don't know if I will. It's frustrating to request a replacement due to a manufacture defect, only to receive a new case with a different defect. I may contact them again, but my faith that this will get resolved with a quality case really has been lost. I may just find somewhere locally that can fix this so that I know it's done correctly, but wonder if the case will hold up long term. All in all, you will be happy with the stands, but be warned that the case may not hold up if yours happens to arrive in good condition.

The pictures of the perp's were very clear, so clear the police knew who they were instantly, from past encounters. One guy even had on a clear mask, sunglasses and a hoodie, and were still able to make identification. The wide angle also, is much bigger than you think. The one guy even thought he could get away with it, because he hugged the building, but because of the wide angle, we were still able to the building and the roof of the building, even though the camera was more focused on the front of the business, in the parking lot area. I have been buying these for everywhere, and would highly recommend them.

These cameras are easy to install but I am a certified electronics expert and computer/systems engineer, so you may need a little help setting it up if you are older, or are not very good at technology. Even with the conversion, or extending the power cable it is great.

review_headline: Flash takes FOREVER to charge, poor performance indoors or at low light, battery life is short.
review_body: We got this camera as a present. My previous camera was a Nikon Coolpix 8100, so the first issue at least for me is that this Canon PowerShot does not have as many automatic modes as cameras in the Nikon Coolpix series. It pretty much has: AUTO, SPORTS, PORTRAIT, FISH-EYE EFFECT (yeah, like it is important to have!), DISCREET, STANDARD, MANUAL, APERTURE PRIORITY (Av), SHUTTER SPEED PRIORITY (Tv), PROGRAM (P), LIVE and HYBRID. It seems as many but I do not know how to use Av, Tv, P, Live and Hybrid and do not have the time to learn, so I would rather have the pre-settings that Nikon has in the Coolpix series.    Also, there's the issue with the power that does not last enough on recordings and with the flash that takes FOREVER to recharge. If you are using the flash and planning to take more than ONE picture, you are in serious trouble. You won't be able to use this camera indoors in places with poor light condition or at night. Imagine being at a wedding and having to ask the bride and groom to hold still their pose for a whole minute because the flash is still charging ... then ooops! someone blinked, please hold in there for another minute because the flash is not ready to go again. Not to mention if you are trying to take a picture of your toddler at night. She/he will never hold still for a minute or 2, so the shot is lost.    I do not like this Canon PowerShot SX280, it is too slow, battery does not last and battery indicator does not perform its duty, to give you time to take out the other battery or go charge it before the current battery is completly depleted of charge. The one thing good is that battery charges to full capacity in 1.5 hours. But again, on a wedding, graduation, or daycare festival, Who has and hour to charge the battery?!! Why there wasn't any previous indication that battery was about 50-60% empty?    I suppose that you can play with aperture, shutter speed and ISO sensitivity to get good pictures in low light conditions or at night... nevertheless, who has the time to experiment with that? Wouldn't it be easier to take out the Fish-Eye Effect and replace it with a Night mode or Low Light Indoor mode?  Do people really consider Fish-Eye Effect one of the main 3 or 4 automatic modes that should be a standard?    Why is that for the $300 price tag, Canon could not include a reliable battery charge indicator or a flash that consumes less power and charges faster?    I think that I will go back to Nikon Coolpix, despite the fact that now Nikon is making ALL its cameras \\"disposables\\", they only live for 1-2 years and then... invariably they break. I suppose that I will have to include a 3 year warranty with it. Anyways, I won't get the warranty with Nikon, it would be like giving them more business for a poor quality job.    In a nutshell, I would not buy this product again and I would not recommend it to anyone.

review_headline: For a sub-$200 camera you won't find better
review_body: I bought this camera because I wanted something I could fit in my pocket, and still have (1) a good optical zoom, (2) quality optical image stabilization, and (3) ready access to the sorts of exposure controls I normally do on my DSLR (for example, underexposing an image to capture a good sunset). product_title: AmazonBasics 70-Inch Pistol Grip Tripod with Bag
review_headline: If you're tired of flimsy, lightweight tripods, this is the one for you
review_body:
Others have done very in-depth reviews on this tripod, so I'm going to keep it simple and just get to the point. After an unfortunate accident involving a cheap tripod and a broken lens, I vowed to get something better equipped to actually support the weight of a DLSR + Lens. The AmazonBasics Tripod is exactly what I was looking for. It is HEAVY. About 8lbs I'd say. And with the legs set wide, there's almost no possibility of this thing tipping. I feel very comfortable extending this to its highest height and trusting my DSLR on it.

The weight and sturdiness was the selling point for me, but the other features are what you'd expect from tripods 3-times this price. The pistol-grip, ball-joint head is the greatest thing I've ever seen. You don't have to loosen or unscrew anything to move the camera. Just pull the trigger and line up your shot. The quick-release plate is super convenient and they even give you an extra in case you want to swap between 2 different cameras. For a full explanation of features, just check out the other reviews.

So in conclusion, this is a serious tripod. If you're just taking family photos or hiking with your friends in the woods, this will probably be overkill. But if you're a serious photographer and need something that can triumph in any condition or environment, the Amazon tripod is the best thing you can get for under $100. I should also mention that the word on the street is that this is the EXACT SAME THING as the similar Ravelli tripod. So if the Ravelli is cheaper, I would just get that instead.

product_title: Sony NEX-6 16.1 MP Compact Interchangeable Lens Digital Camera with 3-Inch LED
review_headline: My goal was to find a light travel option to an excellent but heavy full frame kit maintaining good image quality ...
review_body: I purchased this camera with kit lens new as a two year old model, severely discounted, after reading a lot about mirror less options and trying two Fugifilm cameras with both kit and prime lenses. My goal was to find a light travel option to an excellent but heavy full frame kit maintaining good image quality via an APSc sensor. I see this camera as an inexpensive bridge to future generations of more mature mirror less cameras.  I liked the Fugifilm XT1, kit zoom, 14 mm and other primes but decided against them because of the rather high cost...up to $3000 with a couple of prime lenses added in ...( and because I am not wild about the EV ). Why invest so much in a kit that may not survive the test of time....even a couple of years? I do concede that the setup and controls of the X_mount cameras are more thoughtfully oriented to a serious photographer than those of the Nex 6 and that the Fuji lens selection while very expensive is quite excellent.  However I found that the inconvenient menus of the Nex 6 are irrelevant to my pattern of use. Most of what I prefer to control is very accessible without entering the complicated menus. Specifically  I use aperture control and can quickly adjust from auto to manual focus, adjust ISO, control focus location, bracketing, exposure control without delving into menus.  Although I do not enjoy the image seen through the EV and prefer to use the LCD I can live with it as an aid in bright conditions.    Feature I love about this camera:    Excellent image quality...... even with kit lens if you favor midrange apertures.  Kit lens goes wide...to 24 mm equivalent.  Incredibly light to carry hiking!  Flip up LCD and quiet shutter permit discreet photos in street settings.  Flip up LCD in general a pleasure for framing landscapes and architecture.  Can use legacy 35 mm manual focus lenses with inexpensive adaptor. The focusing aids, both magnification of the image and the bright colored highlights of in focus areas make it a snap tofocus accurately.  A 40 year old Nikkor f 1.4 becomes a superb portrait lens. An 80-200 becomes a 120-300 with a very light, compact camera body option.  Excellent image stabilization combined with auto ISO generate remarkable urban photos at night without a tripod.  Numerous small features such as viewing level, superb video.  For well under $500 this is a winner.

This little product made my summer vacation in the water a super-fun experience. I bought the GoPro for my summer vacation to take video in the ocean, but I was worried about losing the GoPro while swimming in the surf. If you buy this, you won't have to worry.

I would suggest creating a longer lanyard for this handle if you want to swim without constantly knocking this against your arm. I plan on making one out of parachord the next time we use it.

The newer model of the bobber looks like it has a place to attach the lanyard; this would have been nice to have on the model that I bought, but no big deal.

I would recommend this to anyone looking to save themselves from losing their GoPro in the water; the price is great and the product works just fine.

product_title: Sony QX30 Smartphone Attachable Lens Style Camera
review_body:
After playing with this with a couple of days, I like it. It is not perfect, but it is very good. The camera takes awesome pictures and videos - not comparable to my SLR, but pretty darn good. The 30x zoom range is impressive and a great add to a cell phone camera. I used it both on a Moto X (2nd gen) and an iPhone 6. Setup wasn't difficult with either, but using NFC on the Moto X was definitely easier.

There were 3 "cons". None of them are fatal, but buyers should be aware of them before making the purchase:
1) The delay in updating the phone screen via WiFi makes the camera pretty much useless for capturing a still of something that
is moving. This is true even after setting the 2M (lower resolution) for the viewfinder. The camera REALLY needs a lower res
viewfinder option so that the delay can be eliminate.
2) The camera does not focus well if you use the digital zoom. This isn't a problem as the optical zoom is very good and you can
get the same effect as the digital zoom by cropping the resulting picture.
3) The camera has a spring clamp to use to mount on a phone. My Moto X with it's 5.2" display and a low profile case was about
as big a phone as the camera can grip. A larger case or a larger phone likely wouldn't work.

I'm going to keep the camera. In my opinion it is a great throw in the bag camera for travel etc. It provides WAY more capability and quality than any cell phone camera that I've tried. Because of its limitations, I would not consider it to be a replacement for a dedicated camera - if you have room to carry one.

product_title: Sigma 35mm F1.4 DG HSM
review_body:
I absolutely love this lens. Shooting with it I have the confidence that my images can be 'Art' as the name implies. As others have mentioned, it is the sharpest 35mm lens on the market, even straight from f/1.4. Build quality is very solid, and it's not a lightweight lens.

I wanted to mention a few things I've noticed since using it for awhile now that don't get mentioned in every review. First, it has a very flat plane of focus. Meaning if you plan to use it for landscapes, you really need to stop way down, and find the proper hyperlocal distance to make sure everything is sharp from front to back of the image. When you do, the results are magic, corner to corner.

Second, others have sometimes said the bokeh (out of focus blur) on this lens isn't that great. 35mm (and other wide-angle lenses) aren't particularly known for great bokeh anyway, but what I've found with the Sigma is that if you have a lot of busy stuff going on in the foreground or background, the bokeh will be a little nervous. If you keep the out of focus details to a minimum, you'll get a very nice creamy blur. I can't really knock the lens for this, as it's pretty common, and can be worked around.

I haven't shot with Nikon's 35mm f/1.4, but I have with the newer 35mm f1.8G, and it too is a nice lens; very good at landscapes and lighter weight, but not quite as sharp as this Sigma. I wish it were weather-sealed but for the price I can't really complain. It's an excellent complement to the Nikon 85mm f1.8. I just wish Sigma would hurry up and make an equally sharp 24mm f/1.4!

product_title: Galaxy 2 Parent
review_headline: Lack of internal memory makes a super camera unacceptable
review_body:
The camera is excellent (5 stars), but its lack of internal memory storage makes it unacceptable to me. For someone who does not want to add Android apps, the camera may be an excellent choice. The integration with Android apps was part of the camera's appeal to me. The apps that come preinstalled take most of the internal memory, and there is room for only one or two additional apps. I could not install Facebook and Swiftkey without running out of internal memory. I wanted to add apps for additional cloud support (e.g., SugarSync) and photo editing tools, but there is not enough internal storage to allow that. None of the apps on the camera can be moved to an external SD card. With no significant apps installed, I still got an error message saying something like, \\"Available memory is low. Some camera functions may not be available.\\" That's a built-in defect that I cannot overlook.

I love this camera. It has the feature set that I want, including 21x optical zoom, 16 megapixels, 4.8\\" HD LCD touch-screen monitor, excellent pop-up flash, automatic uploading to Dropbox, slow motion, pre-set modes, manual camera control, saveable user configurations, Android apps, etc. Unfortunately, the lack of internal storage space makes it all useless to me.

To add insult to injury, after two days at Disneyland, the gallery app became slow and unresponsive, and some photos displayed incorrectly. (I have attached a sample screenshot where the bottom portion of the photo is misaligned.) I did a factory reset and started over, and it did not solve anything. I would like to install a different photo gallery app (e.g., QuickPic), but there is not enough internal storage space.

In short, after taking about 310 photos, the camera has become unacceptable, despite all of it's wonderful features. I am returning it to Amazon. If a Samsung Galaxy Camera 3 (or even a new model of Camera 2) comes out with 32GB of internal storage space, I will be seriously interested.

review_body:
I am what the industry calls a \\"Prosumer\\" - a consumer who likes a bit of the professional features in my cameras. I don't work professionally, but have enjoyed photography ever since taking a class in 7th grade with my fully manual film Minolta SLR camera. I shoot mostly family, landscapes and auto racing.

First the camera: I upgraded from a very early Canon Rebel XT that lacked many functions (like shooting in RAW, video, etc) and just didn't take very good pictures. This camera, on the other hand, has taken some amazing shots, and the clarity and ability to crop and zoom are simply amazing. The functionality is easy to work with (menus and adjustments are easy to use), and the ability to shoot in RAW + JPEG is something new to me and very much appreciated. With the onboard WiFi and my iPhone app, I can quickly send out the JPEGs while using the RAW images later to touch up in Lightroom or Photoshop. The camera is a good weight (not too flimsy, not too heavy) and the lenses are very good for this price point. In fact, the reason I got this package was specifically to get the 18-140mm lens. BE AWARE that many of the sets sold for this camera only come with the smaller 18-55mm lens. The 18-140mm is a large diameter lens, lets in a great amount of light for low shots, and has the ability to go from wide angle to a good zoom focal length in no time. It really made the package for me. That they also throw in the 55-300mm lens is icing on the cake as my last 300mm lens on the Canon only went down to 70mm and wasn't very good overall. This zoom lens, while slightly narrower than the 18-140mm, is still a good outdoor lens that gives you a wide range of options. I find that for almost every application though, the standard lens is the one to go with. Just be aware that if you stack an IR filter and polarizing filter, you will see a vignetting at 18mm as the wide lens is actually capturing the black ring around the second filter. The articulating screen is another big plus for me as I loved this feature on my first-gen Canon Powershot G1. You will also love the many effects and modes available (color select and miniaturization are my two favorites).

The only downside on the camera so far is that the video mode (which you get to by triggering the live view switch) autofocus is not very good at all. It takes too long and doesn't adjust automatically when you zoom or your subject moves. Pressing the shutter half down will eventually get the video to focus, but it take way too long and doesn't look good at all. I was very pleasantly surprised that the camera found her face and adjusted the exposure properly so you could see the details of her face, even though it was in shadow. product_title: Ravelli APGL4 New Professional 70" Tripod with Adjustable Pistol Grip Head and Heavy Duty Carry Bag
review_headline: Great tripod, but not for everyone.
review_body:
I may have to revise this review in the future, but after putting this thing through its paces for an hour I can say that it so far is exactly what I wanted. I needed a heavy-duty tripod capable of holding a Canon DSLR with a battery grip and a prime lens for extended periods and in external conditions. This is precisely that.

Having said that, here are some of my potential concerns:
- I'm not sold on the long-term viability of the pistol grip ball head. As far as I can tell, I have no control of the level of tension, which means it is spring loaded. Which will eventually fail as that is the nature of springs.
- The retainer screw for the head plate has to be unscrewed too far to allow the plate to be removed. It is perilously close to falling out and getting lost.
- The tension for the vertical pole is a screw rather than a retainer ring. This means that if you crank it down too tight, you risk bending the pole and thus preventing it from moving up and down.

Here is why I like this tripod:
- It's heavy. I see a lot of reviewers of this and other tripods complaining about tripod weight, but I have to disagree. Certainly if you are using a small point n shoot at the family gathering, you probably want a light 'pod with a small footprint. This beast is definitely not for you. I needed something that can handle a significant DSLR and prime lens load without the head snapping off or the 'pod tipping from a light breeze. Seriously, with the range of motion of the legs coupled with the weight, I don't think I'm even going to need to sandbag this thing on location.
- Its footprint is as large or small as you need it to be. This is crucial in awkward or severely uneven spaces, but is also great for retaining stability in unfriendly environments. I'm not going into the arctic tundra or anything, but there are severe winds in my area that made my previous tripod nearly useless outside. This beast has no issues.
- The pistolgrip on the ball head makes in crazy easy to get the camera level. on the other hand, it becomes a bit more difficult to ensure that the tripod itself is level, so you need to pay attention.

In all, this is a great tripod for rugged use and I am very glad I bought it. You have to be methodical in its use, but that's sort of a behavioral pre-requisite for anyone making a living in photography. If you want something to hold a point n shoot camera or only need to use a consumer DSLR with the kit lens indoors, you can find cheaper, lighter tripods to suit your needs.

product_title: Canon EOS M 18.0 MP Compact Systems Camera with 3.0-Inch LCD
review_headline: The best mirrorless camera I've owned
review_body:
The best mirrorless camera I've owned, It's fast and clear. Those shots that I used to miss due to slow shutter are now gone. I keep it on continuous mode. With it on, I'm able to get good shots of kids, dogs, and group activities. The lens that came with this camera is also very good for stock lens. The size is also very portable compared to traditional DSLRs, which was the major reason why I bought it. Don't let that fool you though, because (some may disagree with me) but it can do many of the things DSLR can do, and thanks for this camera, it has delayed my purchase of a DSLR. For me, it's almost a near DSLR replacement. :)

Yea, I may get a DSLR in the future, but greatly delayed due to this one.

Battery life is good on the camera, I can get a good days usual usage out of it. I remember going on a family trip in Branson, taking this with me from 9am - 9pm. We visited attractions and went to shows. I took the camera out often to get shots of actors, objects, family and friend interactions.. etc. I'm constantly turning the camera on and off in the middle. I still have a bit of juice left on it at the end of the day. :)
Of course, I have one or two extra, fully charged, batteries with me at all times but rarely have to use them unless I forgot to charge the current one the night before.

Note: I'm not a professional photographer, merely a photography enthusiast. A big hobby of mine.

product_title: Polaroid Bicycle Mount for the Polaroid CUBE, CUBE+ HD Action Lifestyle Camera
review_headline: A good mount for riding on streets but not for BMX or off road riding!
review_body:
[[VIDEOID:191d412f32638917071f1ec9fb43e1d5]]This is a bicycle handlebar mount for the Polaroid cube camera. I installed it on my wife's bike and it fit nicely and it was tight on the handlebars. It literally installed in a second and the mount did not move around when installed properly. You can twist the camera 360 degrees and also rotate it on the handlebars to set the right recording angle that you want to use. I show that in my video.

The part that mounts onto the 1 inch diameter handle bars has a couple of pads that can fit inside the top of it (Use only one at a time and put the other in a place that you will find it for future use). The pad helps the mount stay more securely on your handlebars and not rotate around the handlebar. Make sure that your handlebars are 1 inch in diameter because if it is larger then the mount will not fit. If they are smaller in diameter it will be too loose.

In our testing the mount performed well but there were a couple of issues that I didn't care for and I deducted a star for them. One is that the camera seems a bit easy to remove from the top mounting platform. It didn't fall off during our riding and bumps but we were on a smooth street. If this is going onto an off road bike or a BMX bike for racing I would feel that it would be knocked off easily. For smooth streets and casual riding it is fine. The mounting platform is also supposed to be removable by pressing two side buttons but I tell you it is a real pain to get it to work. I just wound up pulling back the rear mounting tab to remove the camera. I show this is my video.

Overall I like it but it could be more solid for those that want to use it for racing events or off road riding. After all it is an action camera. I rated it at 4 stars for use on streets and 3 stars or less for any rougher event.

I was supplied a sample for test and evaluation and I didn't promise a review but I did promise that if I gave one it would be fair and honest.

review_headline: A very decent EP.  I think it could be a bit better, but for the price, it's a solid deal to get into Televue.
review_body: Clarity is excellent, as I expected from the Televue name.  This will give you the max theoretical FOV for a 1.25" barrel (which makes me yearn for a 2" barrel focuser...which will require a new telescope...not this year! :D).  My understanding is that these were designed by Nagler, who is the eyepiece guru engineer.  My only complaints are with what everyone else says - you have to be in just the right position, and looking straight-on, or the image disappears.  The top lens is deceptively wide (more due to lens mechanics than any real deceit).  You still have to focus straight down the center.  Part of my problem is being used to cheap eyepieces.  I have found you need to move back from the lens for a better view.  Most eyeglass wearers should be ok with this EP.  The view is much clearer than ANY of my cheaper brands.  No regrets.  It also works well with my 3x Barlow.  One thing I didn't like was that the eyecup came all the way off on my first use when I went to unroll it, and I had to fumble around in the dark to get it back on.  Probably better that it isn't glued, in case it wears out, but it came off too easily (maybe not assembled perfectly).

product_title: Swann SWDVK-US TruBlue D1 3000 600TVL Camera  (Black)
review_headline: Great system. Caught the pumpkin smasher.
review_body:
I have had this running now for two years and it has not disappointed me. I knew that I was not buying a high end system, but even so, this exceeded my expectations. Connection and setup is quite easy (disclosure: I am an engineer) and the cameras switch from night vision (black and white) to day vision (color) quite easily. One of the cameras has stopped doing night vision. The internet access was easy to set up, which I mostly use to view the images from various computers and tablets (All Windows 7 and 8 computers and tablets) within the house, but remote works just as well.

Running the wires, of course, is the most difficult part of installation. Prior to this I had tried a do-it-yourself with wireless IP cameras, but it was difficult to maintain. I must say the all-in-one approach was the best way to go for me, especially at this price.

Side story: Two Halloweens ago, my pumpkin was taken and smashed. I went to my playback on this system to catch the little villains in the act, only to find that a deer had started eating the pumpkin and it had rolled out the street. :)

For Swann: For the next generation: higher resolution, but keep my cameras compatible so I can switch out the ones I need changed, better motion detection, and more PTZ support.

All-in-all, a great purchase.

product_title: DJI Phantom 2 Vision+ Quadcopter Parent
review_body:
This thing is amazing!!! First off, let me give you some background so you know where I'm coming from. I've been apart of the RC world for many years and started flying rc helicopters by learning on a 600 size (54" Rotor span) single rotor hell. Rc helicopters are extremely hard to fly by nature. I even put a go pro on that hell to get some shots from up above. When drones first came out I was immediately interested. When they first came out they were very complicated. I bought a german Mikro Kopter. It cost me about $4000 and that was without a camera or controller. I spent hours upon hours soldiering and building that copter. After is was built I continued to spend a ton of time calibrating and fine tuning the machine. I never crashed, but I always had to put time into and never seamed quite perfect. I lost interest.

I bought this with the hopes that I could just plug and play and have fun and get great images. I had big doubts. It looks like a toy, the controller looks like junk and it only costs $1150 (when I bought on sale). I have had great experiences with DJI products on my other heli's... I took the plunge. After all the experiences I had with all my heli's. All the time of building and setting up. The learning curve of flying. I am very impressed that at this price point you get a quad that handles very well, has great GPS lock, gets great images, has pretty good range, has video downlink, and even though the controller looks like junk,,, it does the job and comes in the box. This thing has everything. Is it the best images, the best flying quality, the best video downlink... absolutely not, but for the price it can't be beat.

The one thing about almost everyone who flies this machine... they completely rely on the gps/navigation system. Make sure you calibrate the compass on every flight. It is easily forgotten. It will fly without the calibration, but it is probably the biggest reason for complaints for it flying away.

Even though DJI came out with the awesome hell and made if available for the every person and not just the rc junkies... It is still a complicated rc machine and not a toy. I highly recommend this bird and you will not be disappointed. My perspective might be slightly different because I know how far multi-rotor heli's have come.

Buy it! Buy it! Buy it!!!

product_title: Holga Shutter Release Set with Cable Release and Mount
review_headline: Works, but cable is cheaply made. Replaced with with a better one.
review_body:
This cable release does what it is supposed to- it depresses the shutter button and holds it there until you release it. Unfortunately it has some flaws.

The disc lock (the little wheel that makes it "stick open") likes to engage whether I want it to or not. It's supposed to release when I let go the button and the lock should only work when I turn it. Instead I press the button and the lock engages, forcing me to flick it to close the shutter. It didn't use to do this but the more I used it the more the lock stuck.

The end of the button that your press to open the shutter likes to unscrew itself while you're trying to make the disc lock stop locking.

The cable eventually failed completely and as a result it wasn't depressing enough to completely open the shutter, which caused me to waste a full roll of film that I had spent hours double exposing. I was not amused.

Fortunately I have a solution- the cable is just a standard mechanical cable release that you would use on any old school film camera. Just unscrew the cable from the plastic mount that goes round your lens, throw it in the garbage where it belongs, and buy a good cable release to put on the mount. I recommend a Gepe cloth covered cable with a t-lock.

product_title: JOBY Wrist Strap for DSLR and Mirrorless Professional Cameras.
review_headline: A Great Option for Active DSLR Users!
review_body:
The Joby DSLR Wrist Strap is a great addition to my working camera kit.

I like to hand-hold my cameras during long, all-day shoots, so I bought one of these to check out. One of the things that drew me to the Joby is its clean and simple design. I appreciate the understated look and lack of a glaring brand name. I was considering the Canon WS-20 strap at first, based on all the positive reviews, but I just couldn't get over the huge "CANON" logo dominating its appearance.

The Joby is well made and supports the weight of my DSLR and pro-level zoom lenses well, although the thinner webbing, which measures approximately 10mm (3/8") wide, can become uncomfortable if the camera is left hanging on your wrist for extended periods.

Of course, the strap is primarily used as a back-up measure in case the camera slips or gets bumped out of my hand, so the thinner strap is a plus in other ways, as it reduces bulk and packs into my camera cases and bags easily.

The sliding loop opens and shuts with ease, allowing all but the biggest-fisted photographers to don the strap quickly and cinch it down comfortably.

I'm a taller guy with medium to medium-large sized hands and I find the overall length of this strap is just right, being not so long as to allow the camera to dangle uncontrollably and not so short that I can't get my hand through the loop easily.

While I have seen the prices fluctuate on Amazon, sometimes making it a better deal than others, I tend to feel this strap is slightly overpriced for what it is. However, I'm happy with my purchase and have ordered multiples for my other camera bodies.

Considering the limited number of good quality straps available at this price point, the Joby represents a very good value for most users. Moreso if you can catch it on the low end of the price range through Amazon ($10 shipped in my case for the Charcoal version!).

Highly recommended.

review_headline: Great Camera ~ Aweful Service from Sony!
review_body:
I actually love the camera and as a long time Sony purchaser have never had issues with them until now.

The issue is with the service department. You see, I have an issue the included lens and hood. After about six months of use the lens hood would no longer stay locked on to the lens. I though, I'll just get a replacement lens hood. So I headed off to the Orlando, FL Sony store. They did not have any replacement hoods in stock so they grabbed one of a demo camera. It had the same issue and barely locked on. They then proceeded to try my hood on there camera and it locked on just fine. After careful inspection they decided the issue was with the lens. They stated there was nothing they could do and gave me a "special" alpha series service number.

I called and was told "no problem", they issued a work order number and told me I would be contacted within three days to set-up a loaner lens. I never received that call and finally called back after one week. Yet again I was told I would be called within three days. Guess what, I never received that call either. After six weeks of multiple calls with no return calls I finally receive "the call". I am told the loaner lens will be shipped out ASAP and that it will be the same lens I am shipping in. To my surprise I receive the lens actually arrive in two days. Guess what? It was a much slower and much less expensive lens that I was sending in. I called and was told to send it back and they would resolve the issue. Well, it now been almost two months since this started and I'm still waiting at this point with no end in sight.

I still love Sony products in general but their service department get a big zero. Great products are no good with non existent service so beware if you are considering purchasing this camera or any other Sony product.

Thanks, a long time and currently very disappointed Sony customer.

product_title: EMPTY
review_headline: Good fit and function and affordable
review_body: Fits my Nikon D7100 quite well and functions perfectly with the camera.    I've read a couple of complaints regarding the number of batteries it can hold and the latch not being secure enough. First off, the Nikon battery grip only holds one battery so what's the beef with this one? I have similar grips for a couple of my Canon DSLRs and they do hold 2 batteries. However, the Canon camera is elongated as compared to the Nikon and their batteries are smaller. Therefore, there's enough room to put 2 batteries in the grip.    As to the latch, on mine you would have to hit it against a brick wall to make the locking mechanism unlatch, and that's a maybe.    The thing that sold me on this kit was the inclusion of two batteries and a charger. The Nikon EN-EL-15 cost about $50 each and has 1900mAH of power. The batteries in this kit are rated at 2500mHA power. If they last half as long as long as the Nikon ones they are a bargain. Throw in a battery charger that includes a car adapter and a European style plug adapter and its hard to beat. The grip kit also includes a second battery carrier that holds 6 AA batteries which I have found useful in the field when the Lithium batteries have been used up.    The battery charger in kit works fine with the factory and kit batteries and vice-verse with the Nikon charger. The kit charger is a little more compact and fits much nicer in the Nikon camera bag that came with the camera (I bought the camera as a kit that included a bag, remote control and two telephoto lenses).    The manual for the grip depicts all of the control buttons but does not explain how to use them or exactly what they do. In most instances though, the naming convention of the controls are self explanatory. There are two thumb wheels; one in the back labeled \\"Main Command Dial\\", and one in the front labeled \\"Sub-command Dial\\".  Not sure what exactly what they do. I have tried using them with menu functions, etc., but nothing seems to happen except with the \\"MainCommand Dial\\". It will interact with some of the menu functions but not all of them. The \\"Sub-command Dial\\" doesn't do anything that I can tell. I will have to research this some more.  A shutter release button is located in the center of a grip function lock switch (locks out the function controls on the grip). There's an AE/AF selection button and a 4-way toggle button with an \\"OK\\" function when pressed. This 4-way works really well, in fact it seems to be significantly faster than the buttons on the camera which perform the same functions. There are two locking wheels, one the front and one on the back of the grip that are used to screw down the grip to the camera. It is identical to the setup on the Nikon MB-D15 battery grip. You can use either one as they both turn in tandem. In fact, after very carefully examining the Nikon MB-D15 battery grip it is difficult to tell the difference between the them. Even the \\"soft rubber\\" grip material looks identical to the Nikon brand.I'm not too sure that they are not the same except one is branded Nikon and the kit is from Vivitar. All the buttons, switches, etc., seem to be virtually identical to the Nikon branded one.    The cleaning tools are mehh... Not much use for me, but for someone that needs them they are a bonus.    All-in-all, this is a very affordable alternative to the Nikon branded battery grip. The build quality and materials are on par with the Nikon brand grip. Functionally the controls on the grip (at least the ones that can figure out what to use them for) work correctly.    Update:  12/29/14    I have used the Vivtar grip and batteries for just a little past 2 months now and so far no complaints. The batteries and grip work quiet well. I'm using two SD cards one for JPEG and the other for RAW pictures simultaneously. It does not seem to use up the battery life on the kit battery as much the factory ones. But then again, the kit batteries have more power than the OEM battery that came with the camera. Istill haven't got around to researching the various buttons on the grip. But to be honest, once I got the camera set up I have not used the ones on the camera (other than switching back and forth between the viewfinder and the LCD display and the on/off switch). So far I would stick with my 5 star rating.

product_title: Think Tank Photo Camera Support Strap Set V2.0
review_body: I am a pro-amateur photographer that does landscapes and portraits.  I use this on my back-country backpack trips works great and keeps the camera accessible and balanced while carrying stuff all day.  After a few backpacking trips carrying my DSLR in a camera bag I started realizing that I was missing a lot of shots because it was too much of a pain to get the camera out, take the shot, then put everything away.  I needed a safe, secure way to carry a camera so it is ready to shoot in a few seconds.  It is only because I had this setup that I felt ok to leave my camera out during a lot of the hikes, and as a result I have been taking a lot more pictures and getting a lot more great shots! This turned taking photos on a hike into a quick and fun process, rather than a cumbersome time eating task. For my backpacking trips I usually carry a 30-50 lbs pack.  I have learned that neck straps cause all kind of issues with long term use for my DSLR systems.  This system integrated on my backpack moves all of the stress to the backpack straps – and even helps to balance my load by shifting weight to the front.  No more neck pain, and fast access.  The camera is pretty fast to release from the straps to give a full range of motion. Depending on how you setup the straps, leaving it attached does limit the range of motion, but is sufficient to get quick grab shots. Make sure to have a screen protector on the camera, the metal clips would often hit the back screen of my DSLR.  It never scratched mine, but hearing metal impact the camera on occasion was a little nerve racking at times.
