review_body:
I'm happy with my choice, having used the camera on a week-long kayak trip. Good photos (not the greatest, but for the money and water tolerance I'm pleased), small size, extensive choice list on touch screen are all big pluses. Other reviewers who note that the screen is difficult to see outdoors are right -- but I managed to get most shots I wanted (point and shoot, right?). I messed up a few shots with my finger covering part of the lens, but I quickly learned.

The buttons on top of the camera aren't very intuitive, so when you give the camera to a stranger to take your picture, s/he may need a moment of instruction -- and won't always be able to see that tricky screen to get a good shot.

There is a "smile shutter" feature that really works -- fun to use and it can be handy in many situations. I haven't tried many of the other features yet, but as I learn each one, I'm more pleased.

I dropped the camera a couple of times and it continues to work just fine. The orange color is great -- much easier to find in a bag, car, whatever.

The kit of extras is great; everything is of reasonable quality. I really appreciated the floating wrist strap; although I didn't wear it on my wrist, it was very helpful -- usually I tucked the floating part in a pocket of my PFD and could quickly reach the camera (in another pocket). I didn't do a good job of applying the clear protective coating to the scratch-prone screen, and it didn't stay adhered as well as I'd like, but I'll try again. The coating did get scratched once but not the camera screen.

I do wish the camera had a stronger zoom for travel. Considering everything, however, I'm pleased with the purchase.

product_title: Smatree SmaCase G160 - Medium Case for Gopro Hero 4/3+/3/2/1 and Accessories (8.6" x6.7" x2.7") - Black & Red
review_headline: Quality case for your GoPro and all those bits and pieces you need to make awesome videos.
review_body: This is a well designed case for carrying one GoPro and most smaller accessories. If you have a larger case that holds everything you own, adding this case to your collection is a must do.  You can use it as a smaller day case where you take just what you need (although more than you think).    When I pulled it out of the box, my impression was that this was a pretty small case and I was skeptical that it could contain everything my current case holds (a GoPole Case, which is great case BTW).  My previous experience with Smatree had been with their excellent Battery and charger set which impressed me very much, so I put my first impression aside and set to work packing the case.    I managed to get the following into this case:  -GoPro  -Floaty Back  -Extra Back  -GoPro Frame  -2 Smatree Batteries  -Smatree Battery Charger  -Smatree Car Adaptor  -2 USB Cables  -Spare Memory Cards  -Various Mounts (approx 20 pieces)    The only things from my GoPole case that I could NOT fit into this case were my Joby Tripod and my GoPole Bobber mount.  These are bigger than the case themselves so I knew they wouldn't fit.    One of the major PROS of this case is the foam padding inside the case.  It provides a secure hold for all of my items especially if your day is going to be particularly active.  The top flap of the case looks like it won't hold much, but Smatree's clever designers find extra space where you expect none. There is a surprising amount of hidden depth in the top flap of the case, and since it is recessed, whatever you manage to get in there will not interfere with the items snuggled in the foam.    Overall the quality of the case is very high and I would definitely recommend adding it to your collection. One last note, as much as I love a brand, Smatree doesn't overdo it by slapping their logo all over the case.  I appreciate that my case is not just an ad for their company and they let their quality speak for themselves.

review_body:
These are awesome lens pouches (especially for the price!). I needed a case for my Nikkor 70-300mm telephoto lens (the largest bag in the group) and it fits perfectly with a bit of room to spare. I decided to get the pack of three, because it was basically the same price as buying a similar single bag. My 18-55mm lens fits well in the medium bag, but may be able to squeeze into the smaller one if needed.

Well-constructed. The seams are all nice and tight and made of good material. There is a handle area (nylon) with a clip on the top. The draw-string is a very nice addition, though the bag does not close all the way due to the basic structure (would have to be a softer/more flexible material I think). The draw-string clip seems durable. The material is strong and soft, but definitely not for rough handling - for example, it wouldn't protect it if you dropped it from a height. I am using them in my normal camera bag to keep the lens protected from general jostling around and bumps.

Someone else mentioned that this would not fit their lens hood - I have mine mounted (backward for storage) on my 70-300mm lens and it still fits in the bag with room to spare. Perhaps they have a thicker hood that takes up more room, not sure.

product_title: Vktech Black Camera 323 Quick Release Plate
review_headline: Looking for a High Quality, General Purpose Plate?  I Found it Here!
review_body:
[[VIDEOID:mo2195PXL9USVU]]There are a LOT of quick release plates on the Amazon market. I simply wanted an extra plate for a new table clamp mount, which is actually for the GoPro series but has a 1/4\\" screw adaptor on it for my Samsung F90 camcorder. So my needs was something that would be generic enough not to cause me any mounting issues.

My initial reasons for choosing this Vktech was a) lots of great reviews, especially in comparison to a couple of \\"look-alike\\" plates at the same price point, b) this is actually one of the less expensive ones relative to the market as a whole, and c) it looked generic enough in design to work for my particular application. And man, even I wasn't quite prepared for the quality I ended up with!

To highlight points from my video review:

* Fits 1/4\\" screw adaptors with it's open bottom design, nice and flat - and although it feels \\"heavy\\", it's only 5 ounces with both plate and mount together.

* Solid metal construction with two extra locking mechanisms. I am not that keen on the one that keeps the release lever locked IN, but the button system that keeps the lever in an OUT position for truly quick re-attachment blows all my tripod integrated release plates out of the water.

* Plate is physically designed to mount in a single orientation. I mention this as my favorite tripod allows me to put the plate in any which way I want.

* I didn't think of it at the time, nor is it actually a practical issue now, but I could wish for an integrated bubble leveler. Something I will have to keep a look out for in the future.

* I looked at the less-than-happy reviews, and all I can say... man, they must have gotten a bum product. The plate on mine is rock-steady inside the mount, both lay perfectly flat, and at least for my purposes with a simple screw adaptor, sits on it without any wibble-wobble.

The biggest selling point to me is the button that keeps the lever in the out position. I can't tell you how many times I have spent fumbling around in low lighting, trying a plate into the mount while pushing the lever open since they rest in a semi-closed state. Aside for vaguely yearning for a bubble leveler, I'd recommend this mount for general purposes without reservation.ps the lever in the out position. product_title: KIWIFOTOS LMA-M42_FX M42 Thread Lens to FUJIFILM FUJIX-PRO1 FX Adapter Ring
review_headline: Fuji X-E2 success with one gripe!
review_body:
This is one of the better-made adapters for MF lenses that I've encountered. Fit and finish are superior, and I much prefer the black-finished thread mount to the shiny chromed ones out there. Just a personal thing.

I had zero problems mounting my SMC Takumar 50mm/1.4 onto this adapter, and then this adapter onto my Fuji X-E2.

The only problem I encountered was in attempting to loosen the set-screws (hex-head) to rotate the lens on the adapter for proper alignment. The included hex-wrench was the wrong size! The 3 hex-head set screws require a 1.5mm hex-wrench, and the included wrench was 1mm. Spin, spin, spin.

Almost all of these cheap-ish adapters have set-screws that are undersized (usually a 1mm flat-head) and made of soft metal, and it's insane to have an adapter fail because of a stripped set-screw, but it's a frequent occurrence. I bought this adapter because I saw it used a hex-wrench, and I guess I should rejoice that it takes 1.5mm hex-heads rather than 1mm, as that will ensure a longer life.

But, good grief -- can't the manufacturer at least include the right sized wrench?

This is nearly a 5 star adapter -- subtract 1 star for failure to include the correct tool.

review_headline: Adjusting to the tx30 after loving the tx5
review_body: I bought the tx30 to replace my tx5 which I loved. I am annoyed that the reviews of the tx30 did not warn that the video files in the tx30 are in a different format and stored in a different place.  This caused me several days of struggle, but I have pretty much solved the difficulties.  The tx30 files are format .mst . When the tx30 is connected to your computer with the supplied usb cable the video files appear in the folder path  Private\AVCHD\BDMV\STREAM and appear as .MTS  files.  In the tx5 the videos appear in MP_ROOT\100ANVO1  as .mp4  files In both cameras the still photos appear in folder DCIM\100MSDCF  as .JPG files.    Added Note:  have found out that the tx30 can shoot in mp4 mode. Just press the Menu button of this camera, go to Settings, go to Shooting Settings and select Movie format. Then select MP4 making it the video file type. The .mp4 files will appear in MP_ROOT\100ANVO1 when camera is connected by usb cable to your computer.    Once I had found the video files and copied them to my computer, I still faced the problem that none of my existing software like Quicktime and Windows Media Player would play the AVCHD .mts videos.  Sony recommends installing \\"Play Memories Home\\" but after downloading I found it would not install on Windows XP computers.  I installed it on my husband's Windows 7 laptop, but it ran very slowly and crashed his computer.  So I would not recommend it unless you have a pretty new computer with 2 G RAM or more.    The good news is that I discovered that my Cyberlink Power Director 9.0.0.2930 could recognize, play, and operate on these .MST video files.  The currently available Cyberlink Power Director 12 Ultra can surely do this, too. This was good for me because I already know the Power Director program.  Even though \\"Play Memories Home\\" is free, I didn't find it very easy to use.  I deleted it from my husband's laptop because it seemed to be slowing it down and causing crashes.    I still give the camera 5 stars because itdoes so many things well, it's small and light and feels great in your hand, it goes underwater, it takes continuous sweep panoramas, all the things I loved about my tx5.  I didn't need the extra pixels (the ts5 is 10 megapixels), but you can set the tx30 lower if you don't want such big files.  I didn't want higher definition video, but again you can select the lowest and reduce even more when you convert the file format.  My problem is that the tx30 is ahead of the ability of my computers. My computers can't play really HD video very well.    A word about my tx5.  I've had it for 4 years, taken it on many trips.  It's been great.  The screen is unscratched.  It's gone snorkeling with me and performed well underwater.  Nice pictures of various fish and coral.  Nice panoramas and video.  What happened was I dropped it (short, about 3 ft).  Everything still worked except the zoom button.  I have sent it back to Sony.  It is out of warranty, but on the phone they said they could fix this kind of problem and predicted the cost would be the standard repair cost of $111.  Probably silly to both repair the tx5 and buy the tx30, but it's a backup.  I originally paid $299 for the tx5 and now the price for a new tx5 is $390.  I paid $195 for the tx30 and it's now $189.82 on Amazon Prime.

review_headline: Another great product from SmallRig that makes it easy to attach shoe-mount accessories to my camera rigs

Great, solid products from SmallRig. I work as a freelancer at the network TV level, but have to keep my gear purchases on a reasonable budget. I've purchased SmallRig products before because of the price and features, and I've always been very happy with the build quality.

I really appreciate how the SmallRig rail clamp allows me to tighten a shoe clamp in place around the shoe-mount accessories I'm mounting. There's even a tiny spring inside the shoe clamp that forces it to expand and release the shoe-mount accessory when you loosen the shoe clamp. Great attention to detail on the part of SmallRig.

I also really appreciate the ratcheting handle on the rod clamp bolt. I've purchased 15mm rod attachments from other manufacturers that don't utilize this simple feature. That can be a huge pain if you have to tighten a rod clamp in a narrow space and need to ratchet the handle back and forth.

I have other SmallRig products, and I will definitely buy from SmallRig again.

My only issue was a separate alarm siren that I purchase to work with the system. According to the instructions, this unit operated from a small wall outlet type power supply. The system also checks all remote battery devices and alerts when a battery needs replacement. I highly recommend this product.

product_title: Simplicity DS-1 Bi-Directional QR Camera Body Plate Arca-Swiss Compatible with Stainless Steel D-Ring SS
review_headline: Nice QR plate for small DSLRs & mirrorless
review_body:
The Desmond DS-1 is a small Arca-compatible plate, measuring 37.5mm in width and length (i.e., a square). It's ideal for large point and shoot, mirrorless (ILC) and compact DSLRs. The bi-directional design allows the camera to be mounted in the clamp side-saddle or front to back, handy when using monopods unable to rotate clamp orientation. It appears very well made: smooth machine work, extra milling for enhanced lightness and black anodized finish. It fits securely in my Hejnar, Sunwayfoto, Desmond and RRS screw clamps.

I bought the DS-1 for a Canon Rebel SL1, supposedly the world's smallest DSLR. Most plates are too big and cover the battery door or extend past the lens mount. The DS-1 sits flush with the front and back edges of the bottom and doesn't cover the battery door (see customer images). The plate is secured to the camera bottom with a stainless steel 1/4\\" D-ring screw. Plate position may be adjusted by sliding the screw in a slot. I'm not a fan of D-ring screws--they snag on the clamp and are fiddly--and replaced it with a 1/4\\" Sunwayfoto hex screw. [[ASIN:B004SNMNFA Sunwayfoto Stainless Steel 1/4-Inch to 3/8-Inch Tripod Adapter / Bushing TN-1 TN1 5]] or [[ASIN:B00D97ZKAQ 10 Pack Cap SS Steel Screws 1/4\\" Tripod Quick Release QR Plate]] work well as replacements. It's good to have spare screws on hand to upgrade existing and future plates.

Another reason I choose the DS-1 is because lacks an anti-twist flange or lip. Why? Universal anti-twist flanges are set at a right angle and tear up the beveled (rounded) edge of EOS cameras. For a proper fit, the flange needs to to matched to the contour of the bottom edge.

Since there is no lip, twisting is controlled with two rubber pads. Unfortunately, they're small and slippery so I upgraded to a larger neoprene pad. I bought a sheet of 2mm thick Neoprene with adhesive backing (the type used to decouple monitors from stands). Neoprene is grippy and molds to the bumps on the underside of the camera when compressed. I cut it so it covered the entire plate surface (38mm x 38mm). The outcome was zero twist in the drop slot with my SL1 and heaviest zoom (15-85 IS USM): 2-second waterfall pics and selfies at the end of a monopod were rock solid!

I also tried the DS-1 on my Olympus E-P3 and it fit: nearly flush with the front and back edges of the bottom and doesn't cover the battery door. The description claims it fits the Canon S110 and S120 so I tried it on a S110 and the DS-1 is silly huge. Yes, it can be adjusted to allow access to the battery door but 1/3 of the plate protrudes pass the bottom edges. Tiny cameras like the S90/100/110/120 are better served with a smaller plate like the Kirk PZ-130 or [[ASIN:B008GN1GJM SUNWAYFOTO 26mm QR Plate DP-26]].

In an ideal world I'd have a custom contoured plate for my SL1 (plus world peace, free-range chickens and a million bucks in checking!). But since that ain't happening, the DS-1 is the next best thing. Yes, the D-ring screw and rubber pad required upgrades for optimal performance, so I deducted a star for that! But considering the low cost and easy improvements, it's an excellent plate for small cameras and among the few that fit a SL1 without covering the battery door. product_title: Lodigimo Retro Digital Diana Camera Black & Silver
review_headline: Hipster Toy Camera That (For Some) Is Fun To Use.
review_body:
This is a camera for \\"toy\\" camera enthusiasts. It claims to digitally recreate the look of the old 1960's plastic toy camera that was often used as carnival prizes, etc. The original was never seriously meant to be used, but became famous as an \\"art\\" camera. Do a search and you'll find a lot more about it.

Basically, somebody recreated in miniature the Diana design, dropped in an old 2 MP \\"COACH\\" (camera on a chip) and a simple plastic lens. I doubt if the face recognition works, as the lens does not focus!

The camera is fragile...just brittle plastic. Do NOT use the included strap, which looks like the cheap ribbon used with 3rd prize medals at a county fair. There is also NO lens cap, which would have been nice to have.

Sadly, the one error all of these Diana wannabees miss is that the original lens was made from non-optical non-quality styrene plastic. It was the same wavy stuff that windshields of model cars were made from, or the little magnifying glasses that used to come in Cracker Jack boxes (before concerns about choking!).

I would like to see someone make this camera with a couple of lenses that would screw into place: one optical plastic and one the original wavy stuff!

Still fun to use! I'll probably include it as an illustration in my 3rd edition of my \\"How To Use The Digital Camera You Just Bought\\" book!

product_title: Canon Waterproof Housing WP-DC44 for Canon PowerShot G1 X Digital Camera
review_body: I got this camera case in 2014, and dive about 30-40 dives a year.  My feelings on this were mixed at first, but now unequivical.  First, I have to say this is my first Canon case.  I've owned 4 Olympus underwater camera housings, going back 9 years, and any camera housing can be subject to flooding.  The buttons are on this case well laid-out, and easy to use.  Originally, I gave this case a 2-star rating, thinking I might have been culpable with the one full flood and two small leaks I'd encountered in the first 18 months of owning the case.  Since then, it has flooded 4 times, destroying more than $2,000 worth of cameras.  Insurance covered some if it, that that's not the point.  Before owning Canon, I'd owned 4 Olympus housings, and in 10 years, and over 600 dives, had one flood.  One.  I sure hope this was an exception to the rule.  I should have taken a hammer to this piece of crap years ago.  Canon:  get your act together!  You make a great camera.  Why only a single O-Ring?  And why oh why didn't I get rid of it when it looked like it might fail again last year.  Ever hopeful, I'd put it off, changing the O-Ring [I did this every year], and making sure the 20 or so tiny [and non-servicable O-Rings for the buttons] were well-lubricated.  Anyway, caution for using this case.   My experience in 200 dives:  4 dead cameras, two near misses.

product_title: Fotasy LH61E 75mm-300mm Lens Hood for Olympus M. Zuiko Digital
review_headline: Very difficult fit but does the job
review_body:
After spending 500 dollars on a lens you would think that olympus would include the hood since the lens is pretty much useless without it, but alas my 75-300 micro 4/3 lens arrived hoodless. Call it my own silly little rebellion (emphasis on "silly") but I just was not going to purchase the olympus hood. Rainbow imaging has always had good alternatives to the brand names and so even though the reviews here on Amazon were mixed, I went with this hood.

When in place the hood works just fine. The problem comes when you actually try to get it in place. This is a VERY rough fit. Very tights and takes a great deal of finagling to get it on. And some times it tricks you into thinking its on when it's not. Taking it off the lens is another chore. Really really really stiff. Backing it onto the lens for storage works better and smoother but still a minor effort.

BOTTOM LINE: I debated between 3 and 4 stars for this one and ultimately went with 4 because when in place the hood does the job it is supposed to do and does not interfere with shooting even at the long end. If you are concerned about ease of fit both putting on and taking off your lens then definitely look elsewhere. This one will frustrate you. If you don't mind fighting with the hood to get it in place then buy it.

product_title: Olympus TG-3 Tough Digital Camera
review_headline: Great macro, fun underwater, sturdy, long battery life- what's not to love?!
review_body:
i love this camera! got it just before a diving trip and am sooooo glad i did! lucky for me it's quite intuitive, so easy to figure out on the road/ in the field.

pro's:
- fantastic macro. truly. several friends have asked what kind of camera i use. not bad for a pocket camera!
- easy to use, intuitive controls and menus, generally well placed buttons and whatnot.
- sturdy, and feels it. i kept it in the side pocket of my bag thru 4wks in indonesia, with not a scratch on it.
- nice underwater settings and correction- forgot to put on underwater mode for part of a dive- what a difference!
- nice photos! very respectable all around point and shoot image quality
- underwater! i accidentally took it to 16.8m and though it was flashing an alarm at me, it survived unscathed. i didn't have a computer on a few dives, but the camera acts as it's own depth meter past 12m or so, giving you some warning. at 15m it flashes a warning on he screen, but keeps working.
- quick! i'm not super technical, so i can't give you exact numbers, but i haven't once been annoyed by the lag time on this camera. i suspect i am used to a certain amount of lag, so less sensitive to it than i used to be, but some digital cameras still make me nuts. not this one.
- battery life- it seemed to go forever! never had a problem with it, and i just got in the habit of recharging it when i got the chance, not because i needed to (phone ran dry infinitely quicker). it would 'sleep' if i didn't use it oftne enough on a dive, so i tended to just keep doing enough to keep it awake for the whole dive (60min)- not a problem during the dive, or the rest of the day.
- price- great deal for the quality and features. i've been on a run of problem cameras (crappy image quality, inconsistent charging, delicate, etc) for several years, but the streak has been broken!!!
- wifi- though it was a bit twitchy initially connecting to my phone (required a reboot once or twice), it mostly worked fine and always transferred my pics. super convenient to be able to use my phone to upload pics and not need to travel with a computer!
- size: i found it perfect for slipping into a pocket on my day pack, or the side pocket on cargo pants. i really liked not worrying about it getting knocked around.

cons: these are nit pics, but perhaps worth noting for some
- the mode select button is easy to move accidentally, so sometimes camera gets switched to a different mode inadvertently while in my pocket. since it usually ends up in macro, i catch it immediately because the camera focus is very unhappy (trying to focus to 1in) and it's easy to switch back.
- only 15m! though the pics wouldn't be much good at deeper depths due to no attached flash, it's a drag for me to limit dives to 15m. meant i only took the camera on my 3rd dive of each day and missed lots of cool photos.
- macro underwater mode is weird. it zooms in super close to the subject, which is hard to adjust to at first (as i mentioned, just got the camera). the pics turned out well, but not many underwater creatures want to sit still while your camera adjusts. the other underwater modes were awesome, i mostly stuck to the underwater action mode, seemed to work well for lots of situations.

overall, i'm super happy with this camera after traveling with it for 6wks. it did well both above and below the water, and held up to some rough travel conditions. i was easily able to transfer pics to my phone, then upload them to the internet for friends and family (even stopped using my phone for most pics because the camera pic quality was so much better and the transfer so relatively easy!). this is the best camera i've had for years, and i'm excited that it seems likely to last me for years to come!

I bought a Panasonic Lumix FZ70 60X zoom camera which uses 55mm filters. I have an older Pentax ESII camera from the 70's that still works, but is just kept for reasons. It uses 49mm base filters and a couple of accessories lenses uses 58mm. These extra filters have just sat for the last dozen years or so. I bought this step up ring to be able to us e the filters (UV, skylight, morn/eve, cloudy, and polarizer) with this new camera. Some reviews of other rings mentioned poor machine, bad threads, poor silk screening, etc. so I was hesitant to order. But I figured for the price........nothing to lose.

All my concerns were groundless. This product is excellent. The appearance is excellent, the quality is good, the threading is clean and precise and it works like a charm. I now have one of my older filters as protection on the front of my new camera's lens and will be able to use my varied assortment as desired. (I had also made my own soft focus, spot focus, and other filters as well) Now I can use all these.

If you have filters readily available and need something within a reasonable range to fit another camera I would highly recommend this product. If you needed to change several sizes, the operation and appearance may look ungangly, but in my case I was only going up one size so the appearance is hardly noticeable. It allows me to use my several hundred dollars worth of filters for only $3.95. How can you go wrong with that?

product_title: Tronsmart SJ4000 Novatek 1080P 30fps 12 Mega Pixels H.264 1.5 Inch 170°Wide Angle Lens Outdoor Waterproof Sports Home Security HD DV/CAR DVR/Camera (Black)
review_headline: Device was DOA, but I could see the potential.
review_body:
First and foremost-- I ordered this device from the seller "GeekBuying", fulfilled by Amazon. I received a genuine SJ4000, NOT a knockoff. So that's a good start.

The device I ordered ended up being DOA. It worked for a couple of days, then started overheating, freezing, and showing scrambled video on the screen. Never even got to try it outside. However, I'll try to approach this from the viewpoint of a non-DOA device.

I ordered this device to replace a GoPro HD Hero 3 Black edition that I'd ordered for a pro-level project last year. I like the idea of having an action cam readily available, but in practice, I've only used my GoPro a handful of times since the initial project I ordered it for. While the GoPro produces fantastic results, I didn't see myself using it for any more paid work, and figured I could sell it (and the LCD backpac), and replace it with something cheaper for personal use.

The SJ4000 produces very good results. I'd say it's in-line with the Sony Action Cam AS10 which I've also previously owned. Heck, it's possibly even better, in terms of video quality. In the brief time I spent with it, the videos were clear, sharp (though maybe a bit over-sharpened), and showed only a moderate amount of compression artifacts. You can find video samples online with a little searching, so I won't go into too much detail here, but overall, things are good.

The main upside to the SJ4000 (vs other Chinese-made "knockoffs") is that it's completely compatible with most GoPro accessories. The mounting system is directly compatible, so there would be no issue using an official GoPro suction cup or head mount with this camera.

It's thicker than a bare GoPro HD Hero 3, BUT thinner than a Hero 3+LCD BacPac combination (which is useful to know, since the SJ4000 has a built-in screen). The device itself is rather lightweight, and it's clear that it's not made out of the highest quality materials. To putit simply, it feels cheap. Even the waterproof housing feels considerably cheaper than its GoPro counterpart. But it gets the job done (assuming you receive a functional unit). And with the large number of mounts and accessories that the SJ4000 comes bundled with, it's quite a deal compared to a comparable GoPro setup.

All this being said, the unit I received was still DOA. I'd never want to bring this into a situation where I intended to capture precious memories or important footage. It's an inexpensive alternative to the name-brand GoPro line, but you get what you pay for.

product_title: NX3000 Style, Color, Config
review_headline: Nice Camera, But You Should Buy an SLR instead
review_body: On Paper the NX3000 is terrific.  It is significantly cheaper than the [[ASIN:B00HV6KGNM Samsung NX30 20.3MP CMOS Smart WiFi & NFC Interchangeable Lens Digital Camera with 18-55mm Lens and 3\\" AMOLED Touch Screen and EVF (Black)]] but has the same image sensor and many of the same features.  It's also categorized as \\"compact\\", implying that you can put it in your pocket or a small case and easily take it hiking or to a selfie party.    In reality, because it uses the same lenses as the Samsung NX line, the NX3000 does not fit comfortably into any compact camera case - and definitely not your pocket.  The display is LCD instead of the AMOLED on the NX30 - meaning it doesn't do well outside in the sun.  The display also can't be tilted into any useful direction - just the selfie flip-up thing - and it's noticeably low resolution.  The camera is uncomfortable, lacking the nice one-handed grip that the NX30 has.  Having used the NX30 extensively, any time I used this camera I couldn't wait to put it down and grab the NX30.  I would also note that it lacks one of my favorite SLR features - the ability to take multiple pictures at the end of a timer (both the Canon Rebel and Samsung NX30 can do this - probably most SLRs)    It does take really good pictures.  That counts for a lot.  The OIS lens - if you get that version - works extremely well and the camera takes SLR-quality pictures.  It also has a selfie mode where it can take a picture automatically if you smile at the camera.  I passed the camera around at gatherings and everyone loved this feature, gimmicky though it might be.  Seriously: you can hand this camera to someone at a party, show them this feature and you won't get the camera back for several hours as the camera gets passed around to everyone there.  So the camera is not a dud.  It works as advertised.    But in the end, I don't think the camera is worth buying.  You'll either be happier with a pocket-friendly point-and-click or a real SLR like the NX30.Spend more or less money, don't be fooled into thinking that the NX3000 occupies some sweet spot in between.

product_title: CowboyStudio Panoramic Gimbal Tripod Head BK-45 Specialized 1/4-Inch Screw For Telephoto Len Camera
review_headline: Beware quality control issues, but if you get a proper copy it's terrific!
review_body:
In 1991, the Wimberley gimbal tripod head changed long-lens photography in an almost revolutionary way. A heavy telephoto lens mounted properly on this device could be balanced in such a way that it would hang "weightlessly" and easily be maneuvered with a finger or two. It was a clear improvement over even the best ballheads, such as the Arca-Swiss B1.

Not surprisingly, over the past twenty-plus years, a number of copycat gimbals have come onto the market. Most recently, Chinese manufacturers have produced knockoff models that are way cheaper than the original Wimberley, and also cheaper than other good quality gimbals, such as those made by Jobu, Kirk, and Really Right Stuff. Enter the Beike BK-45, an inexpensive, Arca-mount equipped, surprisingly compact gimbal that sells for a hundred bucks, more or less.

The CowboyStudio Panoramic Gimbal Tripod is a Beike, imported and distributed by CowboyStudio of Texas. This same model is currently marketed under numerous names, but they all are the BK-45. One actually can buy these gimbal heads from Chinese sellers (via ebay, for example), and in some cases pay a bit less. But buyer beware. I purchased one of these from China not long ago, and it arrived with an annoying defect: the control knob for the swing arm (which controls the "up down" angle) did not tighten at all. The unchangeable level of swing arm dampening was adequate for using the thing (some gimbal manufacturers do not, in fact, allow the head to be fully tightened down, arguing that this is a safety feature). But this knob control is supposed to work, and it did not. To return the thing would have cost me big bucks in postage, so I gave it away and bought a second unit, only slightly more expensive, through Amazon, which I know would exchange it for free were there a problem. Another lesson in penny wise, pound foolish!

So, a warning: a perusal of reviews of the Beike BK-45 quickly reveals that quality control is an issue. More than a few owners have reported the necessity of taking the thing apart, cleaning out the heavy lubricating grease, and relubricating it in order for the unit to function properly. I am no mechanic, so I eschewed this option the first time around. And fortunately, this unit from CowboyStudio works perfectly. The knobs tighten, and the moving parts glide smoothly left-right and up-down. So as it is, I have a remarkably inexpensive tripod gimbal head that will support even the largest telephoto lens for smooth, effortless panning and tilting. Amusingly (I guess), the BK-45 includes a fairly non-functioning compass stuck vertically over the screw that holds the swing arm tighening knob, and an equally nonfunctioning bubble level. At this price point, there are "compromises," I guess.

I have no idea at this point how the unit will stand up to hard, repeated use in the field. I don't tend to beat up my equipment, so for me, ultimate durability is not a primary concern. But even having paid for two of these gimbals, I ended up with a bargain tripod head that works nicely. My recommendation is that if you want to try out a gimbal tripod head, this is a good unit to purchase. And it appears that CowboyStudio makes sure that the units they send out are in good working order. Thumbs up!

product_title: ExpoDisc 2.0 Professional White Balance Filter
review_body: As a pro photographer and cinematographer for mote than 30 years now, the right light balance is indeed a very big deal. However, the Expodisc has never met my expectations. In fact, it has never delivered an acceptable result. It doesn't do mxed light sources well. Daylight is never quite right with it. In reality, I still find an 18% gray card reading the de-facto standard for the best w/b readings. Now, to be honest, if you shoot RAW, in-camera auto light balance is more than sufficient 99% of the time. You can always correct it in Lightroom, DXO or Capture One Pro. If you're a RAW shooter, save your $50 and put it toward gas in your car to shoot another 1000 shots or pay for 5 months of your Adobe Photoshop subscription. If you feel you have the need to get your white balance as close as possible (slides, scientific, etc.), get a collapsable 18% gray card and learn how to do PRE's on your camera. You will save money, get a more accurate white balance read and lose a great deal of frustration in the process.

product_title: Expert Shield - THE Crystal Clear Screen Protector for:
review_body:
Installation was easy.

Short Version:
* clean display
* peel back first protective layer of screen protector
* place screen protector on the display
* squeegee out the air bubbles with a credit card wrapped in the provided cleaning cloth
* peel off the second/opposite protective layer of screen protector

Long Version:
* practice without peeling any of the backing from the screen protector
** I just laid it down, and picked the left edge as a reference point, making a mental note of how far from the edge, and how much gap to leave at the top to "center" the screen protector vertically.
** be sure to practice how you'll hold the screen protector, and the display. I place my left pinky and thumb on the left edge of the display to steady things.
* clean hands (especially the fingertips)
* clean the display with the provided cloth
* peel away the first backing layer (remember your mental image of where to place the screen protector)
* start at the left edge of the display, and align the screen protector as you practiced
* slowly lower the screen protector to the right
* as it makes contact with the display, use your left index finger to follow along, and slide/press down on the screen protector IN THE MIDDLE (this is roughly how I hang wallpaper)
* use a credit card wrapped in the provided cleaning cloth to push out any air bubbles
* celebrate

Despite all my planning + preparation, I trapped an eyelash between the screen protector and the display. I followed the instructions, and used a piece of regular old office tape, taped it to the screen protector (which still had the second/opposite protective layer on), and peeled the screen protector back. I only peeled far enough to expose the lash, keeping enough of the screen protector in contact with the display so I wouldn't have to mess with repositioning it. I used a second piece of tape to remove the eyelash, then lowered the screen protector, and all was well.

Once it's on, it's hard to tell that you have something covering the display. It's clear, and I haven't noticed any increase in glare... there's definitely no *decrease* in glare, but they never promised that so I'm ok.

I usually walk around at festivals with my camera on one of those rapid strap clones, so I like the piece of mind of knowing that the display will be protected against minor bumps.

product_title: Panasonic DMC-GF6KK 16MP Mirrorless Mirrorless Digital Camera with Lens Kit
review_body:
I've been a Panasonic Lumix girl for many years, but until now it was strictly the point and shoot pocket cameras. For people who are looking to buy a bridge camera, something that bridges the gap between point and shoot and a more complex camera, you can't go wrong here. Micro 4/3 technology makes owning a full feature DSLR style camera more streamlined and easy to carry around. For a lot of people, this means more likely to *use*, and more often at that. Be aware that there aren't as many lens options, and the ones that are out there may cost more than their traditional counterparts. That said, I think that the M43 technology fills a need for people who want portability and functionality. The GF6 has reminded me why I loved photography.

Body:
The body on this camera is only slightly larger than my previous pocket cameras. With a pancake lens you really could put the whole thing in your pocket if you wanted to. Because it's a micro 4/3, it's lighter than a DSLR by far, but it feels sturdy and well built in your hand. Everything feels well constructed, from the lens release button to the not-too-slippy mode dial. The only thing that feels like you have to be careful with it at all is the pop-up flash. More on the flash later. The SD chip and battery are located together in the bottom of the camera. The buttons are well placed, but be warned that due to the very small size of the camera it's easy to mash buttons with the palm of your hand, and it's especially hard to access functions that are inside the wheel to the right of the screen. I use the edge of my nail when setting the white balance.

Screen:
The screen is a joy to compose and set up shots from. It's a touchscreen just like on a smart phone, allowing you to adjust your focus target, access feature menus on the fly, scroll through shots you've taken, and more. Because it angles out and flips up, you can take \\"selfies\\" and it will automatically turn on a timer so you can set up the shot just right. The angling screen also allows you to take shots at low and awkward angles much more easily. The legs that support the screen aren't flimsy and hold their position well. Because the camera has no optical viewfinder the screen is always on. Be mindful and buy an extra battery, especially if you plan on extended shooting sessions.

Kit Lens:
The 14-42mm kit lens is very small if you're used to a standard DSLR kit lens in the same range. The profile feels proportional, however, and it's got quite a bit of versatility for such a small package. The focal length can be limiting if you're used to getting up close and personal to your subjects (say, close ups of flowers and such), but for portraits, and non-macro shooting it does the job well, and it's fairly fast. If you want more reach you'll definitely want to supplement with a decent zoom lens, but be prepared for major (lopsided) bulk.

Wifi:
I thought I'd love the wifi feature and being able to conect to my phone, but be warned, that functionality does NOT work with iPhones at this time. It's an Apple limitation, I'm told. I tried using the app with the house wifi as a work around but found it slow and clunky.

Flash:
The built in flash, like most built in flashes, is kind of a joke... IF you use it as is. However, if you use your finger to tilt it back all the way so it's facing the ceiling... you can bounce the flash and get a much, MUCH better photograph, especially when shooting off the cuff portraits. It's amazing how much better and warmer they look when bounced. The spring loaded flash lets you play with the light that way and is pretty neat. I wish it had a hot shoe instead, but since it doesn't, at least there's a saving grace.

Menu:
The menus on the camera are very easy to get around. Unlike my old Pentax, they're bright, intuitively laid out, and simple to use. The scenes mode has plenty of fun options for those who shoot on auto, though remember that you can't access some of them if you have the intelligent auto (iA or iA+) turned on. On screen menus for manual shooting are also easy to use, though they require some getting used to from a more traditional DSLR.uto, though remember that you can't access some of them if you have the intelligent auto (iA or iA+) turned on. review_body:
Powerful, adaptable, quiet, light, and it also looks good. I'm a pro shooter celebrating 30 years at one major daily newspaper. As our staff has had to cut back to trim from budget, I saw these units on sale, and so I was issued two heads with batteries. I've used them to cover rap artists, politicians, as well as MLB and NFL players. I could use them to even light basketball gyms, but that's too much hassle for me these days.

These units really do crank out the flash output, enough to make a great portrait with a brolly in full sunlight, like I just did again, two days ago, and with cloud cover earlier today. They've been shipped and dragged into mainly hot climate conditions (90s and high humidity) and have not had one failure. I've used pro gear including White Lightning and Norman, but don't miss them.

There are less powerful units that I considered, but I wanted the ability to use sunlight as a key light that won't overpower the image, since most cameras shoot at 1/200th or 1/250 second sync. This has just the right juice - but in addition to getting this, consider a decent ND filter - with the sun behind the subject, I had the brolly above and a reflector below and at ISO 100, was pounding him at full power through the battery at f/22. I was concerned about sharpness falling off and the intense depth of field but the image looked terrific - editors mentioned how I made some tasty chicken salad that day.

I've shot in all types of places, some with questionable fuse strength and these have yet to trip a fuse. I love the handles, which make the cumbersome heads easy to secure without fear of dropping. The light is pure and consistent. I know to use 1/2 power in full sun. Its balance means I don't have to second-guess or have fear of change.

The batteries are light, charge well and hold charge. They don't allow for using the modeling lights but I wouldn't want to for that would drain batteries when you need them. The size of the battery means you could have a single head, with AC cable, DC connector, battery and nice strong compact stand, and it would all fit in a small backpack, or even take the center compartment of a Think Tank case. Imagine being able to crank out great portraits at the great salt lake, or in an auto graveyard with this. This unit lets you work where others simply can't, and that's why I got them.

I like some other nice features but there are a couple nits to pick, all about the hardware. The mounting hardware is great because the locking handle (the only plastic - which has been sturdy - which locks an all-metal mount) can actually ratchet. Some handles out there don't which really is needed if you want to move the handle or you're in a tight spot. It also helps when packing to move the handle close to the head. The screws to lock umbrellas can completely unscrew - I almost lost one screw that way. Make sure to screw it back in more when pulling the umbrella out.

review_body:
I got this three days early, but was apprehensive about the documentation. So I put it to the test as soon as I got it home. I hope this helps other flash novices like me. I am using this on a D3300. Here's what I learned:
1. My flash unit is a little touchy about how it takes the batteries. I had to load and unload a few times before it would come on.
2. When you mount it on the camera it picks up the settings right away, however--the camera doesn't take the flash into consideration in it's metering. (I was shooting indoors at night), and I had to experiment with it to get a balanced flash. . I'll explain later about the settings. But the flash works well--I tried all the angles, and the diffuser, and I got very good results in all modes (P,A,S,M).

Note: My flash goes to sleep in less than 30 seconds, I don't know if I can adjust that or not, but it's aggravating to set up the shot and have the flash show SL (sleeping).
3. The JJC receiver and remote initally talked to each other, but I (initially) couldn't get the flash to work on it. I put it aside and tried it again later, and it worked consistently FYI: There is a YouTube video on this that helped me a little bit--look up JJC Receivers--the guy's name is Raphael.
4. Settings on the flash: TTL =through the lens--this is when your flash is mounted on the camera. M is for manual, Strobe is for Strobe (where you keep flashing through the pictures to get an effect like a badly edited movie S1, and S2 are slave modes.
5. I have more experimenting to do but to give you an idea of a fairly good light balanced night portrait, I used the following settings:
ISO 200, f2.8, 1/60, 35mm Nikkor 1.8G prime lens. Altura Flash set on M at 1/16 .0.3EV+ (self portrait with shallow depth of field shot indoors at approximately 10 feet from camera). Then I went with what the camera said I should do: (shutter at 1/2), and it still worked well--I just had to sit very still for the shot not to blur.

I worked with flash mounted on the camera, and also with the flash mounted on the receivers bouncing light off the walls and ceilings. I used both the hard plastic diffuser, and the wide angel diffuser with the bounce card. I did acheive the "catchlights" in my eyes, and I avoided the glare on my glasses. The flash was at 45 degrees or greater in all cases. I hate self portraits, but I must say I was impressed with the results--and having used the built in flash, I can see these are much better quality. I think I'm confident enough to take some good shots of people.

I kept taking shots moving the flash around until I was satisfied with the results. Then I put the camera on P, and left the flash on M with the same settings (the flash remembers the settings it had last when you turn it on), and got identical results.

After so many selfies, I tried putting a Rogue Gel (deep pink) on the diffuser, and the flash refused to fire. I took it off the diffuser, put it on the lens itself, and I got selfie bathed in pink (had it been a background shot behind me as the subject, it would have worked quite nicely). The point I am making here is that the color was deep, and rich, and even. So if you want a flash to produce those qualities using a gel for a background, this one can. I can see where I could use that.

I saw a comment from a photographer who said he was using Eneloop batteries and how they lasted through 400+ shots: I am using Eneloop XX , and they are working well. Again, I had to finesse the batteries in the flash for a few minutes until it came to life.

Final comments: I hope this helps someone in their decision making. This flash is working for me as a new flash photographer. I am satisfied with this purchase, and the service I got from digital goja. I may go back later and get the second flash.or the shot not to blur.

review_headline: Good image stabilization but exposure and contrast issues
review_body:
Camcorder
It's already known that this camera's stabilization feature is outstanding so that saves it from getting a low rating from me.
What really disappointed me was the camera's tendency to seriously over expose in the auto exposure setting. I am not talking here about shots in the sun or extremely bright light. I am talking about, indoor shots and shots in shaded areas or very overcast settings. It seems that the camera naturally has a high contrast (which will tend to make dark spots darker and light spots lighter).
I always have to adjust the EV shift or exposure manually or I will have seriously blown out details (especially on faces). This simply was not the case with my other dslrs or camcorders. If anything, auto exposure and EV shift tends to be a bit on the underexposed side. I've looked at some other people's NX30 footage and noticed a slighter over exposure of skin (not as bad as mine though). What this means is that you'll constantly have to be monitoring something that you may have taken for granted with your other camcorders. This will be further complicated by the fact that there are no external buttons to adjust this. In other words adjusting exposure is not particularly quick.

The touch screen is also very inconsistent. At times it's a tap whilst at other times you have to push down medium or firmly. That of course is very annoying since almost all of the camera's controls are via the screen as opposed to onboard buttons.

Tripod
As you might have expected/ suspected, the larger "Pro" tripod is just ok at best.

Extra battery
The Sony manual warns to use only batteries with the "V" marked. Yet these supplier's replacement battery does not have a V. So am not to sure if the camera is put at risk from using the replacement battery.

I will update on the filters as soon as I get the chance to use them.

product_title: Sony NEX5 Bundle Parent
review_headline: Quality and creativity in a wonderfully small package
review_body:
My mother owns this camera so I already had a chance to use it before I bought it. I would classify myself as a serious amateur photographer right now (previously did professional photography and have had professional training). I have a Nikon DSLR that I enjoy, but the drawback is it's bulky, heavy (in comparison to the Sony), and I have to be intentional about using it. What I love about the Sony is that it is small, lightweight, and takes amazing photos for its size. I also like the creativity features (various shooting modes), the ability to do panoramas, and the fact that you can take beautiful hand-held night photos with automatic exposure being right on, or near right on. This camera is so flexible while maintaining quality and it allows you to be spontaneous and creative. I actually carry this camera with me all the time because it is so small and lightweight (I keep it in my purse and I have a medium-size purse, or I put it in a messenger bag I sometimes carry). No more missing great shots because my camera is at home. I used to work as a photo-journalist and I like shooting unique and day-in-the-life types of shots. Although cell phone cameras can meet the need for some of these types of photos, for me I really like having the option of taking a higher quality photo with various modes and settings in - literally - my back pocket.

That being said, there are a few things I don't like. The biggest drawback for me is the lack of a viewfinder - much too hard to use an LED screen and see what you're really getting, at least for me. I know you can add one (and some day I plan to), but the cost is about $325. And because of it's small size, it can sometimes be awkward using the buttons/dials. But I guess you can't have everything and I am willing to work with these things because the benefits of this camera outweigh the drawbacks.

review_headline: 1) canon 60d w/ 50mm prime 2) canon 60d w/ 28-135 Obviously the 50mm fits easy and has room in the bottom to stick the ...
review_body:
I want to give this case 5 stars but can't.

The strap that is used to hook the case to something is permanently attached to only one side. For how "I" want to use the case, it's on the wrong side. I'm going to end up having to cut the strap off and re-sewing it to the other side of the case for it to completely work for me.

I currently use this in conjunction with the CowboyStudio Quick Neck Shoulder Strap. I attach the case to my belt loop and the shoulder strap is long enough so that the camera can rest in the case while I walk around. When I want to take a picture, I pull the camera out and shoot.

My reason for getting the case is so that while I'm on vacation with my wife and kids, I don't have to worry about the camera bouncing around on my hip as much. I'm also not advertising what kit I'm shooting with to help keep thieves from wanting it quite so much. It helps that the shoulder strap I have has the metal wire that runs through it. These two items together has helped put my mind at ease while traveling.

My two walk around setups that this case is used for are the following:

1) canon 60d w/ 50mm prime
2) canon 60d w/ 28-135

Obviously the 50mm fits easy and has room in the bottom to stick the kit 18-55 if I think I need that for some reason.

The 28-135 is a bit of a stretch, but it's slowly stretching out and making it easier to get the camera/lens in and out.

There is no way of carrying the camera/lens with an add-on flash with this case. And any lens bigger than the 28-135 probably won't fit either.

review_headline: Works--just not the way it's supposed to
review_body:
I bought this battery pack for use with my Nikon SB800 Speedlight. I'm a wedding photographer, and I use bounce flash during receptions. The flash came with almost incomprehensible directions, but it seemed pretty straight-forward. I plugged it into my SB800 as directed, and it did increase the flash recycle times. However, it also made my flash unit unresponsive to any changes in settings or even to being turned off. Nothing but unplugging the batteries would reset the flash and make it usable again.

After searching online, I found this video: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6mufVQnMfKE which shows another user having the same problem. In the comments, someone suggests plugging the PC sync cord (the small, single end) into the camera instead of the flash unit. I tried this, and it did fix my problem. The flash is now responsive to changes while being plugged in.

This product has some kind of design flaw.

review_headline: So Much Quality and Features in so Little Space
review_body:
Really great bag. Very, very happy with my purchase (bought on a popular auction site new for $30 less than this site).

There are so many pockets and spaces and features packed into a very minimal compact bag. When I started to play around with what to put where I was afraid I'd forget where things were because there were so many options!

The SD card pockets, the tucked away rain cover, tucked away tripod holder, tucked away microfiber cloth… So many hidden treasures!

Even the details like the elastic bands to hold excess strap. Very well designed.

And of course the headline feature, being able to swing it around your front and open the pocket which faces you in that position. Easy access to camera and basic accessories without having to take the back pack off.

The minimalist design keeps people from getting curiouser nervous about what you have. I'm not worried about getting held up because it does not look like I'm carrying anything expensive.

I would have loved an optional second strap to wear in backpack mode or just to wear the opposite way or even if they had an optional handle so I don't only put weight on my right shoulder. Of course the back the size isn't that heavy but sometimes my shoulder can get irritated if it carries something all day even if not terribly heavy.

Other than that small request the bag is perfect. Great size, very comfortable on medium journeys, tons of different places to put things, awesome design, tons of hidden features.

product_title: Ravelli Light Weight Aluminum Tripod
review_body:
I've been waiting until I got back to a computer to write this review...that's how much I love this thing.

First off, I've been using this with a Nikon D3200 with both regular and telephoto lens. I'm also a photo novice, so work with me.

It's very lightweight and I was able to strap it to a backpack (Mountainsmith Borealis AT) for most of my Alaska trip and outside of maybe bumping into people (the backpack was rather full) I rarely noticed the weight.

For the price is has got to be the best tripod out there. It's very stable, has the quick-release thing at the top (again, I'm a novice) to pop the camera on and off. You can do portrait and landscape, tilt, rotate, the whole nine yards you'd expect from a full-service tripod. Balance bubbles helped as well. It even can raise up maybe 18" further via crank (awesome for 5'8" me and 5'4" wife). The feet are on ball mounts, so it'll handle most any terrain without slipping. Knobs were very easy to manipulate and even when loose I was able to use the camera as a steady mount while aiming at moving objects. Has a neat little handle that you can use. I used it as a handle with the legs full extended and used it as a makeshift monopod (tightened the tripod leg lock when closed). People on the cruise asked where I got it and I had to tell them the specs on it. Bag is decent quality...handled a lot of abuse. The tripod handled a bit of abuse as well - some scratches but I'm not worrying. VERY fast to set up and put away. Never tilted, went off balance or let me down. EXTREMELY GOOD PRODUCT.

product_title: Canon PowerShot SX260 12.1MP Digital Camera with 3-Inch TFT LCD
review_body:
I purchased the SX260 in January 2013. In April, 2014, the LCD screen darkened when viewing a subject. After contacting Canon Customer Service, they advised that I should mail to their closest repair facility. Upon receipt, I was immediately notified that Canon did not repair such defects but they would send me a new SX260 for $ 150 plus tax. As I had paid slightly more than $ 200 plus tax only16 months prior, I advised that paying over $350.00 for a camera that becomes unusable after 16 months didn't seem like much of deal.

I wrote their Manager of Customer Relations in May, 2014 and expressed my disappointment that Canon manufactured a product that has such a short usage period and that their manner of resolving a defective product seemed a bit unfair. Expecting to get a response saying something like "sorry, we'll try better, etc", I was extremely surprised to get NO RESPONSE whatsoever. I guess they figure that ignoring a dissatisfied customer makes the problem go away!

All I can say to any future purchasers of Canon products, I hope you don't have any problems with their products as I am pretty certain that you won't like their problem resolution strategy.

product_title: Fotodiox 145mm Ultra Slim Neutral Density 1000 10-Stop Filter for WonderPana 145 and 66 Systems
review_headline: Top quality, best on the market for quality/price
review_body:
I bought it together with the 145mm system holder for Tokina 16-28, so I'm inserting the same review here as well:

After reading everything about the topic and reached the last page of the internet :), I finally made my decision and I bought this system about a month ago. I bought this holder and the 145mm ND1000 Ultra Slim version from the Fotodiox website.
The packages arrived in 3-4 days from USA. I have put on the holder onto my 16-28 only once. It's still on it :-) I'm not planning to take it off. I am really happy with this product, delivers superb quality, no loss in detail at all! It DOESN'T cut the corners either because this is the ultra slim version of the ND1000 filter. Maybe a slight magenta cast which is easily correctable.
It's dark, really dark. on a cloudy day you can shoot 30 seconds easily on F8, Iso 100. Around sunset you need 2-4 minutes, nice! If it's really really sunny, you step down under F16 and go under Iso 100.
Of course, it's not easy to use, because you have to set up the picture frame and the focus first, then switch to manual mode, before screwing on the filter. When the filter is on, you can only play with the shutter speed and the F numbers.
Unfortunately the filter doesn't come with a cloth but you will need one when you take it down, put it back all the time, so I've bought a Matin M-6320 Large Microfibre Magic Cleaning Cloth, and I'm keeping the filter in it all the time.

So I'm really happy with this system, I think this is the best solution now in quality/price. Some of my first pictures with it can be seen on my Photoblog: facebook.com/bbzphoto

product_title: lens cleaning cloths
review_headline: Very good product, EXCELLENT  customer care
review_body:
The item arrived promptly, every thing as described. But the most outstanding feature was the customer support of Goja.
First you need to learn from my mistake, the adapter snaps perfectly on my sx510 HS, then you can screw on any 52mm accessory (the hood, any of the filters, etc) at one instant I over tightened the hood to the adapter and couldn't unscrew if (even though both are made of hard material but still I didn't want to try excessive force so I won't break either -yeah I think I might be that strong!:)
So I thought I'll get another adapter ring for the filters and keep the one attached to the hood where it currently is, but since I couldn't find the stand alone ring to purchase, I emailed Goja with the situation asking to buy the ring alone. Within a few hours I got a reply from the customer service rep saying he already made arrangements to send me an extra ring!! Next day I got the shipment notification and tracking number! Chapeaux!
The lesson is, don't tighten the screwing parts more than you should! After all they are supposed to come on and off. But if you do, contact the company and they will help you!!
Bottom line: good product for what it's worth and excellent customer care.

product_title: DJI Phantom 2 Vision+ "V1.0" Quadcopter with FPV HD Video Camera and 3-Axis Gimbal Bundle with Extra Battery
review_headline: DJI Phantom 2 Vision+ (Plus)  The Gimbal System is a Piece of Crap Do Not Buy This Unless You Are Made of Money!
review_body:
So you think you want this, just wait until you buy another to replace the damaged camera gimbal that can't be fixed and because in the beginning replacement camera units were not available. Now picture this at about 50 feet away, 35 feet in elevation your connection between the controller and P2V+ becomes unresponsive, flies into palm fronds sliding down those then flips and drops 12 feet with no visible damage anywhere except a dirt smudge on a prop & a crack in the optional prop guard that you have to buy and install (honestly I've seen some nasty cuts on videos of people cut by blades and you really will want to install these.) But now your camera flops like a fish on land. BTW in case you don't know these only record video with NO SOUND.

Good news the gimbal is non-repairable or serviceable... BUST OUT $680 for a camera unit. Anybody want to buy a couple of good used slightly marred DJI Phantom 2 Vision+'s with new cameras on them??? Joking of course, due to the fragility of these its probably good I have 2 of these now to have a backup unit. I have a rant review of this gimbal system on LiveLeak dot com.

This is a PG video due to language- you have been warned!- http://www.liveleak.com/view?i=58a_1405193854

My channel there has a channel in the channel called "Aloha Kauai Flybys - Aerial Videos of Kauai" if you want to see some of the video these can do I edited.

In my opinion you are ahead getting the Phantom 2 and rigging it with the FPV system, separate gimbal & GoPro, at least you'll have sound on your recordings you can mute. The other plus is you'll be able to replace components that cost a portion of the Phantom 2 Vision+'s camera unit with non-replaceable gimbal. Think of the money you will save in the long run!

Now my situation was compounded by the lack of camera replacements in the beginning. I use this for work & fun of making videos. So I rationalized it was a $400 dollar ding bynot being grounded for over a month because I wanted a couple of extra batteries anyway.

Fortunately I can use these as write off for my work but I am betting most of you cannot. A gimbal independent of a camera component or that is repairable is what is needed. DJI's camera is very heavy in relation to the gimbal, its a machined chuck of aluminum that could be a high impact plastic to save weight and beef up the gimbal durability with sturdier components. A redesign is in order, one that includes a replaceable gimbal independent of the camera system.

This is my 2¢ on this product, it is good but far from being perfect or durable for its intended use and likely mishaps. Sooner or later most of you will crash, when you do if the gimbal goes out of whack it will cost you $680 for starters.

product_title: Olympus TG-3 Tough Digital Camera
review_headline: Would recommend to anyone looking for a non-DSLR camera
review_body:
I normally shoot with a Canon 6D but I have an active family that loves water, the beach, snow, you name it. It's not always feasible to get fun, candid shots of my children with my DSLR so I wanted to find a tough camera that I could throw in my purse but that also takes good pictures. This was my choice and I am not disappointed. Admittedly, I have had it less than a week and I will try to come back and update my review after I have owned it for awhile but my initial impression is that it has exceeded my expectations.

We have already used it in the pool and the water resistant lens cover worked great. There are a few pictures where a water spot got in the way but if I had been paying attention and dunked it in the water again it wouldn't have been a problem. Most of the time, the water just slides right off. My son has already dropped it as well (albeit, he is two so it only fell about two feet), but it's fine and in fact, it doesn't even look like that happened.

I have to mention one of my favorite things about the camera - it's instant focus. It takes pictures faster than any other point and shoot I have owned and I know that is one of the biggest complaints from people that have point and shoots. You will not be disappointed at how fast this camera can take a picture.

And I have to say the quality of the pictures is pretty darn good. I've had several point and shoots in my day and this one takes the cake. I am very happy with what I have seen so far.

product_title: Nikon COOLPIX L610 16 MP Digital Camera with 14x Zoom NIKKOR Glass Lens and 3-inch LCD
review_body: This Nikon camera was terrific in many regards:    good, sharp pictures    easy menu system    convenient access to closeup settings, exposure control, and flash settings    Weaknesses were:    short battery life    short camera life    As with many digital cameras, there were delays in camera startup and shots.  It's frustrating when you are trying to capture that candid moment, but it takes too long and the moment is gone.  It's faster than my previous digital camera, but it's the very expensive cameras that have the super fast warm-ups and focusing.    I found the pictures to be sharp and well exposed in normal lighting.  And with the exposure button on the back, it was easy to adjust exposure settings to compensate for bright or dark backgrounds.    As mentioned by others, the battery life is indeed short - largely due to the large, bright display on the back - - could also be due to only 2 AA batteries.  However, use of flash exposures was a major culprit in the short battery life as well.  But I had no problem with rechargeable batteries, and just kept extras handy in my small camera bag.    While I thought that the camera took excellent pictures, it is not good that it died due to a fatal \\"lens error\\", at only 1 year, 1 month.  In researching potential fixes, I found that the problem is not uncommon for these lens-projecting cameras, so I can't say if it is worse for this camera than for similar cameras.  But the cost of repair would likely come near the cost of a replacement camera, so since home remedies didn't work, I guess I'll be buying another before long.  But this time I'll try to find a sturdier camera.    Update:  9/5/14  Well - - - times, they have a changed.  I noted above that the digital cameras are slow to warm up and to focus for a shot.  But there have been significant improvements.  I purchased the Nikon Coolpix L830 - and while not being that much more expensive, it is significantly faster, not to mention a significant improvement in the zoom range.  But it uses a lens-cap that I keep forgetting to remove, which then reports a \\"lens error\\" - - but I assume that potential forgetfulness was built into the camera and should not create a camera failure.  The drawback is that it is a very boxy camera and will not fit in a shirt pocket, but the boxyness does provide more protection to the lens.

product_title: Dropcam Wi-Fi Wireless Video Monitoring Camera
review_body:
Excellent wide angle, clear picture for live viewing. If you plan to get this camera because it sends you a snapshot of each motion alert, you will be sadly disappointed. Problem is that Dropcam claims to give you a picture for each motion alert delivered to your email. But the picture you get is only visible IN the email at a very small size. When you click on it, you are sent to your live cam to view live video, NOT TO A LARGER PHOTO like you would think. So if you need it to identify someone or something, you are out of luck. If you planned to not pay for the recording service and just go with the email alerts, think again. $99/year is the least you will have to pay with any plan. Another problem is that email alerts are only sent every 30 minutes or more. If you have this camera aiming outside and a car goes by at 3:05, and your house is robbed at 3:10, you will not be alerted to motion and there will be no photo because 30 minutes hasn't passed. You would need to buy the recording service. Also, custom activity zones are only available to paying CVR subscribers. A custom activity zone will allow you to draw a box around the area of the video that you want to be alerted to when there is motion, like a doorway. product_title: NX3000 Style, Color, Config
review_body:
This is a really nice camera. It has a nice retro look and a nice wide screen. It does not have a viewfinder other than the screen. I prefer having both. I guess I am old school. If you are a novice, this camera is very simple to use. I like this camera for many reasons but thins there are a few things that can be improved on (viewfinder? please?).

First, to charge this camera you have to plug the entire thing in. It has a 3.8 V Li-ion battery and the camera does not come with a charger. Unless you get one on your own, you will be stuck having to plug in the entire camera. Second, this camera uses a micro SD card. THe camera DOES NOT come with a sample micro SD card, not even a tiny wee one. That is a bummer as I had to order a new one and wait before I could use the camera. I have a ton of the standard SD cards but had none of the micro-SD ones.

The electric panel is neat because it can flip over so you can take a nice selfie. Selfies are very easy to take and they look really nice. But note that if you have the flash attached, the panel will not flip completely over and it will not lock into place. So, you will still be able to see yourself but upside down. The style is really nice, reminiscent of old camera. I like it. I have the camera in white but I would suggest you select another color. Any scruff will show easily on the camera's body. I don't expect the white to stay white for long.

If you are looking for a nice easy to use camera, this is a good option.

product_title: Fotodiox Lens Mount Adapter - Pentax K AF Mount (PKAF) DSLR Lens to Sony Alpha E-Mount Mirrorless Camera Body with Built-In Aperture Control Dial
review_headline: Works great, fits perfect... small workaround needed with aperture dial
review_body:
Very well made and fits the lens perfectly. This adapter is used on Sony NEX-5N with a Pentax-M 50mm f/1.4 lens.

The adapter includes an aperture control dial. At first, I didn't think this was useful but have enjoyed having it when using the lens for video. For photos, it's nice to use the aperture dial on the lens to know exactly what f-stop it is.

However, I was having trouble with the adapter and the aperture. With the adapter, the lens could only be closed down to f/11.

Luckily, I solved this problem. After mounting the adapter to the lens, I first set the adapter's aperture dial to wide open. Second, I closed down the lens to f/22. This makes it possible for the adapter to now close down to f/22. Not sure if this problem exists with other adapters, but this small workaround is not a deal breaker.

Definitely recommend this Pentax K to NEX adapter, as there are some great Pentax lenses out there. And I was happy to pay more for this Fotodiox adapter just to know that it will be well made and keep my lens mounted safely on my camera.

product_title: SAVEoN Professional 52mm Telephoto Lens + SAVEoN MicroFiber Cleaning Cloth + Lens Tube Adapter + 4PC Macro Close Up Kit for Canon A610, A620, A630
review_body:
Starting with the "good" first. Got my money back after everything was said and done.

Now the bad:

Have a Canon A620, which has similar lens specs to the A610 and A630. Unfortunately, the lens adapter they sent me was for a Canon A650 (it was clearly identified as such on the box) and completely useless. I sent an email to them about this, and also expressed my fear that the lenses they sent me might not fit the adapter that my camera actually needed.

I was told that they had the correct adapter, and another adapter was sent to me, only the second one sent to me was the same one (In the same box!), that I got the first time!

Sent another email out, and eventually the correct adapter was sent, but the fear I expressed in my first email about the lenses not fitting the adapter turned out to be partially true. The telephoto lens was actually made for a 52mm thread, but the macro lenses, which would have been very nice to have, turned out to be totally useless with the adapter for my camera!

After I expressed some more than appropriate outrage in another email, I was given a total refund, and told to keep everything I had received. This means I ended up with two useless adapters for a camera I don't own, a set of macro lenses I can't use, and a telephoto lens and adapter which DO fit my camera.

Lessons learned?- searching for accessories for an outdated camera can be a pain in the butt. You expect that camera outfitters are looking to sell off their inventory of accessories for older cameras... you never expect that they have no idea of what they are actually sending out to you, or whether the products are the correct ones.

Live and learn... so it goes.

product_title: Sigma 18-35mm F1.8 DC HSM Lens (Black)
review_body:
The fastest zoom lens ever made, Canon and Nikon owners have had access for a while. As of July 2014, Pentax shooters can get one, too - which I did. And I am very, very happy about it. This lens will be on my camera probably 80% of the time.

First, the bad news:
1) It's heavy, and mounted to my K-3, it's a beastly combo. I'll live with it.
2) I wish they could have engineered this quality into an 18-50 or thereabouts. (This is probably impossible...but then, this lens seems impossible.) Usually I can just get a little closer to the subject if needed, so it's not such a hardship.
3) It is prone to lens flare, so shots that include a bright sun can be challenging. This one is a bit irritating, but I have another lens I can use in such situations if need be. And after all, most of my work doesn't feature a mid-day sun.
Because of these things, if I could grade it 4.5 instead of 5, I'd do that. But it's too good to rate a 4.

Beyond that, all news is good! The image clarity from this lens is superb - near perfect at center, and very good even at the edges and corners. What's more, that statement holds true across the focal range, and at any aperture, even wide open. Beautifully crisp at 35mm, it's even better at 18 and, as you might expect, best around the middle of its range.

Construction is very solid with both the focus and zoom rings moving smoothly and holding position once set. Autofocus can be fine-tuned manually without switching to manual mode, and the lens length never changes. (Focus and zoom actions happen entirely inside.) Nor does the outer ring rotate, making polarized filters easy to use.

Vignetting and CA's are modest, and stopping down slightly will all but eliminate them. Barrel distortion and pincushion are to be expected with any zoom, but it's controlled and I'm sure a Pentax corrective profile will soon be available for Lightroom 5 users. (It's already there for Canon and Nikon versions.)

While no lens is perfect, this one comes closer than any zoom I know of, and it's on par with the best primes in this focal range, making them redundant. Portraits, landscapes, street shooting - this is a versatile, very high quality lens.

Sigma has come a long way in this business, and they've now asserted themselves as innovation and quality leaders. Yet somehow, they still price like a "value" player. I love this lens and I'm becoming a big Sigma fan, too.
