product_title: Fotodiox EZ-Pro Octagon Softbox 60" with Speedring for Alien Bees Strobe Light B400, B800, B1600
review_body:
I haven't tried many octaboxes before. I come from a filmmaking background, so we use Chimeras all the time, but I can't compare it to Elinchrom or any other brand.

I bought the non-EZ pro 60" octabox first, and hated it. It felt really cheap, especially the Balcar adapter. It took 20 minutes to setup and another 15 minutes to tear down. And I hated having those rods all loose in the bag. Then I bought the EZ pro version. It's vastly better. It's built like a Rifa light or any other octabox that opens like an umbrella. After the first time putting on the inner and outer baffles, setup time is about one minute. You open it like an umbrella (but backwards) and the diffusion and rods are already attached from the last time. Give it another minute to put the eggcrate on and you're ready. Especially for location work, this unit is great to be ready in 2 minutes.

The quality feels solid. The Balcar adapter and speedring feel solid as well. It fits on my Einstein nicely, but I'm thinking about getting the Kasey adapter to lessen the strain on my Einstein (the octabox can give heavy). The eggcrate is nice, not the best or the worst, but it's an eggcrate. It doesn't feel like it'll just rip. All in all, I'm very happy with it. It comes with a bag and a plastic plate to kill the direct light. The plate is cheap but it's job is merely to block the most direct light from your source. Others have complained that it only attaches by sliding on the umbrella rod and it just stays there, without screwing it or attaching it further. Who cares? It stays put.

I don't see the need to spend 500$ or more on an octobox. You want a large soft source that won't break down on you, and isn't expensive, and I think I found it. I've had it for 2 months and it's been great.

review_headline: Batteries do not fit into the charger
review_body:
After receiving this I tried to charge up the batteries only to find that they do not fit into this charger. The batteries are slightly too long to snap into the charger. I ended up damaging one of the batteries by pushing it too hard trying to make it fit. The problem is the same if I try to fit the original Olympus battery that came with my camera into the charger. The charger is not made for the LI-42B battery.

Upon closer inspection, there is an etched notice on the charger that states:
Fits Oly
LI-40B/30B
Fits NIK
ENEL 10
Fits KOD
K7006

I would not advise purchasing this. It is being sold as a mismatched package. The batteries that came with it are LI-42B. I do not know if the listed Nikon batteries will fit in the charger either, as the batteries that came with this are marked "For Olympus Li-42B, Nikon EN-EL 10." If these are the actual size of the Nikon battery, then be aware that they do not fit in the charger either.

They are also marked as Nikon EN-EL10, so if you are intending to charge this size Nikon battery in the charger, be advised that it will not fit even though it is listed on the charger.

review_body: This thing is pretty awesome!  You might think that you could just use a wipe and some cleaner to get the same results, but this is pretty effective and more convenient. This removes them in a snap, with no cleaner needed (and no residue or wipe marks). The pad tip is small like a fingertip, so it can clean right to the edges of the lens glass no problem.  The retractable brush is very handy for flicking off dust, hairs, fur, or whatever other junk inevitably ends up on your lenses.  The pen shape makes it easy to store, and long enough to easily reach into lenses with a hood.  One of the best things about this is that it is made by Nikon, so I don't have to worry about it damaging the optical coatings on my lenses, which is always something I worry about with liquid cleaners.

1/13/14 - UPDATE:
Just received my new frame that nixplay replaced with absolutely no hassle (in fact, they insisted that they send me a new one to replace the defective one even after I turned down their offer to do so), and it is functioning perfectly. It was so easy to set up and get started that something had to be wrong with the first one received. Set up took less than 5 minutes and wasn't complicated in the least. I was able to switch around the pictures that I loaded onto it very easily so until the software is updated with a shuffle feature my pictures are being played out of chronological order which is what I was looking for. We have it on a shelf in the kitchen and everyone who comes over loves it.
I mentioned in my previous review that a touch screen would be good, but now that the frame is working correctly, a touch screen really isn't necessary. It's actually quite nice not to have fingerprints all over it.
All in all, I'm completely satisfied with the nixplay frame. I would recommend it to anyone and am looking forward to the software update where I can load my phone pictures directly on to it. You can't go wrong with trying out the nixplay frame. If you have any problems, customer service doesn't get any better than than at that company. review_body: My kit just arrived about an hour ago so I haven't had much time with it. My review is based off of what immediately stands out to me. First off, the kit is very well packaged. Everything arrived with zero damage. It doesn't come with instructions, but they aren't really needed. Set up is pretty straight forward. From unpacking everything to setup probably takes about 10 minutes at the longest. The stands are light weight, but more than strong enough for the lights and umbrellas. The cords could be a bit longer, but an extension chord is an easy solution to this. The umbrellas are much smaller than what I'm used to working with, and they do feel a bit fragile. I imagine the less you handle them, the less chance you have of damaging them. The bulbs are the biggest let down of the entire kit. As other have stated, these are only 45W bulbs. They are not very bright at all. I have seen a couple of reviews on YouTube where the reviewer has complained about the lights being too dim, but they had the umbrellas facing the wrong way. Turning the umbrellas in the correct direction will provide a good amount more light, but they are still not very bright. I did some test shots with my Canon 5D and a Rokinon 35mm f1.4 as well as a Rokinon 85mm f1.4. I was able to shoot at ISO 100-200 at f1.4 and ISO 200-400 at f2.8. I had to have the umbrellas extremely close to my subject in order to get enough light. The light is a bit blueish as others have noted, but that is easily fixed with a custom white balance set in camera or in post. with the 35mm I was able to keep my shutter speed around 1/40th sec at ISO 100-200. With the 85mm I had to bump the ISO up to about 400 in order to get a fast enough shutter speed.I knew the issue with the lights being dim before I purchased the kit, but it would still be nice if the seller would put the correct wattage in the title of the item. I'll definitely be upgrading the bulbs asap, but for the price of the kit, I cant complain.

product_title: ImogenStudio QCP-A100 +Cam Video Security Accessory for Smartphones (White)
review_headline: Good budget-friendly camera, but the app is slightly annoying.
review_body: Update: The app has updated and now I have zero complaints about this camera.   I bought this camera to use as a baby monitor, because cameras marketed as such are several hundred dollars. $49 was way more in the range of what I wanted to spend. The way the camera works is by connecting to your wi-fi, and the camera is monitored via their iSecurity+ app. I have no complaints about the camera. I was able to set it up in just a few minutes with no issues. It was fairly self-explanatory. The picture is nice and full color. It has a night mode which also works well and allows us to see our baby without going into his room and disturbing him. I was able to mount it to the wall pretty easily and get a good viewing angle.  Now, the app (which I think you NEED to use the camera) is pretty irritating at times:  1) The camera stream times out after 5 minutes, even when I'm on Wi-Fi. I wish it would let me run the camera as long as I wish to, or set up different rules for 4g/wifi so that I can customize how long the camera streams before timing out.  2) After a camera time out, I cannot reload the camera. I have to close out the app, log back in, and reload it (which takes a lot of extra time).  3) A camera can only be synced with one account. For my husband to have access to viewing the camera I had to set him up as a "friend" and give him viewing permissions. It'd be nice if a camera could be linked to several people in the same household, though I can see that this could pose security risks so I can live with this one. At least we have the option to allow him to view via a friend account.  Overall, I would say this camera was worth the money because it was really affordable and it meets our needs. It's nice to be able to pull up the camera on our smartphones instead of having to keep up with a separate monitor. review_body:
Unfortunately, I don't have any other strobes to compare this to; I don't set up my lights all that often (no room for a studio here), so when the power pack for my old Novatron strobes died, I never plunked down the cash to replace it. Instead I use this SPS920 and two remotely triggered Canon Speedlites.

When I first bought this unit (close to 10 years ago now), I quickly got frustrated with it because it was the first time I had ever had a light with built-in slave (automatically firing when it senses a flash burst from another flash). I was trying to trigger it with a Speedlite, and even though I could see the SPS920's flash burst in time with the Speedlite, it always seemed out of sync -- the light from the Speedlite could be seen in the resulting frame but the SPS920 would actually fire a fraction of a second *before* the shutter tripped. Rookie mistake. Turned out to be the pre-flash that most camera systems use to determine TTL flash exposure was triggering the SPS920's burst before the main flash.

So, you'll have to have your flashes in manual mode if you're going to trigger the SPS920 remotely. I've seen some units out there that have pre-flash sensing capabilities that will allow them to ignore the pre-flash and fire at the correct time. However, I've never used one so I can't compare them to this model. Since 1) TTL flash metering would likely be wrong anyway since this strobe is not accounted for in the exposure calculations, and 2) my radio triggers don't support TTL metering anyway, it's safe to say that I'm not missing anything by switching to manual mode on my Speedlites.

I've looked around for similar strobes, especially nice cheap ones that I can play with and are still small enough to be somewhat portable (at least, more so than the Novatron set). There are much cheaper ones out there, of course, but the consistent pattern among those cheaper models is a combination of poor build quality (according to the reviews) and low power (on the rare occasion when a guide number is specified, it tends to be no higher than around 30, compared to this unit's GN of 92).

product_title: Nixplay 8 inch Wi-Fi Cloud Digital Photo Frame. iPhone & Android App, Email, Facebook, Dropbox, Instagram, Flickr & Picasa - W08A
review_body:
Like most people, I bought this frame for my mom so that we could send her pictures of what we were doing and they would magically appear in the frame. My kid is about to go off to Americorps and we will be travelling this summer so it seemed like a great idea. Bottom line is, it is, but right now it takes a little work. Two things up front, first the holy grail, where you can just email a picture to a web address and it just appears in the frame doesn't work...yet. Theoretically this will come next month (Feb) but the implementation date has apparently been pushed a couple times already so don't set your watch. Second, the web site is really picky about web browser and machine types. I use Linux (Ubuntu) and have a chromebook. Even though both have chrome -- the allegedly preferred browser and have the most recent versions -- the web site wouldn't go through the set up process with either of them. I ultimately had to start windows in a VM to get through the set up. After setup, it still complains when I try to use a browser in Linux but it lets me use it. What's so special about MS chrome I don't know.

Ok, once you get a browser that works and do the setup (the setup is pretty easy and mostly consists of pairing the frame to the account you created on the web site) you can start using the frame. Basically you can sync the frame web site with Facebook, Picasa and instagram. That gets pictures on the web site, but you still must manually add things to the frames slideshow to get them to appear in the frame.

Here is the work around we use to get pictures in the frame for my mom so that she doesn't have to mess with it:
1) we set up a picasa account for her (she already has a gmail account so we just used that)
2) we modified the picasa account so we could email pictures to it (you have to go to picasaweb to do this. Right now it forwards you to google plus photos, so you have click the link at the top to go back to picasaweb. Click settings and then scroll down to where it says "upload photos from email." Click that and it will ask you for a password, and then give you a long email address. This address can now be used to email pictures to picasa which will now be accessible by the frame.
3) go to the nixplay web site, log in, and click the picasa link. Pictures emailed to picasa show up in an album called "Dropbox" drag these picture to the slide show.
4) The frame will now display the new pictures (and the old ones) from the slide show.

Once you've done the set up, its essentially a two step process. Email to picassa -- add to slide show. But ultimately that's pretty simple and you can add slides to the frame at will from anywhere. And that, after all, is the whole point. Hopefully when the get the email feature working it will get down to a one step process. For now I have given it four stars because 1) the picky browser problem 2) the poor documentation (come on nixpix create a youtube video that shows how to do this for the non-techy people that these will ultimately be given to) 3) the somewhat complicated process of getting pictures on it.

But for now, as long as you know what your getting into its pretty cool. We are thinking of buying another one for us because once you set it up, the pictures are fun and the screen is pretty and the pictures look great.

review_headline: Better than OEM? Better believe it!
review_body:
Wasabi kit (US Version) VS: Smatree kit (biggest rival) kit & OEM Accessories
Good:
--> Battery Rated Capacity - Wasabi Batteries 1280mAh rated higher than 1200mAh rival brands & 1050mAh OEM
--> Battery Performance - Batteries SIGNIFICANTLY outperform OEM & rival brands in Rec time test (see below)
--> Battery Weight - Wasabi batteries weighted same as OEM 23g each, Rival brands 25g each
--> Battery Core - Li-Poly meets OEM specs and is better than rivals that use Li-Ion
--> AC Adaptor - Compact travel AC adaptor w/ fold up prongs smaller than rival & OEM offerings
--> AC Adaptor - Outputs 3.1A instead 2.1A of rival brand and 2.0A of OEM
--> AC Adaptor - No Bright LED unlike rival AC Adaptor (OEM has no LED)
--> DC Adaptor - 3.1A output matched rival and beats OEM (2.0A)
--> Build Quality - Wasabi matte finish and build quality on par with OEM and better than Smatree's mixture of matte and glossy
Bad:
--> Battery Physical Size - Wasabi Batteries were a noticeably tighter fit in GoPro3 camera
--> AC Adaptor - THIS Wasabi kit only offer US plug (international version is now available), Rival brand offers US & EU Plug compatibility, OEM offers US,UK,EU,& AU
--> DC Adaptor - Wasabi unit is largest physical size unit compared to rival or OEM (smallest)

Most would agree mAh ratings from aftermarket batteries are rarely accurate. Even if rated lower, OEM batteries typically slightly outlast aftermarket products. Coming into the comparison test that is exactly what I expected to find. I was VERY pleasantly surprised to find the Wasabi 21% higher mAh rating over OEM to be fairly accurate. My recording time test yielded 25% longer record time over OEM and 35% longer than the rival Smatree batteries*. I also noticed the Wasabi batteries appeared to retain stored power longer than it's rival, but were comparable to the OEM battery. I believe the primary differences in battery performance between Smatree and Wasabi can be credited to Wasabi using a Lithium-Polymer core, exactly the same as the OEM. Smatree battery is the only one of the three that used a Li-Ion core. The only complaint was that the Wasabi battery had a very snug fit inside the camera. I am unable to test the long -term size variation in the product (since it's new) to see if the batteries will increase/decrease with use, but I expect it to be very minimal due to the use of a Li-Poly core.

Timed Battery Performance*:
OEM 1050mAh - 69:55
Smatree 1200mAh - 64:33
Wasabi 1280mAh - 87:26

*Recording time settings: GoPro3 w/ latest Firmware, Sandisk 32GB CL10, Video mode @ 1080/60fps, NO Wi-Fi, 2 Led flash, Indoors, avg room temp 65F; Batteries used: brand new Wasabi 1280mAh 4.7Wh Li-Poly, brand new Smatree 1200mAh 4.4Wh Li-Ion, 1 month old (charged twice) GoPro OEM 1050mAh 3.885Wh Li-Poly

The OEM and comparable Smatree kits include AC adaptors that feature international outlet support. Perhaps convenient, I don't see this as a huge advantage due to accessibility of USB ports globally. The inclusion of a DC port adds another in-car charging option internationally as well. The Smatree and OEM AC adaptors are physically 50%+ larger than the Wasabi's AC Adaptor that featured foldable prongs. More importantly the Wasabi features 3.1A total output and the other only offer 2.1A and 2.0A. The increased amperage output is a huge advantage in using the AC adaptor to charge large item (tablet) and 2 batteries at once. Something that might be an annoyance to some is that the Smatree AC adaptor feature a VERY light blue LED, while the Wasabi and OEM offerings do not. NOTE: Wasabi is now offering a Worldwide Kit with a AC charger similar to the Smatree kit but with 3.1A and more plug adaptors.

The DC adaptors offered by all 3 kits feature 2 ports and 2.0A (OEM) or 3.1A (Smatree/Wasabi). All disappointingly don't offer replaceable fuses. The Wasabi physical size is the largest of the three, but is only slightly larger. The Wasabi is the only one of the three to feature an LED. The Smatree charger was labeled with a part number YXT-SC029, but that only appears to reference its generic nature.

The Wasabi and Smatree have charging bases and USB cords that are nearly 100% identical, and worked similarly. GoPro's dual charger positions the batteries horizontal instead of vertical. All feature charging LEDS that change color to indicate charging or not charging.
GoPro still appears to be the leader in build quality, but the entire Wasabi kit still feels very much above average. The Wasabi DC charger might have been the largest but it's no-seam exterior construction seemed to be better design than the other 2.

MY VERDICT: The impressive Wasabi batteries and quality AC & DC adaptor makes this kit a MUST buy for any GoPro user working with a budget and needing longer battery performance. product_title: Olympus Floating Foam Strap (Yellow)
review_headline: Works Great with Olympus TG820, But Supplied Strap Not Exactly As Shown
review_body:
I was a bit confused about the various reviews mentioning that this is possibly a cheap knock-off and not an authentic Olympus product and/or wouldn't keep my camera afloat and/or was poorly made, but decided to rely on some of the positive reviews and I'm glad I did. This strap worked perfectly and appears genuine.

DESCRIPTION AND AUTHENTICITY:

The photo above shows a white Olympus logo on the black portion of the strap and mine did not come that way. There are no corporate logos or any other writings anywhere on the strap. However it did come in Olympus packaging that appeared to be authentic, with the Olympus logo prominently displayed on the top cardboard portion of the package that was stapled to the clear plastic bag holding the strap. Otherwise, it appeared exactly as the yellow one in the photo, which is exactly what I was hoping to get.

The body of the strap features 5 linked foam pad segments, all covered in a nylon Cordura-like fabric. There is a spring-activated cinch on the cord portion of the strap that can tighten or loosen the strap around one's arm and there is a detachable loop that one frees from the main strap and can then loop through the strap eyelet on the camera the same as any camera strap.

Olympus makes quality products and this appeared to be an Olympus product; if it's not, it's a high enough quality fake that one would have to question why a company that could do this quality of item wouldn't counterfeit something much more expensive instead.

FLOAT CAPACITY:

I was a bit nervous about using this after reading some older reviews complaining that it would not keep their older (and presumably larger and heavier) waterproof cameras afloat, so I did the sensible thing - I tested it out in a 2' deep hot tub. It easily kept my Olympus Tough TG820 waterproof camera afloat and, in fact, at least the top half of the strap was floating out of the water - if you look at the photos for the strap, it is separated into 5 segments and the center three segments were out of the water, with the camera apparently held afloat just by the two outer foam segments. My TG820 is an all-metal bodied camera that feels quite heavy, approximately double the weight of other point-and-shoot cameras (according to the product details here on Amazon, the TG820 weighs 7.2 oz.). I tested it out in fairly calm ocean waters and it very easily and visibly kept the camera afloat, with the bright yellow strap easy to see. It did its job perfectly well.

FIT AND FUNCTION:

I'm an average size guy with slightly smaller than average wrists and this strap fit me fine. I suppose I would have liked the ability to tighten it all the way snug around my wrist, which I could not do, leaving a gap that was wide enough that I might have been able to sneak my hand out of if I stretched out my fingers and wrist as thin as I could. However, in real life, no one tries to minimize the size of their hand and wrist unless trying to escape from handcuffs and with a normally held hand, I am confident that this strap will not accidentally slide off any man's wrists and probably no women's wrists, either. I used this strap both boogie boarding and snorkeling and had no problems with it in either use.

Another review mentioned a desire for a second, everyday non-floating strap to go with the loop portion that attaches to the camera, but I don't think that's necessary. The loop is pretty thin (but I'm sure it's still probably the equivalent of 100lb test woven fishing line) and will easily slide into the strap eyelet of most cameras without removing the camera's original, non-floating strap. So I just left my original thin cord strap on the camera for use away from water and merely detached the big floating portion of this strap when I wasn't using it in water. The small portion of the end of this strap with clip and loop did not get in the way at all whenusing the camera's original cord strap.

DURABILITY:

As mentioned above, the fabric covering the floating portion of the strap appears plenty durable for many years of use. The snap that holds the floating portion on to the loop portion is made of thick, strong plastic and it requires quite a squeeze on the tabs on either side of the clip to disengage the plastic tabs to separate the floating portion from the thin loop attached to the camera. There is no conceivable way I can imagine that this could come lose accidentally if the tabs are properly and fully seated, with a click, into the snap. In fact, my 8-year old was not able to depress the tabs to separate the two parts of the float, and I had to do it. It's not more effort than the average adult can manage, but it's enough to fasten it very securely.

At least one other reviewer complained that the snap broke and he/she lost the attached camera in the ocean. I do not believe that is attributable to the design of the strap and the strap's snap attachment. I would say that the much more likely explanation would be a) that person did not have the tabs fully clicked in and partially snapped, the snap came undone; b) with any plastics, defects in the materials occasionally can happen (maybe from an air bubble or some contaminant fell into the liquid plastic during the molding process) and that reviewer's camera had the bad luck to have such a rare defect on the snap of his/her strap; and/or c) plastic can weaken with time and exposure to salt water or sunlight and maybe after several years of being in the sun or the owner not rinsing it with fresh water after use in the ocean, the plastic deteriorated and weakened. In any event, testing the integrity of the snap attachment with a few tugs before each use should avoid any unintended detachment of the camera.

CONCLUSION:

This strap was well-made, it functions very well and securely, it is very visible if it should ever accidentally slip off my wrist or away from my hands, and at around ten bucks, the price is right. This simply works well and I recommend it.

product_title: Nikon Df Digital SLR
review_body:
I was trained using a film camera, but never used one professionally. I owned a N70 and rarely used it. I got the D100, then the D200 and later the D300 and loved them all when they were released. All the "D" cameras were used professionally. I also have the 14-24mm 2.8, 24-70mm 2.8 and 70-200mm 2.8. The Df is my first FX camera. I don't care about the retro look, on board flash (cause I use the SB-900 if I need one), video, or the 1/8000 really - it would be nice to have that, but it's not a deal breaker at all. I like that the images are 16MB. I can produce large prints and manage the files easier.

I found the body to be a little challenging on my hands (I have large hands) being that the camera is so small compared to the D300 with the vertical grip. It's clearly not like the D300 which has great ergonomics for my hands. However - I can't stop picking up the camera and shooting with it. I hadn't EVER had a feeling like this before. Because of its small size and light weight I want to bring it around with me everywhere. It's true, this camera will slow you down. It'll make you think about your shot a bit more and that is a really good thing. I was teaching someone about how to use their new Nikon 5300 and he was shooting manual and moving like a bandit. So fast and furious. He was missing what he was doing wrong. This camera forces you a lot more to look at what settings you've got and go from there.

It is a beautiful camera and I LIKE the dials. I can turn a lot of them with the lock with one hand. You just need to spend time with it to figure how best to work with it. Seriously, the dials are awesome and they really are an option if you don't care to use them.

Here's what I wish it had: a low light emitter. My camera focuses great in low light! I'm not sure what other people are complaining about, but my camera is fantastic in low light. The option to have the low light emitter would be nice. I wish it had a better grip. I wish it had a second card slot. That's it.

I also got the special 50mm 1.8. My lens is AWESOME. I have a great copy. Super sharp wide open. If you have this lens and it is soft, return it, but I'm glad I have it. In fact I'm planning of getting more primes!

The battery is better than the D300. Really nice!

Cost - yes compared to other models, its expensive and you're not getting all the features, but here's the deal - you are getting the D4 sensor! That alone is amazing! You really have no idea how awesome this camera is until you have it for a while and shot with it. The price is right. Yes, I wish it had some things included in it, but I'm not returning this baby because of it. I love it.

The TOOL produces AMAZING images and encourages me to use it! Low light capabilities will change the way you shoot.

product_title: Pixel Pro Digital Camera 100M Wireless Shutter Remote Control Release for Canon EOS 1D 1Ds Mark II III IV 5D Mark II 7D 50D 40D 30D 20D 10D
review_body:
If you are hoping for a wireless remote to do HDR bracketting (-2,0,+2 stops) this really isn't it. With the wired release you just press and hold the trigger button. The camera goes through the bracket as quickly as possible and stops even if you are still pressing the trigger. There is no way to do the same with this remote. There seems to be no equivalent to sending a constant trigger signal to the camera. "Continuous" shooting just keeps going. It doesn't stop at the end of the bracket. Firing single shots is too easy to miscount, especially if exposures are long, and too slow.

It seems no wireless trigger short of a Promote or possibly some hybrid arrangement with an Android phone and a wireless adapter (on Canon DSLRs) will be a working alternative. I will also exploring Magic Lantern firmware with may provide the solution.

For non-bracketted shooting this remote seems to work like a charm, however.

review_body:

The carrying handle on the side has proved to be far more useful than I expected when moving from one set-up to another. I was especially thrilled to find that the center column has a tightening nut which allowed me to securely use the tripod even when the legs weren't fully spread. This can provide a little more height and allow you to work within a smaller footprint when needed.

While this is a light-weight, entry level tripod I've been successfully using it on professional shoots and have been impressed. It lacks the smooth, precision adjustment control provided in high-end models, but at this price and low weight, it's an amazing tool. I've even used it to hold my Canon 5D Mark II with 70-200mm zoom lens. That's a lot of weight for this little tripod, but it holds it and I feel safe entrusting it with my gear.

product_title: Neewer 14.37 inch Photography Camera Camcorder Uni-Directional System Condenser Shotgun Interview MIC Microphone for Canon Nikon Sony Olympus Pentax Panasonic and Other HDSLRs DV Camcoders
review_headline: Incrdible!  Better than the videos!  Truly incredible!
review_body: Let me start off by saying that I was a little skeptical.  People were comparing this to the to the Azden SGM-1X, which costs almost six times more ($170 - recommended by many low budget filmmakers).  That was a bit of a red flag to me.  Nevertheless, it had plenty of good reviews and I'm planning a big short film shoot in a couple of months, so I decided to buy this and test it out, with the intention of using it to capture audio on said shoot.  It arrived in a plastic bag, and the box (which bore NO branding, save for a sticker that said \\"Neewer 14.37 Mic\\") was pretty beat up.  The \\"Box\\" was actually just a cardboard sleave holding the plastic case.  Please note that I use the terms \\"case\\" and \\"plastic\\" loosely.  The 'case' is made of a cheap material that feels like the kind used in cheap binders - like a cardboard covered in a thin layer of plastic.  Oh, and good luck getting everything back in it once you take it out...    Well, I took it out and found the following components:    -The 14.37\\" microphone body  -The foam windscreen  -2 mic clips; one for tripods/hotshoes, and one for mic stands  -A 15' XLR to 6.3 mm mono phone-style plug  -6.3 mm mono phone-plug to 3.5 mm mono \\"headphone style\\" plug  -Cheap case with foam inserts and other misc. packing materials    Now, I quickly grabbed the mic, cable, and adapter and then plugged it into my computer.  My first tests in a small room were fantastic!  There was a lot of reverb, but it was mainly the fault of the room, not the mic.  So I took it out to a much larger, much more chaotic room.  I decided to test both modes (There are three modes - off, normal, and tele.  Off is off, normal is a wide pickup area, much like a dynamic/stick/handheld mic, while tele is for longer range recording, picking up mainly what is right in line with it.)  Normal mode sounds quite good, and it has a pretty wide pickup pattern.  This is good for putting on a desktop, recording foley, or doing voiceovers.  The tele mode makes it much more directional.  While this does introduce a little more noise, it's really not bad, especially if you record it loud, such as on a dedicated recorder.  Back to the sound quality, this is at least ten times better than an on board mic, and significantly better than a dynamic/handheld or cheap skype mic.  I had looked up a lot of videos online of this and its twin brother - HTDZ 14.37 inch mic from China (You can find it on Ebay, but it's no cheaper and it comes straight from China with slow shipping - I recommend buying on Amazon from an American seller, that way you can return it if you should get a defective one).  I was VERY surprised that the mic I got was better than the videos!  It captured even relatively quiet, distant sound well, and with a little noise filtering, audio from across the room was usable - very impressive (You ALWAYS want to capture audio as close to the subject as possible - usually within three feet at most.)!    Here's a tip: if you don't have a dedicated recorder, but do have a laptop, you can use your mic-in port and some free audio recording software (like audacity) to record dual system sound (Recording audio and video to different devices - be sure to still record audio with your camera so that you can sync it up in post!).  You could also use a smartphone if it has a dedicated mic in port, or if you buy and adapter for your mic.    There are a couple of issues, but they are pretty minor.  Firstly - power.  This mic requires a AA battery.  It can use phantom power, but it generates an annoying clicking sound.  It works perfectly on batteries, which are supposed to last about 27 hours.  That is incorrect.  I'd say it lasts about 16-20 reliably, since it starts to generate some weird static when the battery is nearly dead.  I'd definitely keep a few batteries on hand while filming.  (Oh, and make sure to turn it off!  It can be rather hard to remember!)  And secondly - component quality.  The box is super cheap.  Absolute junk.  Planto replace it as soon as possible.  Also, the windscreen is not very good.  It's better than nothing, I guess, but that's another thing I'll want to upgrade as soon as possible.    As for the audio quality, I wouldn't say that it's on par with an SGM-1X, at least from what I have heard of both.  I would, however, recommend this mic to anyone who is looking for an upgrade from the built in one on their camera (and it WILL make a huge difference in the quality of your production - especially if you have a lot of dialogue)  Given that it's only $30, I whole-heartedly recommend it.  This should be in every filmmaker's toolbag, no matter what the budget!    Note: I bought mine from BestDealUSA - it shipped fairly quickly and was as advertised, if a bit beat up from shipping in only a plastic bag.    EDIT: 2/23/14  A couple of days ago I took the mic into the field for the first time.  It performed well, with just one slight issue.  The 6.8 (or whatever) mm (1/4\\" 'telephone' plug) to 3.5 mm (1/8\\" 'mini jack,' the kind found on headphones and computer sound cards) adapter proved problematic.  First, it did not want to stay in the camcorder and was quite loose.  Secondly (possible tied to the first one), there were some issues with the sound quality.  It would put out interference, static, or not register as an external mic on the camera.  Wiggling the plug fixed this, but it was tiresome and frusterating.  I went to Radio Shack and boutht a new one (I regret buying there!  It was very overpriced!  Buy on Amazon and save some money!) and it works perfectly.  The audio quality remains fantastic, though you still have to be careful about moving it too fast without a better windscreen.  All in all, still a 5 star product, even with the nuisance of the adapter. (I had been planning to replace it anyway!)    EDIT: 10/23/14  So after upgrading to a new desktop I've encountered a few issue with the mic.  Firstly, there is an odd \\"pop\\" sound every once in a while when recording tothe PC with the included cable.  Changing out the cable fixed this problem.  I should note that I've been pretty rough with the cable, and that I believe this issue is compounded by the weak mic port (it works fine with the original cable on an actual camera with a mic in port).  I'm not deducting points since this isn't a huge issue and it appears to be an isolated incident (only on new PC), but it is something to be aware of.

product_title: Celestron 21024-A FirstScope Telescope with Accessory Kit
review_body:
I purchased this with the kit because it was very cheap and seemed like a good way to try out astronomy to see if it would be something I was passionate about or just dabbling in. Having no training or experience I feel like this was a great starter scope (it's basically point and shoot) aside from one MAJOR issue which is that the eyepiece is in the top center of the tube.

That doesn't seem like a big deal and maybe if I was shorter or younger or had a smaller chest size it would have been OK (I'm a plump 5'5" lady) however for me trying to hunch over the top of the eyepiece to see anything was crippling. After spending a few hours viewing I would have severe pain in between my shoulder blades for 2-3 days. I couldn't find a table tall enough to put this at eye level and because the eyepiece is in such an awkward spot I couldn't sit down and look through it like I would have been able to do if the eyepiece was on the side. I went to the Cloudy Nights telescope forums and some people made suggestions for modifications that may help but that was a little more that I was willing to do. That is a good place to go as a beginner though because they are knowledgeable and helpful.

Even with such painful results I still found myself using this often and the sense of wonder I felt from star watching prompted me to upgrade to the Celestron 127EQ PowerSeeker Telescope which is much more powerful, complicated and very adjustable. I will say that the software that came with this was helpful in familiarizing myself with the sky and preparing for viewing time. The eyepieces are cheap but sufficient and I spent a lot of time using the moon filter and learning by viewing the moon. I did buy a Barlow lens that gave me some more detail even with the plastic eyepieces provided. review_headline: Follow as instructed and it does wonders.
review_body:

- connected the ion Air pro camera to PC to check for updated firmware and charged up to ensure I had enough juice

- Go to Remote tab and you can now see what the camera sees (I did notice live view tend to freeze during recording but hey you need to turn off WiFi PODZ (on the camera) unit once you know it has connection is there so you don't drain the battery.
- After taking picture, you can use your app to view the videos or send to social media.
Also the battery Booster is not really a booster but a charger. you have to take the cover off and connect the booster to camera using USB and it will charge the battery enough for another 2 hours. or you can use it to recharge your Phone. (you will need separate connection for that) so on the go this battery pack (1500 mAH) is ample enough to charge the camera as well as you phones. So far overall operation is good and happy. Lets see how long this will keep up.
By the way I have Galaxy S2 for android device and my kid has iPhone 5S and we both waere able to use our app to check on iON camera view and view the files over the phone.

product_title: Canon EOS Rebel T5i 18.0 MP CMOS Digital Camera with 3-inch Touchscreen and Full HD Movie Mode
review_headline: Ah, finally back in a Canon EOS
review_body:
I had long used Canon DSLRs, but over a year ago, I decided to switch to a mirrorless (Sony NEX-5n) camera as a way to go lighter and supposedly get just as good results. In reality, that's only sometimes the case. I found myself struggling with really limited lens selection (and none of them were great), terrible solutions for external flashes (holy hell Sony), and decent pictures when those two things weren't affecting it.

After the last round of Christmas program photos, and our Christmas family photo, I had enough and decided to come back to a full DSLR. I've read a lot of reviews, compared specs, etc. Seems like all the DSLRs at this level/price have their own pro/cons, but most are good cameras. Some of the things that drew me back to Canon were the following:

Historically good APS-C sensor, now with DIGIC 5 processing
Decent kit lens that will keep you going until you save for some L glass. (Of course, you should always have a nifty 50 lens as well).
Nice touchscreen interface (I didn't think I'd care, but starting to like it)
Nice HD video recording
Silent focusing in video with new STM lenses (No more hearing focusing noises in the audio)
Access to large lens selection
Access to large flash selection

While I haven't had this new body very long, i have been using it a lot, and am really pleased with the decision to stay with Canon here. Photos look great, and I find it easier to get the result I am after. My wife instantly noticed the quality change of some of the kid photos, etc. Tethered shooting works great with the included Canon software. The 18MP photos are plenty of resolution to produce large prints. High ISO shooting up to 3200 looks great, noise becomes more noticeable when you crank past that point.

The focusing system seems to work much better than my old 20D. It's an all around good package.

The only thing I wish it had was wifi integration for remote control from a smartphone/tablet/computer. Other models are beginning to integrate such features, I think Canon should have gone this way.

Additionally, from what i've read, there doesn't seem to be much here over the T4i. If you have that and like it, I can't imagine why you'd be interested in this one. For the rest of us with older models, it's a great upgrade.ontrol from a smartphone/tablet/computer. Other models are beginning to integrate such features, I think Canon should have gone this way.

Additionally, from what i've read, there doesn't seem to be much here over the T4i. If you have that and like it, I can't imagine why you'd be interested in this one. For the rest of us with older models, it's a great upgrade.

A few in flickr apparently have had the same issue. As these have been out for only a couple of months, I am thinking it's probably a firmware issue, but  unacceptable for a ~$1500 package body only. I have the M.Zuiko 75mm f1.8 on order as well and all together has now dented me about three grand - now I am not sure if I made the right decision picking this one.    Wanting to take advantage of the return period and to rule out a lemon, I've initiated a replacement with Amazon (They've been great BTW helping me out on this one) hoping the next one won't fail me as I am now too attached to this camera to let it go.    Hopefully this is just a firmware issue and they will do something to fix it. Planning to call Olympus to make them aware of this issue as well.    I'll update back when I get the new one and get to send time with it.    *****Update - 01/08/2015*****  Apologies for lying quiet after my earlier thoughts a year ago. Amazon customer service was amazing in that a brand new replacement was already on its way before even I shipped out the faulty one. No issues since then and what a delight this camera has been!    I've tried to improve my photographic skills just so I can learn to use this camera better and extract everything that it could offer. My Flickr can be found here.(Most pictures are SOOC except some of the seagull ones) - https://www.flickr.com/photos/23818914@N03/    Like:  1. Menu system. Once used to, very handy and don't have to take the eyes off of the view finder for most changes.   2. Tonal curve adjustment- Highlights can be darkened and shadows could be lightened or vice versa to get better Dynamic Range/Contrast respectively. Fn2 button could be used to do this or any other button could be reprogrammed to do the same.(Unsure if this is a common feature for this level of cameras, but just the fact that you could do this for JPEGs w/o any PP is good enough for me to list it here as I am using RAW only selectively)  3. Color creater could be accessed by pressing the Fn2 and OK button together. Very handy if you want to play with the mood of the picture.   4. Image quality. This is purely from a novice-amateur perspective. I've not used any of its competitors or DSLRs. So I am not comparing the image quality to anything- Just a very satisfying feeling looking at the picture and analyzing it.   5. Good build quality.  6. The 12-40mm build and image quality is great. Pictures are very sharp. (So is 75mm f1.8).  7. Can control the camera through WiFi over smartphone-handy for long exposures.     No Like:   1. Battery indicator not accurate. Have a spare one handy.  2. WiFi App doesn't allow to mass select pictures for importing.  3. Not good for Birds in Flight. Remember this is not coming from an expert, so don't take my word for it. But tracking moving objects seemed a challenge to me.     I don't think my words above are my final thoughts (in a good way) as I am still honing my skills and learning about Photography. I've hardly realized this camera's power, I think. So far so good. If you are like me, coming from a point and shoot and starting to be an amateur or a serious amateur, worth considering this camera.

review_headline: Worked well for about a year. Camera started failing just out of warranty, then completely died.
review_body:

They were both installed outside, and after paying Logitech the annual subscription for their Web Alert Commander service, I was able to setup email alerts and view the captured video segments online. The system worked fine and we were happy with the performance.

However, around September 2013, one of the cameras went inexplicably offline. The cameras are remote from where I live, so on the first opportunity to visit the installation, I attempted to get the offline camera back online. Eventually, through some combination of powering down the camera and pressing the hidden reset button, I was able to get the camera to start responding again; however, within a month, the camera dropped offline again.

On November 23 2013 I contacted Logitech support asking for either a remedy or a replacement (but knowing that this camera is out of its 1 year warranty). I will update this post with progress.

UPDATE: December 18 2013

Logitech made good on the warranty, replacing the unit even though it was outside the warranty plan. The replacement was received December 18.

UPDATE: May 18 2014

The replacement unit is still working well.

product_title: Sony HDR High Definition Handycam 8.9 MP Camcorder with 30x Optical Zoom, and 16 GB Embedded Memory (2012 Model)
review_headline: Better than the newer models and competitors alike.
review_body: This camera is one of the best "budget" cameras to record in all conditions. Consumer camcorders usually have lots of trouble in low light conditions for two reasons, the sensor (the chip that  helps the camera to record "light") is very expensive and simply because optics. When you see a high end camera those are necessarily bulky and very expensive. They are bulky because the optics (size of the lenses) they need to be big to capture more light. Second, The sensor is the single more expensive electronic component  in your camera the bigger  the sensor the better is the camera in low light conditions. This camera has a 1/3" sensor which is even bigger than the one in the 380 model  that supposed to be the next generation after the 260, it has almost the same amount of pixels, etc. I have tried several of these cameras from cheaper Sony (220 /190), JVC everios, Samsung, Panasonic none  of them at this price range compare to the 260 in terms of image quality. I do not care that much about the GPS thing or projectors. I want to watch my videos in a big screen and for me what matters is the quality of the image. If you want to go pro then you have to invest in a very expensive camera. there are two types of users for this kind of cameras. The ones that have control over their environment (such as the ones recording in their living room, your kids activities, etc) and the ones who do not have control at all (those filming church events, concerts, presentations, etc). For the ones who have control over their environment I advice to buy a cheap lightning set to over come any image degradation in low light. That can be made  from home depot working lights ($35 a kit). for the ones recording concerts try playing with your settings if that does not work then get a camera with a bigger sensor/lens if you have budget constraints get this Sony it does a great job for the price.

The binoculars include a few \\"extras\\" that are not necessary but certainly nice to have (shoulder harness to ease neck strain, black carrying case with detachable shoulder strap, lens caps with rain guards, and lens cloth).

Expect quality with these binoculars - You'll be hard pressed to ever use your \\"cheaper\\" binoculars after you view the world through these lenses. Oh well, you can pass the older binoculars down to the kids!

product_title: Nikon D3200 Digital SLR
review_headline: A Very Good Easy To Use Tool For Taking Very Good Pictures
review_body:
I have been an avid amateur photographer since I was young. For many years I used various 35mm cameras and one medium format one that take film. I took thousands of slides and pictures. When digital started with Sony floppy disk cameras I bought one. I used the digital cameras with my work in heavy machines. I graduated to more Sony digitals. I always had high end phones, and those started having better and better digital cameras. I never got rid of my favorite film cameras. These include a 1953 Voightlander Prominent, Olympus OM2n, Olympus XA, Olympus Stylus. I learned to edit pictures early on using Photoshop. I have used Picasa since introduced. I really like Picasa as it is OK for the thousands of pictures of machines I need to quickly edit and add to web sites. Recently I have started using iPhoto. iPhoto IMHO is much more capable than Picasa.

I stopped using film a few years back and have started back using film in the last two years. I started to try and get better pictures with my digital compact and phone cameras. Those work well with scenery pictures at a mid level of quality, but were hopeless taking pictures of pets or children or any action. When I saw the Olympus OMD in chrome I immediately wanted one of those. Looked my my 1980 Olympus OM2n which I have always thought was just about a perfect camera and beautiful. Mine works perfectly after 33 years BTW. So I did months of research on the OMD and then tried to see and hold one in person. There is only one Olympus dealer in San Diego and they kept selling out of them. Once I got to see a black OMD but no chrome. Then Oly started the on again off again sales. I was pressured by going on a long trip last summer so I wanted to get a new DSLR. This was complicated by the fact that Olympus is a smaller sensor format that not everyone likes. No actual live viewfinder. And it costs a lot more than Nikon 3200.

The other camera I considered extensively was the Sony Nex 6. In the past I had only bought Sony digitals and consider them a superior product. The Nex 6 was less money than the Olympus OMD. What turned me towards the Nikon was recommendations. On line recommenders like Nikons. The Sony early last summer had a limited selection of lenses like the ones I wanted. Olympus had want I wanted, but I never could hold one in my hands and it was twice the price of the Nikon 3200. I drove several times to the local camera store to see the Olympus, but no luck.

So I ordered the Nikon and two additional lens from Amazon. As usual Amazon delivered everything fast and in perfect condition. The Nikon has worked flawlessly from day 1. The 3200 is fairly easy to learn. The adjustments and controls take a little time to get used to but are relatively easy. It takes very good digital pictures without much effort. Those who just want to take pictures that are pretty good should just take the standard 18-55mm lens with image stabilization and leave it at that. It works fine for pictures blown up on my 27" computer monitor. The only annoying thing is that with a lens as slow as this one the built in flash is always popping up. Even in shots that don't need a flash. So I find myself setting the camera flash off frequently. I have not used the two additional lenses I bought much. The longer lens a few times for distant scenery. I thought I would use the much faster 35mm lens all the time. So far that is not the case. Before I bought it I did not notice that the 35mm lens did not have image stabilization. When I have used it that has not been an issue. I come from many cameras that did not have IS and always instinctively hold my breath and stay still when shooting.

The Nikon is much larger than my Olympus OM2. I would prefer the OM2 size. But I find the 3200 very comfortable in my hands. Yes it is big, but the size and weight works well. It is a plastic camera. It is well made but very plastic. Much more so than my last Sony compact camera. The Sony has a much more pleasing quality look to it. The comparison between the Voightlander or OM2 in quality appearance and feel is vast. In the distant past I owned a Nikon FM SLR and can attest that Nikon knows how to make a very high quality look and feel camera. The Nikon is not cheap plastic feeling, but rubberized sorta cheap plastic feeling. If you really like Apple products like Mac Books, iPhones, iPads you may not like this product. It is in no way a jewell like thing of beauty like Apple products.

But it takes very good pictures easily. It focuses fairly quickly and comes up with very good color balanced shots on automatic. It has a small view finder. Much much much smaller and less useful than my 33 year old Olympus. For me the viewfinder size and lack of light is the worst feature.

I have most of my film cameras on display in a glass cabinet in my office. The Voightlander is a thing of beauty. It still works well after 60 years. The last time it was cleaned and worked on was 1979. It is hard to use. Mostly because of it's small and dull view finder. Maybe some day I will buy a Leica M3 for the finder. The metal working and gorgeous glass lenses on the Voightlander put a smile on my face just holding it in my eye or hand. The Olympus OM2n is only slightly less so. The metal on the Oly is not as nice but the Olympus easy operation makes up for it. Both the Voightlander and the Olympus are about the same size. The Nikon 3200 as a tool to take pictures is a good camera. The shots I have taken with it at the highest settings on the sharpest (35mm) lens are very good. They are not as good as shots taken with my OM2 and it's 50mm lens with good film in color or detail. However, the Nikon is much easier to use and get good shots with. But I feel absolutely no passion for the 3200 and good photography demands passion.

review_body:

product_title: GoPro Camera CHDH-302HERO3+: Video Camera
review_headline: Has some cool new features, and some dumb new features.
review_body: The Hero3+ has a sleeker look than the more rugged looking Hero3. Both are great cameras, but as stated in other reviews there are some drawbacks. I recently did a shoot where both the Hero3 and Hero3+ were used. The coloring of the 3+ seemed much better and easier to work with when matching it with the DSLRS also used in the shoot. The Hero3+ has a noticeably longer battery life and was mounted to the handlebars of a Harley, while the Hero3 was mounted on a DJI Phantom. Both cameras performed quite well, the Hero3 got some amazing aerial footage of the mountains the ride was on. While the Hero3+ provided extremely smooth footage and really brought out the detail in the road and closeup scenery. Luckily the ride was full of switchbacks so there weren't many areas for the Hero3+ to look soft and out of focus. The wifi ability is a big improvement over the Hero3 and is definitely appreciated. My biggest complaint about the Hero3+ is that the case is junk compared to the Hero3. Mine came with a gash in the white rubber gasket and the latch broke off the third time using it. I wouldn't say I would want one over the other, but the Hero3+ was somewhat disappointing. Hopefully the Hero4 will live up to the hype.

review_body:

Because of my arthritis, I find it difficult to hold my Nikon L820 steady while zooming. So, this will help tremendously.

We had a more heavy-duty tripod that my husband bought years ago when we got our first video camera (one of those bulky heavy ones who hold on your shoulder). It was cumbersome for me to move that thing around for the kind of shooting I do nowadays. But, this new one is lightweight, has a neat carrying handle, pivots easily in all directions, even has a built-in level. The carrying bag is good quality as well. I couldn't ask for a better bang for my buck.

review_headline: Video users, don't stack filters & you might see ghosting
review_body: Just wanted to throw some advice out there for those of you shooting video.  I bought the .6 and .9 Tiffen 77mm filters.  I just did a test on an FS-100 with a Rokinon 35mm prime video lens.  First off, with my setup, two filters cannot be stacked.  The image turns soft.  I didn't expect this based on the other reviews I read before buying these.  With just one filter attached (the .6 or .9) there is some mild to medium color shift (or WB change, I should say), but nothing that can't be tweaked in post.  And, with just one of these filters attached, I picked up some slight ghosting from a bright light source - a computer monitor framed in the upper left third of the shot, reflected dimly in the lower right third of the shot.  Not severe enough to ruin the footage (for me) but it's there.  Your camera/lens combo may yield different results but at least as far as resolution is concerned, the camera I'm using is sharp, so I think it's safe to at least trust the no-stacking suggestion.  Cheers.

product_title: Lightbox Plugable USB 2.0 Digital Microscope for Windows, Mac, Linux (2MP, 10x-50x Optical Zoom, 200x Digital Magnification)
review_headline: Watch out!  Not the same as a Plugable USB 2.0!!!
review_body:
I ordered this through Amazon & received a package from China. The box was not what is shown in the pictures (of a \\"Plugable 2.0 USB Microscope\\" with instructions etc.).
I opened it, thinking \\"as long as it works\\"...
Famous last words - my new iMac did not recognize the device - I downloaded the drivers for the \\"Plugable 2.0\\", since that's what I had as the description from my Amazon order (and the reviews said that you'd get full functionality on macs). No luck.
I tried it on my PC - same thing.

Then I saw that it said \\"Lightbox Plugable USB 2.0\\" rather than just \\"Plugable\\" ([...]
So, I guess I got a knock-off microscope with a name close enough to the real thing (and with pictures of the real thing!!!!), so that people like me wouldn't notice. Apparently, the \\"Plugable\\" software does not recognize the \\"Lightbox\\" device, as it just comments with:
\\"No Device detected, please connect your magnifier directly to your PC USB port\\"

Since I read many good reviews of the \\"Plugable\\" scope (that's why I bought this), I'm sure the original is a good item, but the \\"Lightbox Plugable\\" microscope is essentially just a desktop flashlight at this point. :O(

Hope this helps others avoid my mistake - buyer beware!

product_title: X-Rite ColorMunki Smile
review_headline: If you are serious about your images, don't hesitate to buy this unit!
review_body:
A very useful product for the serious photographer! There is NO way, short of wasting a bunch of money on prints, to guess why your monitor looks so much different than your prints. The ColorMunki solves the problem by accurately calibrating you monitors based on the ambient light in the room where you edit your images.

I taught college level Photoshop classes for 14 years - from intro to advanced classes and have been a BETA tester for Adobe - the number one biggest issue the student were struggling with was getting their monitor to match the output of their printer! Most people handle this process backwards! They try to get the printer to match their monitor(s). Here's the problem: printers are sort of mindless beasts. Most printers have a limited ability to be adjusted. Monitors, on the other hand, can be adjusted easily and accurately.

The second biggest problem is the effects of ambient light and reflections in the monitor. I would tell my students to try and work in the exact same lighting every time they were editing their images. That can be problematic. The X-Rite ColorMunki will solve a host of these problems! It's easy to set up and easy to use. The results are worth the price of admission! You could easily recover the cost of this device with the savings from not having wasted a bunch of money on expensive prints!

product_title: Zeiss 12mm f/2.8 Touit Series for Fujifilm X Series Cameras
review_body:
This lens is an excellent build quality lens. It is mostly metal construction with quality rubber grips. I do have an annoyance about the aperture ring turning too easily, but that is minor given how good the lens is optically (and it is common to all Fuji lenses with aperture rings). My focus ring is tight and nicely weighted, but it won't see much use.

Who is this lens for? Someone wanting a professional quality ultra-wide lens for a Fuji X camera.

✔: Resolution/Sharpness Corner to corner from f/2.8-f/11 (f/2.8 is a tad softer than f/4).
✔: Build Quality
✔: General Image Quality
✘: Hood is tight
✘: Aperture ring turns too easy (accidentally change aperture)
✘: Flare from lights just out of frame if you don't use included hood.

I was shocked at how sharp this lens is. On my X-A1 it is distortion free, and even the RAWs in Lightroom are distortion free, but if you open the RAW files in DCRaw you will see very minor 2% barrel distortion (TV) that is corrected out. This has negligible impact on corner performance as the Touit is as sharp as the Fuji 14mm lens in the corners which is fully optically corrected. Either optical or software corrections can reduce corner performance. Don't let software correction rumors of the Zeiss influence your decision.

So, what everyone is going to ask is why buy the 12mm Zeiss when you can buy the 14mm f/2.8 Fuji for less money? The answer is simple. If you rely on manual focus lenses than the Fuji has much better feel. It has a sliding ring that lets you engage a nice positive manual focus feel and have a built in distance scale. The Fuji is still Focus by Wire, but doesn't feel it. If this is important to you get the Fuji if you don't mind the tighter field of view. The Fuji size is also a little better matched to the cameras since it doesn't flare out at the end.

If you want the widest prime you can get for the system, that is bitingly sharp and an excellent optically (the Fuji is excellent optically too), then get the Zeiss. It is notably wider than the Fuji. So even though the Fuji is a faster focusing, has better manual focusing, and is smaller, I still recommend either lens. The Zeiss is a great choice for the wider field of view, and it produces much nicer starbursts if you shoot night city scenes on a tripod at small apertures. The Fuji has too round of aperture opening.

Yes, the Zeiss is expensive, but after discounts it isn't much more than the Fuji so it makes the lens an equal value.

Verdict: A+, for those that need a pro caliber lens and can live with short comings (mostly in usage with hood and aperture ring).itingly sharp and an excellent optically (the Fuji is excellent optically too), then get the Zeiss. product_title: Case Logic Kilowatt KSB-102 Large Sling Backpack for Pro DSLR and Laptop
review_body:
This bag was purchased with the intent of being able to carry the minimum equipment necessary for a location shoot in neighboring buildings on our manufacturing campus. It also needed to be able to fit in overhead compartments on airplanes for location shoots at our customer locations. While this bag is smartly designed and well made, there are a couple of drawbacks. Yes, the zippers do get stuck going around corners which, at most, is an annoyance I can live with. Overall it is a great bag and is very comfortable to wear and is compact enough to fit in overhead compartments on a commuter sized airplane.

This last issue is both a blessing and a curse. There is simply not enough room in the main compartment. I shoot Canon and use three basic lenses (16-35mm, 24-105mm and 100mm Macro. I shoot really big stuff or very close up details so, luckily, I don't have need of longer, lager lenses). Lens hoods DO NOT FIT while attached to the lens and get relegated to the upper compartment. I travel with a 15" MacBook Pro which fits snuggly and has no room for the power cord which also gets put in the upper compartment. I don't believe a 17" laptop would fit, but I have never tried one. I use three flashes, one fits in the main compartment, the other two go in the upper compartment along with the radio slaves.

I could go on, but let's just say, the upper compartment gets very full of small, yet bulky items since there are only two external pockets, both flat. This would be a much better bag if it was 20% larger (height and width), which would still fit in the overheads. As it stands now, it is a great bag for very minimal equipment.

product_title: Olympus XZ-2
review_headline: Take a look at the Olympus Stylus XZ-2.  I dare you...
review_body:
About me. I'm not photo a equipment expert nor a professional photographer. I am a photo equipment enthusiast and love taking pictures. I have good eyes, good senses, and steady hands and I know quality when I see it. I look at 100% Crops, but I'm not a pixel peeper by any stretch. Here's some of the good stuff I've owned and used: Canon 60D; Canon Pro 1; Canon T4i; Pentax K-5; Pentax K-20; Canon G1X; Canon s95 and s100; Canon SX-40; Sony Apha Nex-6; Sony RX100; Olympus epm2; a couple of point and shoot Nikons that I don't even remember the model numbers; and a ton of glass to support the interchangeables above. Does that make me an expert - not by a long shot. I does makes me moderately informed.

So why the Olympus XZ-2? Like a lot of people I've been on an extended search for a GOOD bridge camera that's high on quality, not too big, not too small, loaded with features, an just simply takes beautiful photos. Because of its lack publicity and unimposing presence in the "favorites" market (have you looked at Snapsort lately - anything Canon or Sony is just about always going to come out on top when compared to anything Canon or Sony), Olympus had never been on my list of favorites either. But like a lot enthusiasts who eventually tire of lugging around the Canon OR Pentax OR Nikon behemoths (all the way down to the G1X) I was still reluctant to trade bulk and weight by sacrificing top of the line features and QUALITY. That's when I started looking at Olympus' line of Pen cameras and their point and shoot line of fix lens counterparts. The search led me first to the Pen epm2. WOW. This lttle gem with all of its available lens and accessories blew me away in both the quality and feature set categories. The epm2 then led me to start looking for an Olympus fixed lens alternative, and that's when I found he Stylus XZ-2. A day after I got it, I am convinced - I guess you could say, I'm a believer. This is one of the coolest "bridge" style camera's I've ever used and I've used some of the best including the Canon G-12 and the G1X as well as the old Pro-1. With its wide 1.8 telephoto lens it's fast, it's accurate, has an articulating screen, it can be fitted with some of the neatest accessories including electronic viewfinders, hot shoe flashes, audio microphone to mention a few. And the botton line - IT TAKES FABULOUS PHOTOS throughout its range of settings. So, Canon/Nikon/Pentax afficianados, want to treat yourself to something really different and really fun and inspiring? Take a look at the Olympus Stylus XZ-2. I dare you.....(heh, heh)

product_title: Samsung EC-DV150FBPBUS 16.2MP Smart Digital Camera with 5.0x Optical Image Stabilized Zoom with 2.7-Inch LCD Screen
review_headline: A Truly Sad Excuse for a Point and Shoot Digital Camera
review_body:
This is the most disappointing excuse for a camera I have ever used. My attraction to it was the front LCD screen, as I was going to a wedding that my young nephews were attending. I thought the front screen would be fun for them and I thought it was an interesting feature.

Being in the camera business for forty years, I knew I wasn't buying a $5,000 camera. I DID expect to get a basic point and shoot camera that could create an acceptable 5 X 7 inch print. As it turns out, I am ill that I took this camera to the wedding rather than buying a $5 disposable film camera or simply using my iPhone.

Other problems with the camera are that the battery only lasts about 200 images before it has to be recharged again; it requires that you recharge the battery while inside the camera, as there is no separate AC charger provided; the built in flash only has a range of about 8 feet even as 400 ISO; and it uses a micro SD card, which should have been clearly disclosed in the Amazon write-up. I had to run to Radio Shack to buy a micro SD card, which was ridiculously expensive.

Do not waste your money on this camera. EVERY one of the 200 images I took tonight are not sharp enough for 4 X 6 prints. If you are ONLY going to view the images you create on an iPhone you are viewing from 5 feet away, then possibly consider it only if you are real fan of useless bells and whistles.

review_headline: Worked great and arrived before expected.
review_body: I ordered this battery a few days before Thanksgiving of 2013.  I was notified that it would arrive the day after Thanksgiving or later.  So I thought, well no videos of Thanksgiving, but at least I should have it for Christmas.  Well, it arrived the day before Thanksgiving.  I put it on the camera and it showed a partial charge, so I put it on the charger.  It was on for only about 5 minutes and the charger shut off.  I knew that wasn't right but tried again.  Same thing happened.  So I looked in the instructions and it suggested if that didn't work to run the battery down.  So I put it on the camcorder and put in a tape and ran it on play.  It only lasted about 10 minutes.  Then I charged it and after about an hour it was fully charged.  I used it on Thanksgiving, but did not recharge it.  I tried it at Christmas and it was fully charged.  I also learned that these lead acid batteries need to be kept fully charged.  The ni-cads used in others should be treated different.  I was told by a guy at Batterys Plus to let the lead acid battery run completly down and charge it only when you need it.  After I read the instructions from Amazons dealer, I realized you don't allow a car battery to run down.  So I think Batterys Plus gave me a bum steer.  I'm satisfied with this purchase and what I learned, as well as the quick delivery, so therefore I gave it a 5 star rating.

review_body:
Although well-built, there are more cost-effective options available. The Lowepro Photo Sport Shoulder bag is small, as far as camera bags go, and will hold a small camera and just a few personal belongings. When I say small camera, I'm talking a mirrorless or very small DSLR (such as a Nikon D5100) with a small-to-medium lens only. Don't plan on bringing extra lenses or a long zoom. The overall aesthetic of this bag seems less like what I would call a camera bag, and more like a purse that happens to have a padded pouch for a camera.

The pouch is a nicely padded cube with a drawstring top. It attaches to velcro anywhere along the bottom of the bag, which allows for a small degree of interior customisation. There are a few zippered pouches inside and out for holding small (and flat) objects. The outer nylon material seems like it will hold up to scrapes well, but there is no additional padding- the camera cube is the only protection you'll get. Although there's just enough space to fit an iPad Air between the padded cube and the outer wall of the bag, be warned that the only barrier between your iPad and the outside world is a thin piece of nylon. Another questionable design choice was the use of plastic "D-rings" to secure the shoulder strap, and no shoulder padding whatsoever. These omissions irk me, given that this is a premium-priced bag from a premium brand.

There are certainly worse bags out there, but there are also better bags for less money. Lowepro's own Passport Sling comes to mind. The Passport Sling is slightly larger, better built and ~$20 LESS than this Photo Sport Shoulder.

product_title: Canon WP-DC24 Waterproof Case for Canon Powershot SD790IS Digital Cameras
review_body:
Fabulous product! Worked perfectly to 100 ft. I had an Olymplus 5000 with underwater case, but have not been able to locate that camera (may have loaned it out some time ago), and was happy to find that a waterproof case was actually made for the Canon SD790 IS which I have had for a few years. It's a great camera, durable and takes great shots. You will need a little practice with the camera's original flash for better pics underwater, and of course, a professional light kit is always great if it's in your budget. The only control you cannot access when underwater with this case is whether you want video or stills. So, you just need to make that decision first, and all is well. Of course, you can always pull a still from your videos when transferred to the computer or editing, so just give it some thought first before diving.

All control buttons worked fine, smoothly and perfectly. And, be sure to follow the instructions concerning the "O" right, keep it clean after ocean or any kind of diving, avoid using grease if possible, or be VERY careful when using it to not overdo it, or get grease on other parts.

One more item, it does not seem to be sold WITH weights, even though you may see a list including them when you see the item, so be sure to find out EXACTLY what is included when you are purchasing, as you may need to buy a weight kit separately.

Other than that - all is just great. It's easy to use, and when you have silica packets from any other devices or shipments, keep them and if they are small enough, they can be used inside this case.

Wonderful product and I would recommend it for this camera.

product_title: Aputure Remote Shutter Release Timer/Intervalometer - 3C Camera Remote for Professional Canon Cameras (Replaces Canon's RS 80-N3)
review_body:
I bought this recently as I decided I wanted to start shooting some time lapse videos using my 5DMkII. I was initially considering the Canon version, but for 1/4 of the price I figured it was worth a gamble. Usually, you get what you pay for, and this isn't an exception.

The whole thing feels cheap, but that's not really a surprise or much of a strike against it. The shutter release is a little clunky, and the jog wheel on the side sticks occasionally. Build quality is cheap, but that's why it's priced how it is.

The battery, when I received it, showed as being "low" but I've used it to shoot continuously on 3 occasions for about 4-5 hours total now and haven't had it die on me. So, it's hard to say if the low battery warning shows prematurely or if they just ship with dead batteries. I'll know when I put new batteries in I guess.

Otherwise, it does what I expect it to do, for a lot cheaper than I was originally going to pay. There are certainly better intervalometers out there with more features and better quality buttons, but this does everything I need right now at a price that's hard to beat.

Being new to intervalometers, I did read the manual when I first got it, and I haven't looked at it since. There really aren't that many functions, but for what I'm doing you don't really need much.
