product_title: BlackRapid RPB-1BB Snapr 20 (Black)
review_headline: Great case that can double as a purse
review_body:
I got this case last August, when I bought my Sony Cyber-Shot DSC-RX100. The camera did not come with a neck strap, doesn't have a grip, and is the most expensive camera I've ever owned, so I was a bit phobic about dropping it. I really liked the sense of security I got from having the camera anchored to the bag strap. Most of the time it works well to use the camera attached to the case strap. At the same time, I've found that it is easy to detatch the camera from the strap when I need to.

As it happened, my husband and I were going on a cruise soon after I bought the camera, and I would need to carry some sort of small handbag to dinner & elsewhere on ship. The central section of the Snapr 20 is a little bit long for my camera, but that meant that I could shove a fold up nylon shopping bag in behind the camera. I used the side pockets to hold my spare battery & SD card, as well as cabin key and any other necessities.

On an everyday basis, I carry my camera in a snug case in my handbag, but when we travel, I like to use a small backpack, and keep valuable items in some sort of small bag in front of me. On the cruise trip, when we went on shore trips, I put my passport, coin purse, and credit cards in a pocket of the camera bag. This meant that I had the important things right under my hands where I could protect them, with less important items (water bottle, umbrella, etc.) in my backpack. It worked wonderfully.

I also got the smaller size Snapr, thinking it would fit my camera better. My camera fits into the smaller case very snugly, and I have not found it as useful as the 20 snapr.

I learned about BlackRapid when I was reading reviews of the camera (which I bought from Amazon) because some people reviewing the camera recommended BlackRapid. I ordered my case from the BlackRapid site. (I think Amazon didn't carry the cases then.)They were very helpful about getting me the case in a rush, and were very responsive to my questions. All in all, I highly recommend the company and their products.

product_title: 700TVL 1/3" Sony CCD Dome Vandalproof CCTV Indoor Security Camera - 36 IR LEDs, Vari-focal 2.8-12mm Manual Zoom Lens
review_headline: Doesn't seem to be 700TVL, spotbeam washout at night.  Beware!
review_body:
I have a lot of experience with CCTV cameras and can honestly say that there is something wrong with all of these cameras I ordered. Upon receiving them, 3 of the 17 were bad, 1 had a crushed DC connector and the other 2 had bad menu control switches on the cord. I thought maybe this just happens in production/packaging. Further testing revealed the following:

DAYTIME:
Overexposed and grainy picture at all daylight levels, could not be adjusted despite all of the features for BLC, Exposure, Lens, etc... At times the image looked worse than a 480TVL camera.

NIGHTIME:
The Infrared forms a spotbeam that completely whites out the center of the image at less than 30 feet and in greater distances washes out the center of the image.
The image is better than a 480TVL but it still doesn't look like other 700TVL units I have with the same specifications.

I have returned 14 of the 17 as of this review. I had to keep 3 of them as they were already in full use.

review_body: Admission: I'm a complete newbie to photography.  I had to take a class that required a DSLR camera.  I looked around, and the cheapest ones for purchase at stores in my area were $700-800.  Way more than I wanted to spend.  I bought a Nikon D1 (I later found out this camera was first issued in 1999) for $100 off ebay, and lo and behold, the thing didn't even work anymore. I sent it back to the seller and got a refund.  But, I still needed a camera.  The Canon Rebel T3 was the cheapest one out there, yet Canon is always a reliable brand, so I knew I wouldn't be disappointed, and so far, everything has been good.  Very easy to set up and meter shots, although the camera is very very picky about focusing, especially when shooting landscapes.  It will not let you take the shot unless everything is as clear as possible.  The Rebel is most definitely less complicated and much more user friendly than almost any other DSLR camera out there, which is definitely good for those like myself who have never used anything other than point-and-shoot cameras prior to purchasing the Rebel.  The price...errrr, maybe it could be a bit lower.  $350-375ish (and not $499) would be appropriate.  I paid $400, which I think was \\"fair.\\"  I'd recommend it to anyone - seems like a great, and relatively lightweight, camera for someone taking photos while on vacation, where a heavy/bulky DSLR would be inconvenient.

product_title: Tiffen Circular Polarizer
review_body: In my experience Tiffen makes a very good filter and this one is no exception. Threads match nicely and the filter seats firmly yet is easily removed. The rotation of the filter is buttery smooth and stays put. The Tiffen adds a nice degree of polarization that gives colors a bit more saturation and contrast with a minor loss of overall transmission. If you're not shooting with a polarizing filter you probably don't realize just how much stray/reflected light is affecting your photo's. Once you see the difference a good filter like this can make you'll wonder why you didn't start using one sooner. Put your UV filter back in the bag and put something in front of your lens that will actually improve every shot. I've spent bigger money on other brands of filter (Hoya, B&W, et al) and I just don't see that money buying me a better filter. Maybe I'm missing something but, \\"the proof of the pudding is in the eating\\" and Tiffen filters do the job for me without breaking my budget.

product_title: Canon PowerShot D20 12.1 MP CMOS Waterproof Digital Camera with 5x Image Stabilized Zoom 28mm Wide-Angle Lens a 3.0-Inch LCD and GPS Tracking
review_headline: Not as Good as the Earlier Model
review_body:
Having owned, and heavily used, two previous Canon PowerShot D10 cameras, we were disappointed by changes in the feature set of the updated PowerShot D20.

Improvements:
1. Larger LCD view screen
2. Underwater macro mode
3. Dedicated video recording button

Disappointments:
1. No \\"sunset\\" mode
2. No \\"children and pets\\" mode
3. No \\"flowers & foliage\\" mode
4. Only one carrying strap placement option (compared to 4 on the previous model)
5. Square-edged design not as easy to slip into pocket or carrying bag

In place of the modes mentioned above, the camera now features \\"toy camera\\" mode, which puts a fuzzy black vignette around the image for a faux-Instagram effect; \\"miniature\\" mode (not to be confused with macro), which creates a fake tilt-shift effect by blurring the top and bottom of the image; and \\"fisheye\\" mode, which creates an artificially distorted center image (but does not capture a wider field of view).

We purchased the D20 because, after two years of heavy underwater snorkeling use, our D10 cameras had begun to show signs of leaking and the D10 is no longer available. Fortunately our D10s are still fully serviceable for non-submerged photography. We will be keeping the D10 cameras for dry-land use, including travel, hiking, and general everyday photography, and the D20, due to the elimination of the modes we most frequently used, will be limited mostly to watersport purposes.

review_body:

Wireless cameras would have been a better choice for me. I ended up having to run my wires over my roof and in the window (otherwise, they would have been all through the house). Although, I'm sure many people would come up with better ideas, lol.
I was aware that there is no hard drive. This isn't a problem for me. I am using the system in conjunction with an alarm system (SC-1000, also on Amazon). The alarm system will alert me when there is activity at my property and I will access the cameras to see what's up. I may purchase a hard drive so my daughter can see what kind of creatures are roaming around in my woods at night. I also have one camera aimed at the door so we can see who's there before opening.
These are not HD cameras and they don't claim to be. The picture is a little grainy (especially at night), but they absolutely serve the purpose intended.
I saw some bad reviews based on pic quality, etc. I can't imagine what people expect for the amount of money they're spending.

Update 9/25/13:
One of the cameras is dead. I will try to get in touch with Zmodo tomorrow, although I read in other reviews that it is nearly impossible.
Also, I am having a hell of a time trying to get the DVR ported out so I can see the cameras from anywhere via internet. However, I can see them on all devices that are on my server.

review_body:

My method of lens cleaning is very simple and very efficient. I shoot the beach often and my lenses get nasty and this metho works very well.

Use a rocket blasted to blow off particles.
Use lens pen brush to dust off stuck particles
Use Tiffen lens tissue paper and my breath to clean the lens of fog/filmy residue
Use the lens pen to clean.
Use pen to hold the lens paper to final clean lens, pushing paper gently around.

Sounds like a lot of work but it isn't and I use this method on my best glass with excellent results.

review_body:
With respect to the camera set up, they are quite simple and easy to use. Out of the box you will enjoy the ease of installation and simplicity of the interface to remote view your cameras. There are however some things that everyone should be aware of:

- If you plan to use multiple cameras >3 on your network, please plan to have available more than 5 meg of upload availability. There is conflicting information provided from Dropcam reps vs what is provided on the website as to how much bandwidth and speed you need per camera.

- Dropcam reps (Cliff in particular) will not own any of the problem and will try to \\"shove\\" the problem off on your ISP. I have spoken with 3 other individuals using multi camera systems and all report the same issue

- Try this if you have a multi camera system...... check your ping times with the cams on and then with them off......... how do they react? Try a speed test with the cams on vs off....... the cameras should not impact download speeds.

All in all if you need 1 camera you will likely be fine with Dropcam.... if you have more or need more than 1 camera... BUYER BEWARE!

One final thing.... Dropcam will not offer to work with you on refunding the purchase price... you can only contact Amazon.

Thanks Dropcam!

Mike

product_title: Fujifilm X20 12MP Digital Camera with 2.8-Inch LCD
review_body:
[[ASIN:B00AV3XH9W Fujifilm X20 Silver 12 Digital Camera with 2.8-Inch LCD (Silver)]]

After researching the Sony RX100, Sony NEX6, Canon G1X, Panasonic GF6 I concluded that the Fujifilm X20 was a perfect fit for me. I recently graduated from a Nikon D5000 and was terribly disappointed with results. I was looking for a camera with the quality of a DSLR with the size, weight and portability of a point and shoot. It was daunting for me to think about hauling the big DSLR and lenses around with me when I travel to Europe in the fall. When I travel the camera never leaves my possession so therefore size and weight are a huge consideration. I consider myself an average amateur photographer who likes the flexibility of a camera that I can control as well as having a fully automatic point and shoot.

The first thing you will immediately notice with the X20 is that there is no shutter lag. You don't miss those candid shots because the camera is processing the last shot. The flash recovery is quick and the photos are crystal clear. The fast 28mm-112mm, f2.4 zoom lens gets the job done. You will notice the sharpness of each photo first thing. For example I took a picture of my dog from about 15 feet and her eyes were discernibly brown. The clearness of her eyes never showed up when I took similar shots with the D5000, they typically looked black and I could never get the eyes fully in focus. The color and contrast is spot on. I do not have to spend considerable time in post-production working in Photoshop fixing the color and contrast. This is a huge plus when you take a significant number of shots.

I highly recommend this camera for folks like me who are photo enthusiasts but have reached a point where you no longer want to haul around sizable DSLR and lenses but still want the control and quality.

PS: Check out the sensor CMOS 2/3, optical zoom 4x, 12mp (don't get hung up on megapixels the sensor size trumps mp).

I wanted to have a couple extra batteries to ensure I'd be able to safely travel and have adequate camera power... dead batteries can ruin a trip pretty quickly.

Consider that a single Canon NB-11L battery is roughy $20. The NB-11L by Canon is rated at 3.6V and 680mAh. On the other hand, the Wasabi NB-11L kit includes TWO NB-11L batteries rated at 900mAh*, PLUS you get a charger that is comparable to the Canon charger, AND a car charger cable, AND an International adapter plug all for about the same cost as a single Canon NB-11L. How can you go wrong?

*Some people have complained that the actual capacity of Wasabi batteries are not as claimed. Perhaps. But even if the rated capacity is a bit lower than the Canon NB-11L, it is still giving you two batteries plus all the extras for about the same price. For my money, I'll settle for a bit less given the cost savings I'm realizing.

I bought a similar Wasabi Kit for my GoPro Hero3 Black and can say that the Wasabi battery life is practically identical to the GoPro battery life. As I use this Canon NB-11L equivalent battery, I'll add to my review if necessary.

For now, I'm completely happy with my purchase and have saved a lot of money compared to buying a Canon branded backup battery.

review_body:
I own this camera along with 7 fixed Nightowl 600 TVL cameras. I bought this camera for its night vision capability (which most PTZ don't have), and for its focal length distance (22x Zoom). Even thou the resolution is somewhat lower than my 600 TVL cameras, you cannot tell the difference unless you expand the video from the grid screen view, and even then its still good, you won't miss a thing.

The only drawback I found is the size of the camera. It is huge, I try to get the size before I bought it, but it was not listed anywhere. It is about 8\\" to 10\\". So big that I could not mount it at the front of the house. It look somewhat illegal...more like a neighborhood watch camera that belongs on a light pole.

Setting up the camera was easy. Test it before you install it. That way if you mount it and it don't work, you will know that wire size or similar is causing the problem. If you have a DVR with PTZ output, you do not need a separate controller to operate the camera. You do not need to mess with the camera dip switches either. PTZ output usually marked +TX and -TX or simply + and - and have a green color connector. The blue wire of the camera is + and the brown wire is - so connect likewise. Once the camera is powered and the video cable is connected, use the mouse from your DVR to control it. Select PTZ and you will see the control interface.

If your camera work when you test it at the DVR and don't work when installed, 1. make sure you are using the supplied 5A power supply that came with the camera. 2. make sure the wire that goes to the camera is large enough to carry the current required by the camera. If the wire is too small, the video will show, but no rotation or zoom. (NOTE: regular video wire sold for video camera can only be used for the video). Use a different wire for the power and RS485 control. Use 18 gauge wire for up to about 140 feet.

Overall, this is a good PTZ camera for the price. It has one of the best night vision clarity you ever seen. (There is no glare in mine as someone mention) It will make your 600-700 TVL cameras look like a joke at night.

I still need to test how the camera performs in cold weather and the reliably of it.

product_title: Yongnuo RF-603 C3 2.4GHz Wireless Flash Trigger/Wireless Shutter Release Transceiver Kit for Canon 1D/5D/7D/50D/40D/30D/20D/10D Series
review_headline: Works as advertised, but plug is too tight (reviewed as shutter trigger)
review_body:
I was delighted to find a wireless shutter trigger for my 5D. I often get the urge to experiment w/ light setups when there is no one around to shoot, so this works perfectly for self-portraits. It doesn't seem to fire every time, however, though that's not a huge issue. Just push the button again. The ability to hold the trigger half-way down for focus is a nice feature. The one negative I found was the 3-prong female plug. First, it's not keyed in a way to determine which way it plugs in, so takes a bit of studying the pin alignment to get it on (to save future buyers the trouble: the cord faces the front of the camera for proper orientation). The fit is also very tight, so while inserting it, I'm always worried that the resistance might be coming from a pin bending vs. the tight fit. These 2 issues w/ the plug are why I dinged it 2 stars.

I know that these are also popular as flash triggers. I don't know if I'd recommend them for that, unless you have only one light. I'd spend a little extra for Cactus triggers, as they make it possible to meter each light individually (w/out turning the other lights off), then firing up to 4 together.

Note that the picture is not accurate. This shows a 3.5mm cord for flash triggering, which almost stopped me from ordering it, since I wanted the shutter trigger. This model actually has the Canon 3-pin cord for shutter release. If you want to use it for flash, purchase a different model, or this model & an additional 3.5mm cord.

product_title: Lowepro Outback Camera Beltpack (Black)
review_headline: Great for the photographer on the go!
review_body: First off let me list all my gear and how I got it to fit.  I have a Nikon D7000 with battery grip, Nikon 17-55mm f/2.8 lens, Nikon 35mm 1.8g lens, a Sigma 50-150mm f/2.8 OS HSM lens, and a Nikon SB-700 Speedlight.  The main center compartment easily can fit the Nikon D7000 with the battery grip and the 17-55mm lens attached with the hood on.  It can also easily fit the camera body with battery grip and the 50-150mm lens attached but you have to reverse the hood.  I can store the 50-150mm lens with the hood reversed in either side compartment, no problem.  To store the 17-55mm lens is a little bit tricky cause it's a fat lens and with it's hood on either forward or reversed it's too tight to fit in a side compartment.  You can leave the hood at home but I like to use my lenses with their hoods on.  Without the hood on it can fit into the side compartment no problem.  So what I do is store the 17-55mm lens in one side compartment, put the small 35mm lens in the other side compartment and the take the 17-55mm hood, turn it sideways and drop it in on top of the 35mm lens.  The SB-700 then has to go in the front pouch.  The problem is there's no padding on the front pouch so I have to be careful what might bump into my bag.  Alternatively you can store the SB-700 in the side compartment but because it's such a huge flash you won't be able to fit anything else in that pouch.  Anyways I think for what it does it's a good bag.  You can go with a backpack for easier weight carrying but when you need faster access to your gear this bag is the way to go.  With all my gear stored in the bag it's probably 10 lbs+ I end up carrying around my waist.  The shoulder strap helps to steady the weight.  My only gripe is I wish they put more padding around the waist belt and the shoulder strap to help ease the strain of lugging all your gear for long periods at a time.  Otherwise it's a fantastic bag and I would definitely recommend it.

review_headline: Wow!  This is a fantastic frame!
review_body:
After looking at reviews for many other frames and feeling like I'd never find one that worked and fit my needs, I'm pleased to say that this frame delivers on all accounts! I don't use it for movies or music, but it is equipped for that. I just wanted something to show our wedding photos and some recent trip photos. And it had to be big enough and bright enough to be seen from across our living room/kitchen area.

I purchased a Nix 12" a week ago and was very disappointed with the brightness and overall color. It was dim, colors were faded...couldn't really see it well even when right in front of it. So that got boxed back up.

Then I saw the review for the Impecca. The user gave it great kudos for brightness and color, and said it was strong on both elements. I definitely agree! I have it up on top of our mantel and the viewing quality seems excellent at many angles. I can clearly see the pictures and true color even from across the large room. I also noticed that this frame was new to Amazon in 2013, which indicated newer technology than most of the other frames offered...check the dates. This frame has upgraded brightness ratios and resolution...which are key factors in a frame this large.

The actual frame itself is quite nice too. Looks like a nice wood frame with black mat...not some plastic border or plastic-y looking thing. It's definitely worthy of being on the mantel. The back is plastic, and the kickstand seems a bit cheap, but it works and no one sees it anyway. The part you do see looks very nice. And feels substantial as well.

Right out of the box I was able to plug in my SD card and have it start showing the sideshow. It comes with a remote but also has buttons on the back side you can use to work the menus.

It arrived on time, and though the exterior box looked like someone had done the Riverdance on it, the contents were fine.

I found another web site that was selling it for $198 but that didn't include shipping and was standard delivery time (about a week). I got mine in two days from Amazon.

I did find the menus and settings to be pretty self explanatory and basic, but I'm fairly tech savvy so I don't know how a technically challenged person would feel. The instruction book that was included was straightforward as well.

The menus were a tad clunky, but I've come to expect that from owning other digital frames. They are enough to get the job done. If you are looking for fancy or frills...you probably should show your photos on your computer or TV.

I originally had trouble getting it to play my photos in random order even after selecting "random" in settings, but I figured out that if you started the slide show from within the pic viewing pane it worked fine. Just a quirk I guess.

I have about 900 photos of varying format and size on it, and they all play just fine and look great. Other frames only work with jpeg files, but this one does multiple digital formats...which is a bonus.

Anyway, I don't usually write reviews. But after such a long and frustrating search for a quality digital frame, I wanted to help others and give folks the confidence to make this purchase. review_body:
I didn't purchase my 7D in Amazon, but I wanted to put in my thoughts on the camera. Like I said in the title, sensor technology has improved by leaps and bounds since this camera was first introduced, but having said that, I feel this camera is great. I'm not a professional photographer, but I consider myself an advanced amateur and know my way around this camera.

I think to really get the best of this camera is by shooting in RAW. Why? To get the most out of its sensor. I've shot 1600 to 3200 ISO and even though you can see grain, with software such as Lightroom or Photoshop you can easily correct and get usable shots. The camera is rugged and I haven't had any issues with it so far and with the feature set coming with this camera, you can't ask for more.

Naturally, if I someday would be able to upgrade, I'm going with the top of the line EOS 1D X. Some people might consider me crazy to spend close to 7 grand for a camera, but when you enjoy what you do and can get the best out there, why not? But right now I can't and I'm enjoying my 7D to the max. I'm learning every nook and cranny in this camera to get the most out of it and in my humble opinion, you can't go wrong if you purchase one. Just wanted to give my opinion hopeful it will help.

product_title: 4 way Macro Shot Focusing Focus Rail Slider for CANON NIKON SONY Camera
review_headline: OK for the Price and Purpose but Messy
review_body:
PROS:
1. The double-stack slider works as advertised. You can make very fine adjustments to slide a mounted camera left, right, forward, and backward. Besides the rubber padding, everything else is made of metal. As a result, the whole setup is heavy and sturdy.

2. If you happen to need a quantity of two of 2-way sliders, this purchase may save you some money because the top slider and the bottom one are identical.

CONS:
1. A special grease/goo (the same stuff used in a fluid head of a video tripod) is applied along the rack and on the pinion. This goo does help to make the movement smooth and fluid. (You can see it by zooming in really close to the picture of the underside.) However, this stuff is very messy and sticky, and I anticipate that it will attract and collect a lot of dust over time. It will stick to your hands during operation, and it is hard to remove.

2. If you are one of the DIY people who try to make this slider as part of a steady-cam jib, this slider will add a lot of weight to your camera (the steady part), forcing you to use more counterweights for balancing.

Overall, this slider is well-built, and I would recommend it to others for the price and purpose.

product_title: Sony Cyber-shot DSC-RX100 Digital Camera (Black) with 32GB Deluxe Accessory Bundle
review_headline: Never thought I'd love a Sony camera so much
review_body:
I've had some great cameras, and until I got this I was using a combination of a Nikon P7000 and a Nikon D3 (each for different reasons). This camera came out and the sensor had me intrigued, so I gave it a try...and I'm so happy I did.

First, Sony doesn't instantly come to mind when thinking about cutting edge products these days...and last year I ended up buying two new Sony cameras, this one and their helmet cam (which is a little less impressive but adequate among equally adequate competitors).

The RX100 takes great photos and video, and is very compact...almost so much so, though, that it's a little tough to hold for large hands, and the surface is a little slick. To solve this and other challenges, I outfitted mine with a Richard Franiec machined and color matched aluminum grip and a CarrySpeed magnetic filter setup. Problems solved.

I also love the different effect modes. This is a keeper, and because of it I find myself carrying the D3 way less. The P7000 is now my daughter's camera.

product_title: Dolica WT-1003 67-Inch Lightweight Monopod
review_body:
I just purchased this last week, and it has been excellent in use so far. It's incredibly light, and incredibly sturdy, especially for the price. I paid twice as much for a significantly worse tripod. The segments slide smoothly and quickly with minimal effort, the clasps are plastic, but feel very sturdy, the foam handle is well cushioned, and the spike/rubber foot combination is great for both indoor and outdoor use. There is minimal flex in the monopod, even when fully extended.

My biggest issue with this product is that the camera mount doesn't flip to hold the camera both horizontally and vertically, but it's not listed as having that capability in the description, and this isn't too problematic for me. I'd take off half a star at most, but since Amazon doesn't allow for half star increments, I rounded up.

This comes with a carrying case that feels fairly good, though I'm not sure how much I'll use it.

product_title: Foscam FI9821W Indoor Pan/Tilt H.264 720p Wireless IP Camera, 1/5" Color CMOS Sensor, F: 3.6mm F:2.4 (IR Lens), IEEE 802.11b/g/n Wireless Connectivity, White
review_body:
This camera is awesome. Ignore the negative reviews, as most of those people must not have any basic knowledge of networking. All I have to say that this product is absolutely fantastic for us. We have it above our twins' crib and it provides fantastic Video (including infared at night) and sound! I have installed the Foscam Chrome plugin on all my PC's and I have no issues watching the crib from on our local network or from the Internet. Since it is a standard IP camera, I have also installed the app 'IPCamViewer' on all of my android devices for $5 (My Samsung GSIII, My wife's Samsung GSIII, and my Nexus 10) and now I can use an of my already purchased devices as baby monitors. I can Tilt and Pan, have access to infrared for night viewing, and can listen in on that room all from any number of devices. I did a TON of research on baby monitors, and the functionality that this IPCam provides for us is unparalleled.

It truly is a great product.

review_headline: Does not make sense for Fuji x100s
review_body: This a very low quality microphone. It is not any better than the built in mic in Fuji x100s. It also does not appear to be cutting down on any camera handling noise. The mic shoe does not connect electronically to the camera so you must use an extension cord and adopter (included). Once you plug in the adopter it will be in the way of the Fuji x100s control knobs and makes the camera impossible to hold. As much as I like the Fuji x100s this mic is a complete disappointment. It is possible that if you have some fuji camera that has no built in mic you could use it. But for this price there are much better mics. This has the quality of telephone head set. What Fuji must do is something that Canon has done for their stuff where they use a high fidelity (not telephone quality) and fully integrated via shoe mount, no cable etc. I do not write negative reviews but I made an exception for this to save fellow photographers frustration.

product_title: Dropcam Wi-Fi Wireless Video Monitoring Camera
review_body:
I have tried many, many wifi cameras to monitor my elderly parents at their home and this camera is, without a doubt, THE one for my purposes. Set up, indeed, was done in no time and no need to know about \\"port forwarding\\". If you can plug in a USB cable to the USB port on your computer, you can set up this camera.

The picture is clean, crisp, and the sound amazing. I can read the newspaper headlines with this thing!

Best of all is two-way audio without the need for an external speaker. No....wait...better yet, best of all, this thing is less expensive than the other wifi camera's I've tried. Want to watch your baby? Get this camera. Want to watch Fido? Get this camera. Want to be able watch and talk to your family when you arent there? Get this camera!

As for the bandwidth usage, for my purposes, I dont have the camera 'on' all the time but simply slide the button to 'on' when I want to check in. My parents appreciate the fact that they can tell whether the camera is off or on.

review_headline: Great camera - package has what you need to get started.
review_body:
I've used a couple of $150 - $200 point and shoot digital cameras. In particular, I never liked the power zoom function, I guess I am too used to the 35mm's with manual zoom. Our video camera was old too.
Within a few minutes of charging the battery I was shooting great stills and video.
The focus speed and image quality especially in lower light conditions is fantastic!!
It can work as a point and shoot or allow all the manual settings you might want.

I'm very pleased with this camera and would highly recommend it to anyone who wants to step up.

Follow-up 22 July, 2013:
After using this camera for over a month; I'm still impressed!
I remain amazed at how fast this camera is (focus and low light). I took some action shots a couple weeks ago of the kids jumping rope. Lot's of fast movement of subjects - wow! not a single fuzzy out-of-focus shot.

My one small gripe is glare on the screen in bright outdoor conditions. This makes it harder to use in those conditions. This was the one reason I really would have liked to get the NEX6, with it's built in view finder, but just couldn't bare the extra $300.
I considering ordering a \\"Delkin Devices DU3.0-M Universal Pop-Up Shade for 3.0-Inch LCD Screens\\". I will update this review if/after I've ordered and used the shade.

review_headline: My new GH3 has sat on the shelf since I got this!
review_body:
I'm a dedicated Panny shooter. Started with their FZ50 superzoom about 6 years ago and in recent years have stepped up. I own both a GH2 and also the new GH3 4/3 models. Both those have their own great features and strong points, but now that I've had the FZ200 I see they do not have the convenience and light weight that makes it my first choice when I wanna grab a few quick shots.

Image quality is EXCELLENT. I prefer to shoot JPG (tho this'll do RAW) and like to use Photoshop CS6 to enhance every image I post. FZ200 images are a joy to edit requiring less work than those from either GH2 or GH3.

I shoot mostly at the max telephoto end of the zoom with subjects being birds and wildlife or boaters out on the lake. The OIS works great even with my old man's shakes and the f2.8 aperture gives me benefit in low light and for depth of field control.

product_title: Foscam Outdoor Wireless/Wired IP Camera with 4mm Lens
review_headline: Good product and value, for the moderately tech savvyy
review_body:
I've finally gotten my system working reliably after a couple of weeks ironing out the software setup bugs. My system consists of (1)outdoor F18905W and (3)indoor F18910W cameras. Getting the cameras to work on my internal WIFI system was pretty straight forward following the directions that came with the units. However, getting it to work remotely was a challenge and required a few calls to FOSCAM tech support (be prepared for very long wait times). Tech support is very helpful and knowledgeable setting up the system to work remotely, although they could not completelely solve my intermittent problems with my camera's getting hungup. Turning my Wireless \\"N\\" router back to \\"B&G\\" and trying different manual (vs. auto) WIFI channels helped make it more stable. FOSCAM claims this is an issue with my \\"new\\" Router, I'm not sure about that but its working acceptably now with the current settings (hangs up every few days requiring a router reset). FOSCAM could not help me access my cameras reliably from a remote (outside of WIFI network) PC without using the Iphone APP; they claim my DS is too slow and that the APP uses less data and therefore is best (this is OK for my purposes). I really like how well the cameras work with the FOSCAM pro Iphone app, I use it all the time. The email alerts also work great so that I don't need to continually check on the cameras.

Pros:
Works great with the FOSCAM Pro Iphone app (well worth the $6 app cost). Email alarm feature works great, be prepared to play around with the sensitivity settings to avoid nuisance alerts (light changes, etc). Camera hardware all seems to work well although I had to buy a sturdier outdoor mounting arm for $12 on an auction site.

Cons:
Can't login externally from a remote PC, only works with my Iphone app which is OK for my purposes. FOSCAM claims this is caused by my slow DSL service. Cameras occassionally get hungup (every few days), my solution is to unplug the routerand allow it to reset (I've setup an outlet timer to periodically do this).

Overall, I'm pleased with the value of this product and would recommend it to people not afraid to spend some time with tech support playing around with router and camera settings.

product_title: Sony Alpha - SLT-A33 Digital Camera
review_body: Bought this in the Spring of 2011 not long after it came out (had looked at Sony NEX5 and did not like it). I was a Canon guy for years and a prior Sony buy (DSCH1) convinced me to stay with Sony. The A33 took some getting used to (a bit complicated) but then again, I am one of those folks who hates reading instruction books. It is a flat out amazing camera. The standard 18-55mm lens creates very sharp images even very close-up. The 55-200mm lens is also very sharp. I bought a Sony 75-300mm lens but it is not at all as sharp as the others and I don't recommend it (I may see if it can be returned and checked). product_title: Tamron SP AF 2x Pro Teleconverter
review_headline: Works well, but don't expect miracles
review_body:
I use this with my Nikon D600 and 80-200mm f/2.8 AF-D lens. I've had my 80-200 for a few years now and it is a great lens for low light shooting and I tend to use the 80-200mm range much more than I would the 200-400mm range so that's why I decided to go with a teleconverter instead of buying an 80-400 f/4.5-5.6 VR lens. The cost is about the same for the older version and about $1200 cheaper than the new 80-400 lens so there is real money involved. If you primarily shoot above 200mm, then it might be worth getting the 80-400 instead and maybe getting a prime 85mm for faster needs or portraits. I myself am debating this.

So anyway, this teleconverter autofocuses just fine on my f/2.8 lens though a little sluggish. You have to realize that you lose 2 full stops of light...that's a lot of light so you will have to bump up your ISO a little to raise the shutter speed. Also, without VR, YOU HAVE TO USE A TRIPOD! There is no getting around this if you want sharp pictures. If possible, I would even suggest using a remote shutter cable because any movement is magnified many times over for distant subjects like birds. If your shot is stable, you will get a reasonably sharp picture. It's not perfect but then you're doubling your focal length for $225 so you can't get too choosy.

Biggest annoyance is that the EXIF data is not translated so as far as the camera knows, there is no teleconverter on.

Bottom line, if you accept this for what it is, it's great. Maybe not quite as the Nikon, but then this is less than half the price, and it works with AF-D lenses.

product_title: Mini HD Waterproof Camera Watch Video Recorder
review_headline: Neither a great watch or a great video recorder
review_body:
I bought the watch thinking it would be cool to have a Li Ion powered rechargeable watch. WRONG, the watch component functions completely separately from the video. Even has its own battery which can and will die. Please refer to one of other reviews on which battery size to purchase to replace the battery for the watch function. Again, this battery does not apply to the rechargeable one that provides video recording functionality. You can still take recordings even if the watch stops telling time.

Whatever, I can still take video underwater which is also kind of fun.
here's how to work the damn thing:
let's label the buttons 2,3,8,9 and10 according to the hours they are closest to, for example the button at 3:00 will be 3.
this said, the buttons at 2 and 9 aren't buttons but screw on caps. I bet this thing isn't waterproof without the caps so don't lose them.
Cap 2 covers the microphone and does not unscrew completely by design. I would describe it as a presta head for a bicycle inner tube.
Cap 9 covers the usb interface. The interface is a 2.5mm RCA style jack. The supplied interface cable is a usb to 2.5mm jack.
I know this thing said MP3 somewhere but that's a misprint and before you ask, it's not a media player of any kind.
Don't expect to be able to find a replacement cable for this easily. Also, if your computer doesn't recognize the device, try plugging it directly to a motherboard usb outlet as mine does not work through a USB hub.
Button 3 is actually just a pull out knob to set the time, nothing new there.
Button 10 is for taking photos or recording audio (will get more into this later)
Button 8 is for toggling standby mode or taking video.

The camera is set so that 6:00 is oriented at the top. (makes perfect sense if you're recording others and not yourself)
The functionality is similar to a camcorder in that there's an on/off state and a standby/recording state though it is difficult to tell which you are currently in.
To start, hold down button 8 for 3 seconds.
If you see flashing red lights then no lights after you've released the button, then the recorder/camera feature is turned off.
If upon release you see a solid blue light then you're in standby mode. This blue light should remain on until you press something else. if it flashes red again, please see my update at the bottom.
Now that you're in standby, you can do one of three things:
1. take a picture.
a. press button 10 briefly to take a picture. The LED should go red, then return to blue which means you're back in standby
2. record audio
a. press and hold button 10 for 3 seconds to start recording audio. Remember to unscrew cap 2.
b. pressing button 10 briefly will save your recording and return you to standby mode.
c. pressing and holding button 10 for 3 seconds will save your recording and power off the recorder.
3. record video
a. briefly press button 8 to start recording video.
b. briefly pressing button 8 again doesn't seem to interrupt the video recording
b. pressing and holding button 8 saves the video and will power off the recorder

Another reviewer has posted means of setting the time and date for the recording functions. I've personally tested it and it works like a charm.

USB and connecting to the computer:
I've had the best luck getting this thing to work with a PC by leaving it in standby mode and plugging it in.
the RCA jack should insert all the way into the watch. Do not remove the RCA jack from the watch while the USB side is plugged in, it may short and cause a power surge error in your PC and render the USB ports dead. (a simple reboot of the PC will fix this).
Once plugged in, the watch should show up as a removable disk with 3 directories:
1. IMAGE
2. RECORD
3. VIDEO
you'll notice that this thing records video in AVI, soI suspect you might be able to plug it directly into some other media players such as televisions and watch without going through a PC at all.
The audio is in WAV format and the images are JPEG's (.JPG)
This thing also works fine with Windows 8 (no surprise there)

P.S. On a humorous note. I got a kick out of some stock video left on mine showing the watch being worked on by some un-suspecting Chinese worker (I recognize the mandarin they were speaking). I would have loved to tell you that they were plotting to take over the U.S. by spying on us with these watches, but it was just a long video of the ceiling occasionally interrupted by a woman standing over while working over the sound of an annoying auto-greet message playing in the background over and over (and over and over).


Use the \\"Safely Remove Hardware\\" feature within windows when ejecting the USB connection, otherwise it can be left in a weird state where it won't go into standby mode. Please take a look at the comments section as this seems to be a common problem.
1. connect via USB
2. wait for the drives to show up, (disconnect/unplug without the safely remove hardware option and reconnect if the usb drive doesn't show up)
3. right click on the safely remove hardware icon next to the clock on windows machines (looks like a usb connector with a green checkmark)
4. Select the USB disk and wait for a couple seconds
5. unplug your USB connection
this is a good rule to follow for any USB device. Though for this stupid watch, it's particularly important.

product_title: Bluecell Light Brown leather classic DC digital camera protection case/bag/cover for Fujifilm X10 EXR CMOS with f2.0-f2.8 4x Optical Zoom Lens

review_body:
Although designed for the x10 (and it has \\"X10\\" subtly embossed on the top), it fits the x20 perfectly. With the case in place, all of the x20's buttons are fully accessible. The case is an old-fashioned, \\"ever ready\\" style, meaning that pictures can be taken quickly by flipping the top flap up, without having to fully remove the case from the camera. I have the silver-and-black version of the x20, and it looks great with that. Something about the brown color of this case really enhances the vintage style of the camera. The leather looks and feels very nice - it is hard to believe this case is so much cheaper than the official Fuji case.
The case has two parts - a bottom part that attaches to the camera via straps that snap around the strap lugs, and a top cover, which attaches to the bottom section with two snaps, and which folds over the camera and secures with a magnetic fastener. You take pictures by opening the top cover, or you can easily remove the top cover completely, for example if you are going to be shooting for a while and don't want it in the way. The bottom portion of the case has to be removed to access the battery and memory card, but that is not difficult to do.
The case does add a bit of bulk, so the very small x20 isn't quite as small with the case on. But it s still quite compact. I actually find that the leather case makes it more comfortable to hold the camera - the x20 is so slim that it can feel slightly too delicate in my hands, but the case gives it just enough extra thickness to be comfortable.
The case comes with a matching brown leather neckstrap, which attaches to the camera lugs to replace the original Fuji neckstrap that is supplied with the camera. The brown leather strap is very soft, matches the case perfectly, and feels very luxurious - the side that goes against your neck is soft and feels slightly cushioned, so when the strap is directly on your neck when (e.g., when you wear it with a tee shirt), it feels alot more comfortable than the original Fuji strap. It is also about 10\\" longer than the Fuji strap, which taller users may find helpful.
Overall I'm very happy with this case and would buy it again.
The case I bought is from Bluecell, but Amazon currently sells other cases that appear identical under different names. There is no manufacturer name on the case itself, just an \\"x10\\" embossed on the top of the camera.

product_title: Sony HDR-CX220 High Definition Handycam Camcorder with 2.7-Inch LCD
review_body:
The SONY CX-220 is the low end camera in SONY's Camcorder line based on the Exmor R 8.9 Megapixel image capture element. From a practical perspective, low end can be measured in a number of ways.

First, it's about half the price of the top of the line camera in the series, the CX-260.

Second, it has no internal memory, which requires that you use an SD card to record your videos. Other cameras in the series include 8 and 16 Gigabytes of internal memory. The internal memory can occasionally useful, but SD cards are inexpensive and easy to carry along. Given that you'll need a 32GB card to do upwards of 2 hours of highest quality video, the lack of internal memory is no real handicap.

Third, it it has a smaller external zoom (27x as opposed to the 30x in the CX-260). Again, there may be circumstances where the extra zoom matters, but you'll need a tripod to take advantage of it. Of slightly greater concern, in this regard, is the starting point for the zoom. While all of the cameras in Sony's Exmor R line are described as "wide angle", the CS-220's wide angle isn't quite as wide as other cameras in the series, which means you may have to position slightly further from the scene to capture everything you want to have in the frame. This is a practical issue for me as I most frequently use my video cameras to record Chorus concerts, which usually involve a wide frame. This shouldn't be an issue unless you are shooting in a small space (like a classroom) and want to capture the full width of the room. There are sometimes limits on how far you can back up the camera. It hasn't been an issue in auditoriums.

Fourth, it comes with a weaker battery than other cameras in the series. The CX-260 comes with Sony's FV-50 battery, which I've found can easily handle two hours of continuous video, but the CX-220 comes with Sony's FV-30 battery, which is rated as having about half the power of the FV-50 and needs a stretchto do an hour and thirty minutes of continuous video. This is offset somewhat by the CX-220 relatively stingy power use. The CX-220 will run a good 20 minutes longer than the CX-260 on the FV-50 battery. For longer videos or videos that do a lot of zooming (something I do very little of in my concert videos), either camera will benefit from the more powerful FV-70 battery, which should be good for upwards of 4 hours of highest quality video. My CX-220 clocks in at nearly 5 hours with an FV-70 battery.

Fifth, the CX-220 doesn't come with a Sony battery charger, but is instead documented as charging up using a USB cable. Several reviewers have complained about this, but I don't see an issue. From a practical perspective I nearly always have a USB charger with me, and it's nice not having to bring yet another charger along when traveling. If, moreover, you need a larger battery (like the FV-70, you'll probably find that the cost of the battery charger is small compared with the price of the battery and get them bundled (as I did). Finally, if your first camera is a higher end Sony Exmor R series camera like the CX-260, your existing Sony charger will charge up your CX-220 as well.

Sixth, the CX-220 uses button controls rather than touch screen controls, as the CX-260 does. I find the touch screen controls easier to use than the CX-220's button controls, but your milage may vary. Bigger fingers, and those who obsess about finger oil on screens, will probably prefer the CX-220's button controls.

Finally, there are more menu options, most of which you'll probably never use, and some flashy bells and whistles like an electronically controlled lens cover on the higher end R-Seres cameras. If you want super-slow motion or to have the camera protect the lens when the camera turns off, the CX-260 is probably the better camera for you. If they don't, you can get the same high quality video from either camera. Both cameras have thesame imaging element and record the same highest quality video. If those differences make a difference to you one way or the other, you can probably stop here, but I've titled this review "excellent second camera" and you may be interested in knowing why.

I obtained a SONY CX-260 camcorder six months ago with the specific intent of shooting concert videos. I've been shooting concert video on and off for most of 30 years now, but I was looking to step up a level to an HD prosumer camcorder that I could edit into high quality HD streaming video for distribution on Youtube. I already had a camera that could shoot 1080P video, but that could only record for about 30 minutes at a time. I also had a 720P camcorder and a somewhat better than 720P camcorder, so I was well positioned to shoot video with insets and closeups. What I needed was a second camera that chould shoot a continuous 1080P stream that I could use as a base for cuts and insets. After looking at a lot lot of prosumer camcorders and reviews, I concluded that the Sony CX-260 would best meet my needs based on its ability to record at better than 1080P (about four times better), its relatively high audio and video quality in low to moderate indoor light, its relatively long battery life, and its reasonable price (about $360). It has more than lived up to my expectations. For examples of video shot with this camera see the HD videos at [...]

That said, I've wanted to do better. One of the key restrictions on my filming of these videos is that I'm singing in the choruses. I can't exit stage right and return to restart a camera during the concert. I pretty much have to set up the cameras and forget about them. The CX-260 has really helped with that insofar as it has enough pixels to do high quality digital zooms while I'm editiing. That allows me to focus in on a soloist or small ensemble without losing the HD resolution (something I do a lot of in the referenced Youtubevideos). What I haven't always had is the routine ability to cut between different camera angles while retaining HD quality. I've been searching for a second HD camcorder for a couple of months now. The obvious answer was to get another CX-260, but I was looking to spend less than $200 and get something that could approach (not necessarily match, but approach) that quality.

The CX-220 more than meets those criteria, if only because it is able to match the video quality of CX-260 video for less than $200, not quite half the price of the CX-260. Aside from the slightly smaller optical zoom it has the same imaging components and records at the same high resolution. When I load video from both cameras into editing software I simply cannot tell which camera I loaded the video from unless I clearly label it when I import it. I can do the same levels of digital zoom without apparent loss of quality, and I can cut from one camera to the other seamlessly, which not only helps to make the edited video more entertaining, but allows me to show elements (typically people) that are hidden from one angle using the other angle.

If you are an amateur looking to shoot high quality home video, the CX-220 could be an excellent choice for you. If you are looking to create professional looking videos with excellent prosumer equipment, the CX-220 makes an excellent second camera.

product_title: GoPro HERO3
review_headline: Sold my GoPro 2 to raise money to buy this one. Big mistake.
review_body:
I bought this version in mid-January after selling my GoPro 2 to a friend. Right out of the box it had issues, even after updating the firmware. Freezes, poor battery life with conservative settings, will not transfer files via the USB cable on a Windows 7 PC, having to do hard resets often. This version should not have been released.

I figured it was just a hiccup that would be addressed in future versions of firmware updates, but four months later and still having the same problems. I will be returning this for a refund/credit tomorrow.

As for the function of the camera when it DOES work, I miss the simplicity of the previous versions. The WiFi is a nice little option that has become standard on the Black Edition, but I think the sacrifice of battery life is not worth it. The included remote probably has some good uses for some users, but I am sure most of us will put it back in the box after messing with it once or twice. The only things I see as being an actual improvement are the additional resolution/framerate options and the redesigned door latching system.

This version, even with all of its hyped functions, is not worth the money. Even if it were offered at half price, it still would not be worth it because it fails to do what previous versions did reliably.

You can access the DVR with your phone or computer as long as you have it set up properly and their phone support personnel will be happy to make sure that you are in business right away.

product_title: Canon EF 50mm f/1.8 II Camera Lens
review_body:
This is the cheapest Canon lens you can get. And it is a MUST for any hobbyist's kit, and is in fact working it's way into my paid work as well.

Okay, first off, on film or full frame (35mm) sensor sized DSLRs, this will provide the oft-sought-after 50mm focus length. This has been explained a million ways, but the simplest explanation is that the human eye itself has around that same viewing angle, so pictures taken on the 50mm range will produce a very comfortable image, something we are used to seeing, and this works very well for close-ups or portraits.

If you have a crop sensored DSLR (of which I do, T2i and 7D) the range is changed due to the crop magnification, but this will still produce a nice 80mm equivalent focal length, and still produces that comfortable feel you want in portraits. This will slightly widen the space between the lens and the subject, but not tremendously, and you will find where it is comfortable in a hurry.

This lens has a very wide aperture, but surprisingly considering the price even out at f/1.8 the image is quite sharp, and just a notch or two lower will produce some of the sharpest shots you've seen. I will note that with an aperture set so wide, you will have a super shallow depth of field, which may be confusing initially. For example, my emergency test model (my 16 year old cat) had to put up with me doing macro shots, and I was able to get his eye in perfect focus, with his nose (closer) blurred and his ears (father) also blurred. Absolutely stunning in how fine it goes. This will dial down to as far as f/22, which is almost infinity as almost everything is focused, but this isn't really where you want to have this lens fit overall due to the 5 bladed aperture window, which I will explain more below.

I picked this up initially as a once-in-a-while lens for studio work, where my go-to lens at f/3.6 (which had to be dialed at f/5.6 due to wide softness) sometimes just has be pushing the ISO into grain to produce the images I need. Working at f/1.8 produces good quality, while allowing me to jump from 1/60s to 1/120s and drop the ISO from 3200 to 800, and the improvement in image quality is amazing. Cleaner movements with no blur, and very true color with very minimal visible grain.

As far as construction goes, remember that this is plastic, even down to the mounting ring, so keep this in mind. This lens will not tolerate the abuse I sadly inflict on my other lenses, and I advise that this should never be on the camera when it is in a slung-over-the-shoulder not-using-it situation. The f/1.4 or f/1.2L would be a lot tougher, and if this lens continues to dominate on my shooting as it is right now, I will have no choice but to pick up a better lens because I WILL KILL THIS, with out a doubt.

As I said above, the 5-blade window will produce some odd effects, so this is really the only part that I had to take a star off. In bright sunlight or a strobed studio, this won't really affect image quality tremendously; the bokeh won't be as buttery as the f/1.4 or f/1.2L, or even alternatives like Sigma's f/1.4, but they are still quite smooth. Note though that when getting into high contrast, especially night photography, bright objects will be skewed into 5 pointed stars, and this can be distracting or even ruin what would be a very nice shot. Similarly, at very tight apertures (f/22) this same effect can intrude on your photos, so it would be a better idea to widen the lens up a bit and drop the shutter time and ISO to compensate.

product_title: JVC GC-XA1 Adixxion HD Action Video Camera with 1.5-Inch LCD - Black
review_headline: Best Action Cam Value for the Money
review_body:
I have been eyeing a GoPro for a while but hesitated to make the plunge due to the cost. I shoot HD video with high end Canon DSLRs so I knew that any action cam would not come close to the quality I get with a DSLR and L series lens. However, I don't necessarily want to mount that gear on my Jeep to have a rock fly up and crack the lens, or worse. I was pleased to see that the action cam market has become more competitive and that I had options. After reviewing a fair mount of footage from the GoPro Hero 3 Black, I decided that the quality of 4K video was not high enough to convince me to drop the extra cash. At then end of the day, an action cam sensor is not going to come close to comparing to higher end video cameras and SLRS. I had a few different recording needs: Jeep trail cam, timelapse, and possibly to use as an auxiliary camera for wedding video.

I chose the JVC Adixxion after watching a number of online comparisons. It seemed to me that the white balance and exposure adjustment were better on the JVC. I have been pleased with the performance of both, in real life. I have driven through dark interstate tunnels that have abrupt transitions to daylight and been very pleased with the JVC responded. I am also extremely pleased with the image stability.I also like the way you can mount and record in either portrait or landscape mode and the built in standard tripod screw mounts. This makes the camera compatible with existing equipment and the standard Gorilla Pods out of the box. I have successfully paired it with both my Android tablet and my PC. The LCD seems like a must. I am not sure how GoPro users do without it. I am also pleased to be able to record while charging via USB. My car charger for my phone has a USB port that I am able to plug a longer camera cable into and charger while driving and recording.

The one complaint I have read is about the sound quality, and in particular when there is any type of wind noise. For now, I have remedied it with a strip of gaffer tape and plan to find a piece of earphone foam for a more permanent solution. The sound is OK. Truthfully, I would probably rarely use the sound from any action cam because I prefer a higher quality audio than any action cam would deliver and not likely interested in integrating road noise into my video production.

I wish that JVC had created user forums so that there was a central community of users. I have found information and reviews spread out across the net.

In terms of accesories, I use the roll bar mount and am quite pleased with it. right now, I have it mounted on my safari style roof rack. It would work at other points on my Jeep as well. I have also purchased the Wasabi power package, which includes 2 extra batteries and a dedicated charger, which allows me to do a lot more recording.

I purchased mine NIB on eBay for under $150. This was by far the best choice for the money for me. product_title: Elk Products ELK952 In-Line Telco Surge Protectr
review_headline: Installs easily, with a few extra parts
review_body:
I ordered this protector for my DSL modem even though that's not the real purpose for which this product is designed. I ordered it because my AT&T DSL went down at the central office and when it came back, my DSL modem had died so I had to buy a new one (an Actiontec). The ELK-952 surge protector's got RJ-45 (Ethernet) connectors and sockets and residential DSL lines currently use the smaller RJ-11 (telephone) connectors. No matter, the RJ-11 plug on the DSL cable from the phone jack fits nicely in the RJ-45 socket in this protector. There's a bit of extra room on either side but the fit is nice and snug.

The surge protector's other end is supposed to go to your equipment (supposedly a security system but it's a DSL modem in my case). The surge protector's RJ-45 plug won't fit in the modem's RJ-11 jack so I purchased two items: an RJ-45 to RJ-45 straight-thru inline coupler and a second, short DSL cable with RJ-11 plugs. The pair of items cost another $5. Add the thru coupler to the surge protector's RJ-45 cable and plug one end of the new DSL cable into the other end of the coupler. Plug the new DSL cable's RJ-11 plug at the other end into the modem to complete the phone-jack connection. It all snaps together.

The final step is to ground the earth wire on the surge protector. I crimped a spade lug to the green earth wire and locked it under a screw on my grounded power strip. You might prefer to use the screw holding the cover on an ac electrical duplex outlet.

No perceptible difference in DSL performance. That's good. Protected? We'll see.

product_title: Pentax K-30 Weather-Sealed 16 MP CMOS Digital SLR
review_headline: Simply the best DSLR in it's class
review_body:
I've been a Pentax user since their initial foray into the DSLR's and this is the best of the lot.

While I've been with Pentax for awhile I'm no fanboy. Before this upgrade from a Pentax Kr I researched all the major brands Nikon, Canon, Sony and Olympus however when I matched them up against each other the K30 was by far the most camera for the money.

I'm into still photography so the one area that Pentax lags behind (video) wasn't much of a concern for me. I seriously considered dumping Pentax and going with another brand but at this level of camera the drawbacks to the other brands were just to many. Those camera were nothing more than point and shoots on steroids. They had none to little room for the growing photographer unless of course you bought a higher level of camera.

This camera offers so many features that are usually found on camera's hundreds of $ more expensive.

* Weather and dust sealing
* Electronic level
* 100% view through the viewfinder
* Lens Auto Focus Fine Adjustment for up to 20 different lenses
* Focus Peaking
* Programmable Front and Rear Wheels
* It not only has aperture and shutter priority (Tv, Av) it also has TAv(shutter-aperture priority ,Automatic Exposure)
* Two USER Modes to save your favorite settings

....and much more....

The best though is the cameras exceptional IQ and handling of noise. I am no longer concerned with shooting at 3200 ISO and even up to 6400. ISO 3200 shots need little to no work while 6400 may need some depending on its use.

Many fan-boys of other brands will point out the lack of lenses for Pentax. I have never found this to be the case there is a lens for everything I do. I've got 5 lenses some primes including the 100 mm Micro lens, and the Pentax 18-250mm, I've not wanted for anything.

While this camera may be classified as entry level by some it has many features of a prosumer camera athundreds of $ less. It's an easy enough camera for a beginner and has enough room for even the intermediate photographer to grow.

I would highly recommend this camera to anyone considering a DSLR whether a beginner or intermediate user this camera will satisfy.

Amazon did their usual wonderful job in getting this camera to me on time and also a shout out for Emmy Photography for offering the great Price. Thanks to both.

product_title: Nikon COOLPIX P330 12.2 MP Digital Camera with 5x Zoom
review_body:
If you had a P300 you were probably very happy with it. P300 always took very good low light photos, but there was a lot of noise processing, making pictures somewhat soft. P330 with a larger sensor and options to regulate noise reduction help make photos even better. I was not near US so I couldn't buy the camera from Amazon, I bought it in Hong Kong.... for about $20 more. I also considered Olympus XZ-10, as they had it available in Hong Kong. It is a nice camera, but I found some sample pics on the internet that raised concerns about quality of daytime pics in bright light. So I chose to stay loyal to Nikon and I don't regret it. I haven't had too much time to test it fully, but so far I am impressed with speed of focus, excellent macro, great low light capability. Only thing I would trade is GPS for a function ring on the front. Build quality is fantastic. Overall, especially for the price and compactness, a great pocket camera.

I did notice some comments regarding the power button. I have no fingernails to speak of, and I have zero problems turning the camera on. Yes, you have to give it a solid press... it is a mechanism to prevent the camera from turning on in you pocket by an accidental press (your finger will go on the power button when you pull it out of the pocket), possibly breaking the lens. There is a slight lag in the first set of menus, but once you get in the menu there is no lag, in any case that can be resolved by a firmware update. I think the quality is great. Camera turns on quickly, playback is instant. No issues. In the end, in this segment people are in it for the compactness & picture quality. I think this camera delivers great value for the price.

product_title: Nikon 60mm f/2.8G ED Auto Focus-S Micro-Nikkor Lens for Nikon DSLR Cameras - Fixed
review_headline: great for macro, bad for anything else
review_body:
Like many people before me, i bought this lens with dreams of having a 2 for 1 macro/portrait lens combo. After some real world testing, i have realized this lens doesn't quite live up to the aforementioned dream.
As a macro lens i have nothing but great words to say, as do others so i won't bore anyone with those details.

As a portrait lens, some things of note:
1. This lens seems to have great troubles focusing on anything more than about 5 feet away in anything but perfect lighting conditions. At one point, I stood trying to focus on a tree with some moderately harsh backlighting and the thing just would not focus. It THOUGHT it locked focus but upon zooming in, it was not.
2. Spherecromatism on this thing is pretty severe wide open. If you are somewhat close to the subject and don't have EXACT focus, specular reflections on the eye will appear as magenta or green blobs, depending on front or back focus.
3. Bokeh on this lens isn't what its hyped to be, at least not for me, and it doesn't handle out of focus highlights very gracefully.
4. As another reviewer stated, this lens flares up very easily if there is any type of adverse back lighting.

In a studio environment these problems would mostly become minor nuisances, but in the real world they are deal killers. Sorry, i really wanted to like this lens, but i could not. If you are expecting to use this as a portrait lens, i would think twice, except for studio use. Even the 'ED' glass and 'Nanocoating' can't save it.
Clearly Nikon had to make some compromises to get the extreme flat sharpness.

review_body:
This is a our first DSLR and we purchased it for quasi commercial purposes. We are a small business and bought the camera to take pictures of our products for online sales as well as for personal use.

We are extremely pleased with the camera for the price. The photo quality has been a huge step up from the point and shoot that we had been using (Stylus Tough). The camera body is light and compact. It's hard to take pictures if you don't have the camera with you, so size was a selling point for us.

Battery life seems good. So far our limiting factor has been our card size not our battery life. This camera takes both JPEGs and Raw photos, so anyone moving into their first DSLR should be prepared to invest in some memory, the pictures are huge.

This camera has been budget friendly for a new business. About 2 years ago we purchased a Stylus tough for only marginally less, and the resultant pictures were pretty lousy (in fact we usually opted to use our phones instead). So we have been quite pleased to see a slight step up in price resulted in a huge jump in quality and flexibility.

We liked that this camera came with a lens (great for a first time buyer). We will likely be adding a 55-200 mm zoom lens in the next few months.

Some of the downsides to the camera: the small size of the view finder, the low resolution in the lcd screen and that it is not weatherproofed.

The weatherproofing is a bit of an issue, since we spend a lot of time on the water. Our next camera (likely a few years down the road) will be weatherproofed.
