product_title: Professional BG-E9 Battery Grip + 2 LP-E6 Batteries for Canon EOS 60D Digital SLR Camera
review_headline: Every included product failed within 15 months of purchase
review_body:
I'm going to divide this review into two parts: The grip and the batteries.

The first thing to fail was the grip. I was doing on assignment when it just stopped working. Using the 6-AA magazine, I was forced to go back and get an LP-E6 costing me time and shots. All the batteries were charged properly, I verified later. The grip completely failed. After that day, not even the LP-E6 battery magazine worked.

As far as quality goes, if you take out the part where it fails, the grip was alright. As far as quality goes, it doesn't compare. For the price, the quality is what you can expect.

Overall, the grip is not worth the money. 50 bucks compared to 250 seems like a great deal, but at the end of the day I ended up spending the 250 anyway, and it cost me pictures. It's not reliable.

About the batteries: I've recently upgraded to the 5Dmk2, which is now my primary camera. I continued to use the LP-E6 style batteries included in this package deal with my new camera. On two more shoots, these batteries have failed. Luckily, I had extra batteries with me, so I didn't lose any shots.

Now, both of the batteries just blink when plugged in. They aren't recognized by the camera as plugged in. I use a battery grip on the 5Dmk2, and it just recognizes the functioning battery.

Canon's branded LP-E6 batteries are way too expensive, so I can understand the appeal for these. However, they've both failed. Luckily, they haven't caused problems inside of the camera.

I own some other non-Canon batteries. I've never had any problems with Opteka. That's just my experience.

Good luck. Stay away from this product.

product_title: Canon Remote Shutter Release for Canon Rebel
review_body:
I needed a shutter remote so I could take long night exposures with my Canon T2i in bulb mode. I ordered this on Sunday, April 29, and received in on Wednesday, May 2. It came with my regular mail, in a bubble wrap envelope. The box doesn't have a brand name on it, but on the remote itself is says \\"Progo(tm)\\". Though very similar, it's obviously not the same exact remote I see in the photo here on Amazon. However, I'd imagine it works just as well. The actual remote is very light and plasticy. There is a little texture on the front and back for grip, otherwise it's very smooth. I measured the cord at 35.5 inches long (just about 3 feet) and the remote on the end adds another three inches, making for a total of 38.5 inches long. This should be all I ever need. NO BATTERIES REQUIRED. As I press the button down, I can just barely feel it click as it reaches the halfway point, which of course focuses the camera (if auto-focus is enabled). I press it down all the way, and it takes the photo. Simple as that... I've tried one photo using bulb mode on my camera. I pressed the button down all the way, then locked it into place by sliding it up. I took a nice 40-second exposure in my room with zero camera shake! I tried playing around with the remote while the button was locked into place, flicking it and lightly hitting it, and the button didn't come out of the locked position. It's nice and tight, so I don't have to worry about it sliding out during a long night exposure.

Overall, I'm very pleased with this product. I can't wait to use it with my camera mounted on a tripod :) If you want to see it in use, there is actually a video on Youtube featuring the same exact remote I got. Make sure you type in the brand name I mentioned and look for the title \\"Remote Camera Shutter Release Unboxing and Review\\" by dorrmann.

A little reminder for those who also plan on using this device for long exposures: Remember to turn Image Stabilization OFF when using yourcamera on a tripod.

review_body:
I own two of these camera's - both bought here on Amazon - one back in December 2009 and the other last month, August 2012. I keep one in my briefcase and one in my truck's console. I am not a professional photographer. The primary function of these cameras for me is everyday stuff for when I don't feel like carrying my full size Canon DSLR. That said I just don't understand how there are so many negative reviews for bad picture quality (and even one because the person dropped and broke it - it's a camera, not a rubber ball) - and I end up with two cameras that take excellent photographs. The odds would appear to certainly not be in my favor. At least one of these according to all the reviews should be a piece of crap camera - if not both.

Maybe I'm doing something wrong? I did review the manual before using to familiarize myself with the controls - maybe that was a mistake. I also don't judge quality by the camera screen - instead I download to my computer. That could be the problem there you think? I don't use the manual controls very often - mostly just the auto modes with the occasional selection of a specific scene to match the conditions. Starting to get bummed out here, really would like to jump on the bandwagon.

Seriously folks - own two as I said and they both take excellent pictures. I like the array of controls it comes with. I like the size and weight. Battery life is very good. I love the slide up/down front that covers the lens. Throw a 16 gig card in it and you can take over 7,000 pictures without downloading.

Does it take the same quality photographs as my $2,000.00 Canon? No. Of course not. Most people couldn't tell the difference though.

When I get a little time here I'll upload a few photos so the EXIF data can be viewed and quality compared.

product_title: Fotodiox Pro, Premium Grade Tripod Lens Collar for Canon EOS EF USM Lens 70-300mm F4-5.6L IS, as Canon Tripod Mount Ring C
review_body:
Fotodiox always sells quality accessories (I've ordered from them a few times), and this is mount ring is no exception. The color is a close match to the lens, and it feels like a well-machined piece of metal (fitting of the lens that mounts to it).

You're probably not going to leave the ring on when you're not using a tripod. I've read from other users of this lens and they say the ring provides leverage, but I didn't feel that way - it's kind of in the way when you're handholding. When you give the knob a half turn to tighten it around the lens, it makes a good, tight grip, and the rubber on the inside of the ring gives good protection for your lens - there's no metal-on-metal contact to speak of. However, be advised that the knob doesn't secure (unless I was doing something wrong) and can easily turn (especially when handholding), slightly loosening the ring. But there is NO DANGER whatsoever of the lens falling. There's a latch the keeps the ring from opening, and it functions very securely. I've never used the Canon ring so I can't say if it's the same way with that one, just thought readers should be aware. I still have no qualms about using this ring.

I was going to give it 4 stars because of the knob issue, but then I thought \\"It's not going to move a bit when mounted on a tripod,\\" and I thought about how much Canon is trying to rip people off with the cost of their mount ring (which should've come with an L lens this expensive and weighty anyway). And I bumped it back up to 5 stars. Highly recommended.

product_title: Sony Cyber-shot DSC-TX66 18.2 MP Digital Camera with 5x Optical Zoom and 3.3-inch OLED
review_headline: I really want to love this camera... (and now, I do - pl see update)
review_body:
but I end up only liking it. (updated on June 11, 2012)
Pros:
- Tiny size that rivals even the slickest smartphones
- Highly responsive touch screen interface (a first in this segment?)
- Negligible delay in \\"shooting\\" or focusing.
- Context-aware help files on the interactive screen (useful given the relatively new touchscreen interface)
- A reasonable alternative to lugging around a HD-video camcorder (it records in 29 min segments, so prepare for some minor editing to splice videos etc. having used this only once, I will update the review after more uses).

Cons:
- A flimsy-looking battery compartment and the need to carry around the charger (not a fun situation if you tend to go on long treks like I do). Overall, it looks so delicate that you will be tense handling it ( fear of dropping it or denting/scratching...)
- Some gimmicky special effects that may appeal to children but can be easily attained in both Android and iphone apps for less than 5$. [An exception is the partial color feature that works exceptionally well when there is a stark contrast in the subject (bright colored flowers and green leaves, for example) - this is a feature that is worthy of some exploration if you are into art photography].
- Despite the 18M resolution (also think larger file sizes), the photo quality is not comparable to those from DSLRs even for the same focal range (this one has an equivalent of 26-130 mm).

Ironically, a child may be better suited to handle the interface/controls but the camera looks so delicate, a child probably shouldn't handle it. Despite the innovative interface and brag-worthy ability to shoot in 3D (more money to spend on 3D TV and glasses?), tons of features packed into a tiny sleek design, the price point makes it difficult for an enthusiastic endorsement. At this price range, you must value the weight/size of the camera far more than the need to take better pictures with a DSLR...orlove the touchscreen interface to such extent that you will pay up from other options in this segment.

Update on 6/12/12
After a round of video capture using this camera for dance recitals, this has become my default device for all video recording (and for most pictures). The ease of high res video recording is absolutely breath-taking. The ease of set up, sharpness of the picture, the audio capture, response to zoom in recording mode - all aspects are very well worth the price. The compact size is truly deceiving when it comes to video capture.

review_headline: A Video Review of the Nikon D3200 Camera
review_body:
[[VIDEOID:mo32PSYEYNXY35Z]]I will have to warn you, before investing too much time in this review you should understand that I have geared it for the novice/Intermediate photographer and not for the advanced user. I say that because the D3200 is certainly a camera that is worthy for an advanced or professional photographer. In fact, the D3200 is a marvel since it is possible for a novice to take professional looking photographs with only a few hours of study, but it will also allow a professional all of the capability that they would want for premium quality prints.

Notes -

Image Quality - Absolutely top-notch - the Nikon D3200 takes super crisp photos with excellent color representation. The additional functionality allows more advanced users to maximize light, shutter speed, and zoom/focal points.

Why 24.2MP? - Why does someone want a camera with such high resolution? Well the answer is pretty straight-forward. A high resolution camera will allow you to zoom and crop any portion of your photograph without worrying about the image becoming grainy. This will allow you to zoom to a small area of interest and blow-it-up to a full scale print.

Multiple ISO Sensitivity Settings - The various ISO settings allow for changing light sensitivity without loss of image quality. This is similar to the \\"speed setting\\" of film cameras and the 100,400, etc films of previous years.

- Fit and Functionality - The Nikon D3200 feels great in you hands. While it is not *pocket sized* compared to the cheaper smaller cameras it is still light enough that you will not be fatigued after a day of shooting.

- Outputs/Inputs - The Nikon D3200 has inputs for a mic and GPS and it has HDMI and a standard AV output.

- VIdeo - The D3200 will take up to 20minutes of video at 1080P - the video quality is excellent.... I am not sure I would call it the equivalent of a full 1080P camcorder (Due to image stabilization and frame speed) it will certiainly work in a pinch.

- Burst Mode - The camera will take 4photos/second in a burst. This will help you find the *right* shot even during an accidental blink. If you have never used a camera with burst mode you will be amazed at how much easier this makes in taking photos of children.

Buffer - The Nikon D3200 has an internal buffer of (up to) 100 photos. This will allow you take a multitude of high resolution photos without having to wait for the camera to write to your memory card. On the topic of memory cards you will certainly only want to buy class 10 memory cards.

Camera Modes -

- Portrait - Used for Portraits with soft natural-looking skin tones. If the subject is far from the camera the background details will be softened.
- Night Portrait - Use for a natural balance between the main subject and the background in portraits taken in low light.
- Landscape - For vivid landscape shots when ample light is present.
- Sports - Fast shutter speeds freeze motion in order to capture fast acting sports moments.
- Close-up - For close up photos of flowers, photos, and small images taken at very close range.
- Child Use for snapshots of children. Clothing and background details are vividly rendered while skin tones remain soft and natural.

Final Verdict - Whether you a re a novice, intermediate, or advanced photographer you will likely be very pleased with the Nikon D3200. While you will need to spend a few hours with the manual all levels of photographers will be able to take stunning photographs. Highly Recommended!

review_headline: Not what I thought it would be
review_body:
I bought a Nikon Coolpix L120 camera, and while waiting to get it, looked for batteries and a charger for it. This charger states it's FOR the Nikon Coolpix L120, so came up in search. The Nikon chargers and batteries only come with 4 batteries and are much more expensive.
I saw that the extra 4 batteries with this were lower power (2900) but assumed they would also work, since it's FOR THE NIKON COOLPIX L120!
I got the camera and charger/batteries (from different places) The camera works with non rechargeable batteries but hardly works with the rechargeables. And I set the camera to \\"rechargeable\\". The 3100 batteries work for awhile, but the 2900 (even though I charged them till the red lights went out and left them an hour after to be sure) will turn the camera on, take 2 or 3 pictures than die and camera says \\"battery exhausted\\".
The camera manual tells the kind of batteries it uses, and for rechargeable says \\"4 EN MH2 rechargeable NI-MH batters...\\" and \\"EN-MH1 can't be used\\"
Are the ones that come with this charger maybe MH1? Who knows, where does it say?
And it says on the listing (for sale) they are for the Nikon Coolpix L120 camera.
I don't know what to do now, can I now buy more powerful batteries, maybe the ones made by Nikon and will they charge in this charger? Can I charge bigger, more powerful batteries in this? Do I now have to buy more batteries and another charger?
I was wary about buying a Nikon because it takes AA batteries, my Canon Rebel (I love but wanted more zoom and video) uses a square battery that comes with a charger (not AA, etc) The battery needs charging about once a week. I have had cameras that take regular batteries before and even with a charger it's a hassle.
I just thought batteries and a charger that says it's FOR the camera I bought would work.
I looked over many reviews, at least for cameras before I decided on the one I got (I am on limited income, too) but apparently didn't see reviews for this battery charger and batteries, beforehand.
It might be useful, charging batteries for my remote and other things I have that take batteries, but I'm going to have to buy something else for the Nikon Coolpix L120...
I know, I could probably return it, but that's a hassle, too and the bigger size batteries (if I keep them charged) seem to work for awhile.
LATER... I found the batteries work better when charged for a longer time. I now leave them plugged in overnight or all day. Even after the charged light goes off. The directions say to leave them plugged in for 30 mins after the light says they are charged, but I am leaving them longer. There are 2 sets of batteries so I eave one set in overnight and then the other all day. next time I buy a camera I will get one with a rechargable battery to use with it and not \\"sepeaate\\" AA, etc. ones. (which isn't the fault of the charger)

review_body:
(Update August 20, 2012) Accessory Genie, evidently as part of their routine customer follow-up, sent an email requesting information as to my satisfaction or concerns with my purchase of this camera pack. After I responded directing them to the original review, and simply mentioning the single flaw (along with an attached picture), they took it upon themselves to offer me a 10% refund, which I accepted. This offer on their part was evidently after reading the review. The entire correspondence with them was very satisfactory - especially as it was initiated by them - with email responses, and the refund, which were quick and very courteous. They evidently care about customer satisfaction. Ten percent may not seem to be much, but I'm perfectly happy with it as the flaw/damage was relatively easy to repair and now has minimal impact on the performance of that pocket, much less on the entire backpack.

(Original Review August 03, 2012) This backpack is made by/for Vivitar (apparently the DKS-18 model) and works well to carry, and provide easy access to, an SLR (digital or film), lenses, and several accessories. The sling feature works reasonably well from either side. The pack stands vertically pretty well even when reasonably full. Each flap is lined with a zippered mesh pocket to provide see-through storage for the user's choice of miscellaneous bits and pieces, keeping them in place and easily available.

The dividers in the main compartment are sturdy and can be readily repositioned using the hook-and-loop fastenings that are found in most camera bags. The bottom and top of the main compartment are fully covered with the loop fabric as are the sides of the longer dividers. The hook strips on the dividers are full-height and about an inch (2.5cm) wide. These features help provide stability to contents once all the dividers are in place. Although only one retention strap is provided, probably to reduce costs, it's not too difficult to find or even make more if desired.

For some reason, the card that had been attached to the backpack identifying it as a Vivitar product was removed prior to shipping. This was unquestionably intentional as the plastic bag covering the backpack had been cut to provide access to the card. The purpose in removing the card is unclear as permanently attached Vivitar labels were still in place. In addition, there was a small (1/2-inch (slightly > 1cm)) cut in the netting of the pocket on the inside of the upper flap. It is unclear whether this was a manufacturing defect or the result of removing some other attached item. I was able to repair this cut to my satisfaction, but it was disturbing. Had this damage gone unrepaired, it would have readily increased in size with use of the pocket.

The computer pocket would not accommodate my 17-inch HP notebook but would be fine for a smaller laptop, netbook, or any iPad. Note that I never intended to use this pocket for my notebook; the pocket just came as part of the design. If it was desired to include a computer, my choice would be a decidedly smaller and much lighter notebook or tablet. As with all but the most expensive similar cases, I'm not sure how comfortable it would be as a backpack while carrying the largest notebook that could fit into the compartment. This would significantly stiffen the section closest to the wearer's back and would probably diminish the ability of the pack to conform to the wearer. Again, this is an issue common to all such cases except those with the very best back shaping and padding, thereby substantially increasing price.

The back of the pack is well padded as are the straps. The straps are long enough to be sufficient for all but the very largest user (definitely over 6.5 feet tall or waist greater than 46 inches). Free ends of the shoulder and waist straps tuck away into retainers to keep them from flapping around. The strap to go across the chest can easily be lengthened/shortened but there is no provision for vertical adjustment of this strap. While this should not be an issue for most guys, some petite women might find it's placement uncomfortable. Fortunately, this strap is not necessary for casual backpack usage and is not used at all in the sling configurations.

The straps easily convert to the sling placement and the unused straps can be tucked into the padding to be kept out of the way and invisible. The youtube.com videos for the similar but substantially more expensive Tamrac Evolution 8 backpacks (just enter 'Tamrac Evolution 8' in the youtube search bar), show many features, including sling configuration, common to this Vivitar pack.

The additional items (Accessory Genie Cleaning Kit with Microfiber Cloth , Accessory Bag , and Airbrush) included with the bag were (IMO) low in quality and obviously included just to sweeten the pot so they could be mentioned in the description. Anyone spending the money for an SLR and lenses would probably want to buy cleaning supplies that would work properly without risking damage to the camera. Many choices are available, but those included in this kit are definitely inadequate. Rather than the 'Microfiber Cloth', lens tissues are available from many manufacturers and suppliers. Two such are [[ASIN:B001LQ5XLS Rosco Lens Tissue 4\\"x6\\" 100 Sheet Booklet]] and [[ASIN:B005WG6WS6 Cosmos ® 80 PCS Camera Lens cleaning tissue paper cleaner + Cosmos cable tie]]. While I use microfiber cloths for my eyeglasses, the risk of scratching camera lenses and their multilayer coatings is too great for me. Microfiber lens cloths are expected to be reused, risking grinding miniscule particles against the lens. Using a fresh, clean lens tissue is much safer, especially when combined with a high-quality cleaning fluid, such as [[ASIN:B000F34FVM Purosol All Natural Lens Cleaner 1oz.]], and only after blowing off any/all loose dust or grit.

The 'Airbrush' in the kit is insufficient in at least three ways: the rubber bulb does not blow enough air to dislodge any but the very loosest dust, the brush interferes with the air flow, and bristles cannot be readily protected from damage when not in use. Effective dust blowers are pretty much limited to the Giottos Rocket Blasters, such as [[ASIN:B000L9OIQ2 Giottos AA1920 Rocket Air Blaster Small (Black)]], or [[ASIN:B00017LSPI Giottos AA1900 Rocket Air Blaster Large - Black]], due to quality of construction and effectiveness. Others are less effective or have other design/construction flaws or issues. Canned air is practical but also has limitations.

To be safe, brushes must be soft and have some way to be protected from damage and dust/debris when not in use. Many are retractable which at least protects them from most problems when stored. Keeping them in a 'zippy' bag provides the rest of the protection.

That it is designed to accept a tripod and includes a rain cover (in the top compartment) may be seen as extras but were also on my list of necessities. By the way, if it was ever desired to use this pack for something other than a camera bag, say as a standard daypack, all the internal dividers, even the bottom of the top compartment, are designed to be removed leaving an empty shell with very ready access from the top, sides, and front (as viewed from behind the wearer).

In its price range, I have found no other camera pack that works as well and has as many features as this Vivitar case. The few negatives are primarily due to limitations imposed by the price range and are minimal as practical considerations for all but the most demanding users. These will find themselves needing to pay much more for backpacks to suit their needs. This case will suit most users very well until their needs outstrip its capabilities. review_body: This camcorder appears to be a great performer, except that you cannot shoot HD in anything less than 60p. Yes, you can convert the footage to 30p or less, but we all know that this prevents you from employing the \\"180 degree shutter\\" rule to get smooth motion at anything less than 60p. product_title: Canon PowerShot ELPH 320 16.1MP Digital Camera with 3.2-Inch TFT LCD
review_headline: Not what I expected, Canon seems to have cheaped out over the years.
review_body:
I used to sell cameras a few years back and had always wanted a Canon because of they quality, they used to have nice heavy casing, almost a metal feeling. The casing on this unit is very cheap plastic. It looks like it's going to scratch very easy, so I have to be careful with it. The door that you open to put the battery in also seems very cheap and flimsy.

I liked the idea of having a touch screen and more importantly, wifi. The touch screen is not very good as other ratings has indicated. It's not like a cell phone touch screen, it seems slow and outdated. It's not too bad because you can use your fingernail and it works well that way. The menu is complicated and takes some getting used to. Everything is touch screen except for the review button, the picture taking button, the on/off button, zoom and switching it to auto mode, everything else is done via the touch screen, so if you're not a fan of touch screens, this is not the camera for you.

The wifi works and I can directly post my pictures to facebook. Again, it's not like transfering pictures from a cell phone, but works ok. If this is the reason you're looking at this camera, you could always buy an eye-fi card which uses wifi to transfer images to your computer, that way you can make pretty much any camera transfer photos through your wifi connection. Had I been able to try this camera before I bought it, I probably would have done this and bought a different camera.

Overall, it's a decent camera and the price wasn't extremelly bad, but it's just not the quality that I'm used to seeing from Canon. I've only had it a few hours, so as far as reliability, I'm not sure, but so far so good.

product_title: Vivitar 8 MP Compact System Camera with 2.4-Inch LCD Body Only
review_body: I'm a PADI certified diver and I bought this camera to use when I go scuba diving.  I got it at a clearance price of around $50.  I've had it around a year and so far it's worked good.  Before you consider the quality of the photos to be junk understand how underwater photography works.  Things are a LOT different and light changes a lot under water.  In a swimming pool not as much but in open water (lakes, oceans, rivers) water is not as clear.  The first color you lose as you go deeper is red.  This affects your photos and is NOT the camera's fault.  The high end cameras use special filters and color correction programs to fix this issue.  Also the high end cameras have the strobe (flash) off to the side at a 45 degree angle which is the best for underwater (you ALWAYS use a flash underwater even on sunny days to help with colors and photo quality etc).  This camera has the flash right above the lens which is not ideal.  This is a good camera for a great price.  Like anything else, you get what you pay for.  If you want photos with quality good enough for National Geographic then this is not the camera for you.  Most of the water leaking issues can be prevented by inspecting, cleaning and lubricating the O-ring seal.  Even though it's only rated to 30 feet I've taken it routinely to around 45 ft with no problems.  Had I paid $600 then I would be very disapponted with the functions and photo quality but considering it's low cost, it's well worth it.  Disposible cameras are around $12 and then you have to pay developing fees.  So even if you only use this camera a few times you break even.  Considering water proof housings for non-waterproof cameras are between $150-$200 this is a great deal.  I would buy another one even if this one wears out at some point.

review_body: I bought this kit the day after I received my RX100. Went on a 7-day cruise four days later. Charged the Sony battery and the two Bowers. Used the Bower charger on the Sony battery and it worked just fine. Day 1 of the trip loaded a Bower battery in the RX100 and never looked back. Took 700 pictures in a week and did a partial internal charge on the same Bower battery in the camera one time. Carried the Sony battery and the other Bower in my camera case and never used them. I did a lot of viewing and deleting as I went. I took nine short videos (average of 2 minutes) and the rest were the 700 shots at 20MP using the two-minute shutdown feature on the camera to conserve battery life. The battery indicator on the camera stayed full a long time before it showed usage. A minor issue since I had two others ready to go. The Bowers are rated at 1800 mAh. Sony at 1240 mAh. Some say the higher rating is exaggerated but I would be hard to convince at this point. Very good bargain since the Sony battery is a little less than twice the price for the kit. I sold digital cameras for almost eight years, owned 5 high-end Sonys from the F505 to the R1, which I still travel with. product_title: BlackRapid RS-7 Curve Camera Strap
review_body:
I have tried several different camera straps over the years, from the stiff and uncomfortable straps which come with cameras to neoprene wonders intended to reduce the burden of carrying a heavy DSLR, but the Black Rapid RS-7 hits the target like no other. The design is marvelously simple yet effective, crossing the body with the strap to hang the weight of the camera on the opposite shoulder, allowing the camera to hang at the perfect point for grasping with the hand, and the camera to slide along the length of the strap into perfect shooting position.

The only shortcoming I have found is that the shoulder pad tends to creep, leaving the shoulder and migrating down the chest or the back as the camera is moved along the strap. A simple change of material contacting the shoulder would prevent this. I have other straps with rubberized materials which grip clothing and this material would keep the shoulder pad where it belongs. To solve the problem I ordered the BRAD accessory strap, which keeps the RS-7 from creeping by adding a connection under the arm from back to front but also adds a layer of complexity to an otherwise elegantly simple idea, and looking a little dorky to boot. Now I feel like I'm wearing some sort of posture correction device when I'm shooting.

However, the Black Rapid is still the best option for anyone who is tired of a heavy DSLR rig hanging around the neck. You'll be glad you bought it.

review_headline: Reasonably well engineered, with a few minor issues.

Some of the cap-screws have been replaced by knobs, which may be different than the knobs in the picture.
2) There is a degree scale on the side of the unit, but the knob masks a pretty large area, making it difficult to see exactly where you are.
3) There is a compass in the knob that holds the wedge to the tripod. Unfortunately, the threaded rod that screws into the knob is a) likely to be magnetized just enough to skew the needle b) unlikely to be fully tightened without popping the compass out.

product_title: Bluecell Brown Color NEX-7 leather classic DC digital camera protection case/bag/cover for Sony Nex 7 with 18-55mm Lens Camera
review_headline: NOT A GOOD FIT FOR NEX 7
review_body:
There are very few camera cases for the NEX-7 on the market right now, and this is one of them. The price is good, but I would not recommend it for the following reasons:

1. The case indeed fits the camera body and the 18-55 kit lens, but it is loose, bulky, and at least for the lens, there is ample room for the lens to move around inside the housing.
2. There is a large (massive actually) tripod adapted screw that connects the camera to the body portion of the case. It is clumsy, and is the only thing that is securing the case to the body. It is difficult and tedious to unscrew.
3. The clumsy screw makes it impossible to place the camera flat on a surface. With the case attached, the camera will tip onto the lens or to one side.
4. The lens portion of the case is, as mentioned, too large, and it attaches to the body portion of the case with two large, bottom mounted snaps. These snap securely, but when opened, the lens portion hangs below the camera. It is sufficiently bulky to affect camera balance, and it gets in the way of shooting.
5. With the case attached, there is no access to the battery/SD card door or to the video and mic inputs/outputs.

The construction of the case is what you might expect at this price, evincing a strong chemical smell, and provoking serious doubt as to whether this is leather or some man-made material. I think that a NEX 7 likely deserves something nicer, or at least something that will not hinder its small form factor or shooting abilities.

product_title: Nikon COOLPIX AW100 16 MP CMOS Waterproof Digital Camera with GPS and Full HD 1080p Video
review_body:

I'm an avid photographer, but not dependent on having a fancy camera. My last point-and-shoot more than lived up to my expectations, letting me take snapshots, close-ups of flowers, and landscape photos. But I REALLY wanted a waterproof camera so I tried this one.

The photos were washed out and often out of focus. Even when mostly in focus, the focus was often soft around the edges. The color quality was lousy - both washed out and too dark in the same image. Close-ups were a nightmare - I had to delete almost all of the pictures I took of tropical flowers because they were SO out of focus - and landscapes were better but still solidly in the mediocre range. And the user interface (button placement etc) was clunky too.

I was less dissatisfied with the underwater shots... but then, my expectations were lower. I expected a memento from the trip, not an image I could hang on a wall, and that's what I got. Overall I've never had so much trouble with a camera!

product_title: Dakota Alert DCPA-2500 Duty Cycle Probe Alert 2500' Kit (Black White)
review_headline: Great Product and Terrific range (600' in my case)
review_body: Installed this a week ago. Had a buried probe driveway alert at my last house and like knowing when someone is coming up my long driveway, without all the false alarms associated with motion detectors, so I got this for the new house. I buried the probe 8 to 10 inches in the ground. The probe is magnetic and senses metal so it only alerts to metal, like cars, ATV's and lawnmowers. My house is over 600 feet from where I buried the probe and I haven't missed a single vehicle since installation, even with the receiver panel being inside my house, wall mounted and on the opposite side of the house, from the transmitter box.  This system will be in the ground for many, many years. I like to head off problems before they start so I wanted to offer the probe and wiring all the protection I could. Since I was going to have to dig a small trench to bury everything, I figured putting it in conduit would keep the wire from getting nicked or corroded in the ground. I went to Lowe's and grabbed a couple of lengths of PVC pipe and fittings. I needed about 18" of 1.5" pipe to go around the probe and used 1/2" PVC pipe for the wire itself. The unit comes with 50' of wire on the probe. I only needed 15'. I didn't want to cut the wire since I wanted the option of moving this setup to a different location in the future, that might need the extra wire. So what I did was put an 18" piece of 4" pvc pipe inline right before the transmitter box. I just let the 1/2" pvc run wild into the 4" section of pvc on both ends of the 4" section. There's a gap between the 1/2" pvc pipes and I just looped up all the excess wire and kept it within the 4" pvc pipe. I duct taped both ends of the 4" pvc around the 1/2" pvc to keep dirt from getting in the 4" pvc. I could have easily shortened the wire because it just goes to 2 wire clamps on the circuit board and you have to take the 2 wires loose to put the wire in conduit anyway. Even with using conduit, it only took an hour or so to dig the 12 foot long little trench for conduit and probe and finish the installation.  I did place the probe and transmitter at an opening in my fence where the driveway comes through. This meant a car couldn't dodge to the left or right and miss tripping the alert. If you can find a similiar choke point, along your driveway, you'll never have a missed alert.  I buried the probe parallel to my gravel driveway about a foot or so off to the side of the gravel where the ground was much easier to dig in than the driveway itself.  You don't have to put the probe and wire in conduit but it doesn't take much time or effort to do it and makes it much less likely the wire will ever get nicked and knock out the system. This system is rated to 2500' but I only needed a little over 600'. I can't say about longer distances, since I haven't tried them, but it is working great with my 600'. Contrary to another review of this product I read before buying it, I found the quality of construction of the transmitter and receiver to be good. The transmitter box is a nice heavy waterproof plastic box with a door, with the circuit board and batteries within it.  I also bought the birdhouse cover for the transmitter box that Dakota sells. It has grooves that perfectly fit the transmitter box. Because of the grooves, the birdhouse easily slides down over the transmitter box and is secure. UV rays make plastic weak and brittle so the birdhouse should add extra years to life of the system and also makes it so you don't notice the black plastic transmitter box.  My ground is flat with a few trees between the transmitter at the entrance and the receiver in the house. I like a heads up when company is coming, so I love my new Dakota system. The receiver is more sophisticated than my old system. It has several functions like, telling me through LED blinks how many times someone has come in or out of the driveway while I was gone, several different chime choices, great volume, 5 minute system delay with push of a button, so you can leave early in the  morning without tripping the chime as you pass the probe and waking everyone up. I had a couple of questions while installing and called the maker. They answered the phone immediately and knew the answers. Great Product and price.  One last thing. I installed this while no one else was at my house. Didn't think I would be able to test it since I didn't have anyone to listen for the chime while I was in the car tripping it. Using the function that makes the LED flash showing how many times it's been tripped since the last reset, I was able to leave, come back and confirm the system had been tripped twice. So I was able to install it and test it, by myself. If you need super long distance, they also have a MURS system that uses a probe, rated to a couple of miles and includes voice communication (seemed more like a commercial system and way more distance and features than I needed).  UPDATE July 2013: It's been well over a year since I installed this. I've had zero problems and I'm very pleased with my purchase. I don't know if it's because I put my wiring and probe in PVC conduit, which breaks its contact with the earth, but the system never gives false alerts because of lightning storms, which we have plenty of in this area.  I don't have a lot of traffic, but after a year, I still haven't had to install new batteries in the transmitter. I should swap them out anyway though, so they don't corrode. The inside unit is plugged into the wall, so no batteries. It's never missed a car coming, except when one of my teenagers sometimes turns it off to sneak out LOL, sad but true.  UPDATE March 2016: Still going strong.

product_title: CowboyStudio Mini Table Top Tripod
review_body:
What were you expecting for $15? For that much money it's a pretty good bargain.

First the bad: it's very cheaply made. The legs open wide but they don't open against hard stops, so the whole thing is a bit flexy when set up. The leg extensions only give you about another maybe 1.5\\" of length, so they probably just should have made one piece legs that were a bit longer. The bubble level is useless because it's on the fore-aft tilt axis, rather than the left right, where you would want it to be to correct for the horizon being horizontal. Yeah, I guess you could rotate your camera 90 degs so that it works, but then the flip portrait/landscape hinge is oriented wrong. Sigh. The 'fluid' head is not fluid in the least, and what looks like the tilt up-down axis tightening screw is actually the rotate left right axis screw. There is a little suction cup thing on the bottom of the riser tube. What that's supposed to do I'm not sure. I guess if you mounted the camera on a sloping car hood, you might be able to suck the cup down to keep it from sliding off. Hope your camera's not too expensive.

On the other hand, I still like this tripod because it has a quick release plate, and because of that portrait/landscape quick flip hinge. A lot of mini-pods don't have either.

For those wondering, the quick release plate is not compatible in size with any other quick release I've ever seen. It's 37mm squar-ish with beveled edges. But the bevels are only on two sides rather than all four so you can't quickly rotate your camera on the mount receiver to try and take advantage of that bubble level. If you were wondering if this fit into the Sima Quick Connect system, that plate is a bit smaller at about 36mm. I actually am using the Sima plates and those adapters, and made that plate fit into this tripod by gluing a little 1mm thick metal shim into the mount plate. Works fine, and the Sima plates have bevels on all 4 edges.

It folds up to a pretty small length, but it's pretty chunky so not something you're going to shove in your pocket or anything.

So I'm only giving it 3 stars but I still like it and plan to use it.

I'm using it with a Sony NEX-5n at the moment, which is a pretty small camera. If you have a bigger SLR or something with a larger zoom, this might be borderline too small and flexy.

product_title: ContourROAM Hands-free HD Camcorder
review_body:
We are using this as a car dash cam. The video is adequate, but low quality HD. The resolution may be there, but the CCD or whatever it is that is actually capturing the image is not the best. It has a few dead/flickering pixels. They aren't really all that visible while the camera is in motion, but at a dead stop you can just see them. License plates are not readable in low light conditions, and even during the day using the HD setting they can be difficult. The Storyteller software that you can download with the device is pretty much useless. It does not have any editing features at all, unfortunately you're forced to download it in order to change the camera settings. It's main function is to offload the video to your computer or upload it to the manufacturer's version of YouTube. That way, everyone can see how cool the Contour is and all the cool people using it. Don't bother using it, just use YouTube or whatever your favorite video sharing service is.

Drawbacks as a dash cam:

Cannot charge or power the device and record video at the same time. Once the battery is dead, that's it. Gotta re-charge it before you can record more video.

Laser level feature is useless in daylight and has very short visible range. Not even sure why the product has it. Can't think of any use for the camera that it would be needed.

Limited recording time/no continuous loop recording time. Once the memory card is full, you're done. You need to hook it up to a computer to delete unwanted files, and unless you've got someone in the car with a PC that can do it for you on the road, or a spare memory card, you're done.

Must use camera software to change settings, there are no buttons on the camera that allow you to do this on the fly.

Storyteller software has no editing capability.

The Good parts:

It's very small and unobtrusive. Does not occupy or block your vision when mounted in the car.

Big on/off switch. Makes it easy to use.

Size again - Small size means its easy to toss in the glove box, backpack or whatever so it isn't left in the car to tempt thieves.

Wide field of view. 170 degrees means you can capture a lot of action.

Decent battery life.

Decent memory capacity. Enough for several hours of driving footage.

This thing is tough. While I wouldn't want to drop it on the glass lens end, the device is solidly built and can stand some knocks.

Low light video is good compared to many devices, but it cannot handle high contrast lighting.

Other thoughts:

Whenever we see something we want to note (i.e. wreck, stupid driver) we turn the device off and wait a few seconds, then turn it back on. This ends the file and saves it, then starts a new one. That way we know the event is at the end of the clip and don't need to go searching through an hour-long clip to find it.

It should have the option to overwrite the oldest file on memory.

DO NOT BUY:

Another battery. You cannot change the internal one on the fly, so don't bother getting one unless you plan on needing it in the future.

The car charger, for the previously mentioned charging/recording issue. Unless you simply plan on charging it in the car; but then you're going to need another memory card, too, as the card will likely be full if you've run the battery down while recording.

The suction-cup mount. See my review there about the problems with it.

OVERALL:

Adequate for around-town driving. Plan on hooking it up to your computer every time you're finished for the day to delete all the unwanted files residing on the chip, and offload the ones you wish to keep. If you don't, your card will be full and the camera will no longer record. Video quality is acceptable, but not HD-worthy. Operation, once set up, is pretty foolproof. We used the included adhesive helmet mount and stuck it dead-center on our dash overlooking the hood. Works fine.

review_body:

This case is ideal for my use on hikes. The case fits on to an existing strap on my bag, so no worries that it doesn't have velcro. I much prefer the solid strap on the bag, but if I were going to use it on my belt, I would understand the inconvenience.

I carry a spare battery on longer hikes and the small pouch on the outside offers more than enough space (I could probably fit two if I needed both). The front zipper would certainly hold a spare memory card, but I rarely take enough pictures to warrant bringing one.

Protection is key for me and this case delivers. Not only does the case shed water (only had a light rain on our last hike), but it also offers enough padding that an accidental drop from my bag was not a concern. I'm pretty careful with my camera, so I imagine this is all the protection I need. I dropped it from about waist-high when we were loading back up to return home and it bounced harmlessly on the trail.

Basically this seems like a pretty minimalist case. Not a lot of extra room, but certainly enough for my day hikes. product_title: Tamron AF 70-300mm f/4.0-5.6 SP Di USD XLD Digital SLR Cameras
review_body:
The Vibration Control (VC) on this lens is quite amazing. I'm using this on a Nikon D5100 and with the camera mounted on a lightweight tripod with VC turned off and the lens on full zoom, tapping on the tripod with my finger causes obvious vibrations in the camera monitor. Turning on VC and doing the same tapping produces a rock solid image. It's really quite a difference between off and on. With VC on it's like the image is locked in place.

If you listen closely, you can hear the VC working but it's very quiet when it's doing it's thing. I can force the camera to take blurry motion shots through this lens but if I give it half a chance by not swinging it around, it stabilizes typical heartbeat and hand shake vibrations even when set to full zoom. If you always shoot from a tripod its not as important, but if you do a lot of handheld photography it's a big deal and it works quite well.

The auto focus is very effective. It takes about half a second for auto focus to seek it's focus spot. Fast enough considering what it gives you. Sharp focus.

There are no visible aberrations even at full zoom. Colors are accurate and vibrant.

Even the very first handheld zoom shot of a Cardinal on the bird feeder in the front yard was a keeper. Very easy to set up and use.

I have no complaints. I'd buy this lens again.

product_title: Panasonic BL-C121A Wireless Network Camera
review_headline: Great as a petcam... during daytime hours
review_body:
I purchased this camera to use as a petcam indoors while at work to keep an eye on our new puppy. The video is pretty clear when on the home network and while watching from the internet. The camera includes a motion sensor and microphone. You can use the motion sensor to trigger notifications to you via email and/or to record a video for up to 10 seconds (the video is not emailed to you, just the notification). The microphone works good, but you cannot hear the sound on the Iphone, which sucks, but this is not the camera's fault but Apple's. What may be one of the camera's/server's fault is that I have not been able to get it to work on my Blackberry. I keep getting a 403 error message when I try to load the page. Then again, it could be my fault as I haven't researched the issue for a possible solution yet. Regarding setup of the camera, it took some time, but I can't say that its really hard. The part that took me the longest was to set up the email timer triggers: You can set it up so that the camera emails you a photo image every hour (other options are every second or every minute, no in-betweens). For setting this up, you cannot use most free email services like Hotmail or Google, so we used our Verizon email account. Verizon's web instructions to setup email software like Outlook was to use port 465, but it actually worked on port number 587 (took me all day to figure this out through lots of Google searching). In the end, this was the setup that worked: \\"SMTP Server IP Address or Host Name: outgoing.verizon.net\\", \\"Port No. 587\\", then select \\"SMTP authentication\\" and enter your Verizon email user name (without the \\"verizon.net\\") and your password. Once I got the right port number, the email feature is GREAT! Now, even though I can't watch the video feed on my Blackberry, I receive photos every hour on my email.

The biggest problem I have with this camera, and the reason I give it 4 stars and not 5 is that image quality severely diminishes when there is no natural light. Come sunset, the image becomes very grainy. I turned on all the lights in close vicinity of the camera, and still, the image is grainy and nothing like it is with natural light. You can kinda still tell where the puppy is, but the image is very grainy. In darkness, you cannot see anything at all. I will try to post images of these, so you can see the difference between natural light, indoor lights, and darkness.

Overall, I am happy with the camera but for the price, image quality should be better with indoor lights (it IS an indoor camera).

review_headline: Panasonic Lumix DMC-GF3 Micro Four Thirds w 14-42 lens Update
review_body:
I am not a pro photographer. I don't usually make money off of my photos but I like good photos. I am mainly a very enthusiastic amateur portrait photographer. Anything that gets in front of my camera is fair game so.

The camera:
I bought this camera to fit a specific niche. I'm not looking to retire my DSLR. I don't want a bunch of lenses for this camera. I have all Pro Glass for my DSLR. I'm not going to shoot any production videos with this camera as my DSLR shoots also video. The niche was for me to have available a camera that is smaller and lighter than my DSLR with nearly the same range coverage. During a trip to Europe a few years ago I realized that nearly half of the several thousand photos I took were with my P&S. I realized in some situations a smaller camera can be advantageous. I've seen these micro four thirds in action and I liked the idea of being able to shoot RAW instead of JPEG. This is a personal preference. I didn't buy this camera to replace my DSLR. For me it is a walk around / scout camera. The size and weight advantage this camera are evident at 17 ounces it beats carrying my 5 pound DSLR. I also got a 45-200 lens to go along with my 'kit' so at somewhere just over 2.5 pounds I have nearly as much range as 30 pounds of DSLR and three lenses with flash.

I like the fact that I'm able to 'set up' the different modes to my liking. I tend to use more sharpness to my photos and I have that ability with this camera.

dislikes out of the box: This is the second Panasonic camera that I have. Both of them have this really flimsy battery/card access door. There is no question that anywhere near water this could be a problem. There was also a noticeable gap along the bottom where the two halves of the body joined.

Overall I like the camera's size. It is a little awkward feeling in the beginning simply because of the lens being nearly as big as the camera. This awkwardness quickly goes away. For me out of the box the camera is pretty simple to operate. The small pamphlet type of instructions are mainly people who don't know about cameras to get the pieces of the camera to fit together. If you are familiar with cameras then it really isn't very useful. The instruction manual is on a disc. I'd prefer a real manual as I tend to carry my camera manuals in my camera bag or a cheat sheet.

I've had this camera for about a month. I've done a few different 'events' with it. The first night I had it I took it to my photo club meet and took photos indoors shooting at ISO 1600. The results of those photos weren't bad. A little more noise in the darker areas of the room but that is to be expected at higher ISOs. I experimented with the Auto ISO and found that it wasn't as intuitive as I like. I tried a couple shots with the AI mode and figured that didn't work for me. I experimented with ISO 3200 in a restaurant party room and found that there was way to much noise for my liking.

I've taken close to 500 photos with this camera in a month. In most situations this camera is really nice to have around. I did take it along on a photo club outing and I gotta tell you that in direct sunlight was a major fail. Nearly all of those helpful screen aids become nearly impossible to see.

The LED screen has many features and I like them for the most part. The touch screen is really nice. The menu selection isn't as intuitive as I'd like, but I typically tend to not change settings all that often during a shoot. I tend to run several of the 'accessory' style features like the histogram, display and grid. These seem to use a lot of battery power. I spent nearly twelve hours on a short road trip with this camera taking nearly a hundred photos and by the time I got home I had two bars on the battery. Not great but then again with all the extra stuff on the LED going too it really isn't all that bad. I typically like to leave my cameras on whenI'm walking around. I turned this camera on and off during the long day. I worked around the bright sunlight and when I was out of the direct sun the camera functioned very well.

I tried to use the editing program that came with the camera. I have already several editing programs and really didn't need this program taking space on my computer. Part of the reason I don't use this camera's editing program is that the first time you open the program it will attempt to catalog every photo on your computer and external drive. As I have several thousand photos on my external drive this takes a very long time. I just modified my work flow a bit as the Panasonic RAW files apparently covered by my version of Photo Shop, but are in Lightroom. So instead of having the program automatically download the new photos into their own folder I create it and cut and paste them. I've noticed that the Panasonic movie files don't transfer automatically. You need to move them yourself.

Conclusion:
The camera fits pretty well the niche I wanted it to fill. There really isn't a macro capability with this camera unless you get a macro lens. I'm pretty much back to using my P&S for that. There are times when a macro lens is handy. The camera has a macro selection but that tends to be more of a bokeh style function than macro.
The camera strap is to short and the small nature of the body means that finding something longer might be an issue unless you come up with a hack. A couple of small key ring holders would work to put a longer strap on. The battery life is a little short especially if you are using the 45-200 lens with the IS switch.
The camera won't fit in your pocket if you don't have a pancake lens on it. You'll need a bag. I have a small military surplus bag that I carry the camera in. I don't so much like the idea of a wrist strap as they aren't all that practical for me.

If you are looking for a nice camera that takes good quality photos, is easy to operate and yet has DSLR capabilities then this is a camera worth taking a look.

review_headline: Everything is a good value at the right price
review_body: This is the only positive review I've written where I have mostly negative things to say about the product.  The web interface is not good.  It requires an ActiveX control for full functionality, and to make matters worse the signed cert on the control expires a month or two ago, and now to get it to work on new machines, I have to set the clock back, install the control, then set it forward.  That is probably a deal breaker for many, and should be.  Searches online for the issue yielded such helpful bits as a Turkish distributor complaining about the problem and the manufacturer response to set the clock back.  I've bought 9 of these so far, and one did not work.  The other 8 worked, excepting the problem above and that one of them would reboot if you attempted to pan/tilt it - there was some goofy fix for it involving doing something during the startup calibration process, but I forgot what it was - after it was done though, it worked as expected.  The interface for configuring e-mail alerts is terrible, requiring literally hundreds of clicks for each camera to individually click on and off each hour that you want or don't want motion monitored.  The alerts can only send a series of 6 snap shots, no more, and no video (this can be remedied by purchasing dedicated controller/DVR software to run on a server). Despite all of that, I'd probably still recommend them.  For the number I needed, I would have paid at least $1000-$2000 more for another camera with PTZ capability and wireless.  Once I learned the quirks, they were fast to set up and deploy.  I don't have any complaints about the image quality, and when I connect them to a controller, iPhone, or Android app, they work as expected.  They also have two-way microphone capability and night vision - very well equipped for the price.  So, if you have a high tolerance for poorly made and supported software, the hardware capabilities of the camera are a good value for the price - especially when using them with 3rd party apps and not their own web interface.  Oh yeah - one last note regarding poorly supported - the manufacturer offers no warranty or return policy, asking you to work the the reseller, I bought it form some random Amazon 3rd party vendor who did nothing after 30 days, and I didn't get around to opening one of the batches until that had already passed, so I am stuck with the one dead unit. product_title: Leica X2 16.5MP Compact System Camera with 2.7-Inch TFT LCD- Body Only
review_body:
Couldn't decide between the Leica X2 and the Fuji X100 so I ordered both :)

Bit of background - I've been shooting with D-SLRs since the Nikon D70. My current body is a D300 with the 70-200VR, 17-55DX and 12-24DX. When city touring, lugging all that gear is cumbersome not only when shooting but when traveling: getting it through security, worried about leaving it in your hotel room, etc. These new micro bodies with high quality sensors are right in my wheelhouse.

My girlfriend took the X100 and I took the Leica X2 out for an afternoon of shooting around San Francisco. At the end of the day, we got back and she conducted a blind test (yes, she is amazing :) and more often than not I preferred the look of the Fuji and for the shots with Velvia enabled, even more so.

Observations from a day of shooting:
- I'm unsure why I've read some call this \\"pocketable\\" because unless you're wearing cargo shorts, no way.
- The lack of integrated viewfinder turned out to be a dealbreaker for me, an SLR shooter at heart. No matter how hard I tried to convince myself it would be OK to shoot with the LCD back, I kept banging my nose into the back of the camera when I raised it to my eye to peek through a viewfinder that didn't exist. I realize the Oly VF is the same (and half the price) of the Leica VF. Still it's an extra $200+ and for me really buzzkills the sleek design of the Leica.
- Compared with the features of the X100's LCD while shooting, felt left out in the wind. The engineers at Leica couldn't think of anything useful to do with the LCD during live view?

I desperately wanted the Leica to be my favourite. It's a beautiful and sturdy piece of equipment garnering more queries and positive comments during one day of street shooting than nearly 10 years of the D70, D200 an D300 combined. Unfortunately technology has caught up with the Leica brand name / price differential. $1000 more for the Leica red dot over the X100 was a no-brainer for me.

If you're just hell-bent on the Leica name and the look of the body, please rent one before buying.

Sad to return it. I'll check out the X3 though :)

Summary:
- In a blind test, preferred the Fuji shots.
- No integrated VF was clunky. Kudos to those of you who can get along without one.
- Extraordinarily low tech for the price. You'll feel like you're using a digital camera from the 90s.
- Extraordinarily little for the price.

UPDATE 11/23/2012 - Took the X100 to Europe and couldn't have been happier. product_title: Fujifilm X-Pro 1 16MP Digital Camera with APS-C X-Trans CMOS Sensor
review_headline: You can pay far less than full retail price for this camera
review_body:
As the owner of a Nikon D700 camera with the newest Nikkor 35mm prime, 24-70mm and 70-200mm zoom lenses, it took only one long holiday trip for me to recognize it was not practical as a travel camera. When I learned of the Fujifilm X-Pro1, it was a godsend, for I knew I could never justify the purchase of a Leica rangefinder with its lenses.

With one exception*, I'm not going to address the craftsmanship or technological prowess of my new Fujifilm X-Pro 1 camera body, as I can add nothing to the experts' reviews. What I can address, however, is the bargain to be had purchasing this item \\"used\\" from Amazon Warehouse Deals or an alternate used reseller sanctioned by Amazon. I compared prices of a \\"new\\" body from Amazon for $1699 v. \\"used-very good\\" from Amazon Warehouse for $1222 v. \\"used-like new\\" from Amazon Warehouse for $1274 and \\"used-like new\\" from OneCall for $1247 (I know it's hard to believe, but these were the prices displayed at the time I made my purchases).

I opted for the \\"used-like new\\" and decided against the aftermarket warranty, even though the ad copy cautioned that the body, as it is used, may not qualify for the factory warranty.

On 14 June I placed the order for the \\"used-like new\\" body from Amazon Warehouse for $1274, as well as for the Fujinon XF 35mm \\"used-like new\\" lens from Amazon Warehouse for $533 and the XF 18mm lens \\"used-like new\\" for $521 (also from Amazon Warehouse). I selected super saver free shipping. On 21 June, all items arrived intact in the same box via UPS. When I opened the original Fujifilm box containing the camera body I was pleasantly surprised to see that it was in pristine condition, giving the appearance of \\"new\\" with all accessories, literature, CD-ROM and warranty certificate. True, the box had been opened and resealed, and Amazon Warehouse had obscured the original body SKU and serial number on the box, but those are the only discrepancies from new as far as I could tell.

The Fujinon XF 35mm lens, contained in its original Fujifilm lens box with lens SKU and serial number stickers intact, likewise appears to be \\"new\\" rather than \\"like new\\". All materials are present and free of any fingerprints, smudges or blemishes (lens, front and rear caps, hood w/cover, lens bag, owner's manual, service locations information sheet and original factory warranty certificate with registration instructions).

Because I wasn't certain what I would find when I opened my Amazon Warehouse camera body, I decided to also separately purchase the \\"used-like new\\" body from OneCall for $1247 because the ad copy stated \\"brand new, open box ...\\" It arrived on 22 June from OneCall. Indeed, this body does appear to be absolutely brand new and unmolested, with SKU and serial number stickers intact on the resealed original box and all items in their original sealed cellophane bags.

I have elected to keep the camera body from OneCall and return for refund the body I purchased from Amazon Warehouse, because the OneCall body is $27 less than the body from Amazon Warehouse and, subjectively, the OneCall original box and contents appeared \\"newer\\" than its Warehouse twin. But, before making that decision, I mounted the 35mm lens on both bodies and tried them out. Unsurprisingly, they all function exactly as I expected. I have now registered the OneCall camera body and the Warehouse lens online with the manufacturer.

As I said, I'll leave the discussion of the camera's merits to the experts, but for the price savings for this body and lens, I couldn't be happier.

And, I couldn't be happier with my order's arrival date, because now I'm looking forward to taking my new, incredibly lightweight and compact traveling camera to Europe next week for the 2012 Tour de France.

NB: I will be returning the 18mm lens, because unlike the 35mm lens, it was not accompanied by its lens bag or warranty certificate. The little spacein the box dedicated for those items was empty. I realize that I could contact Amazon and arrange for an exchange or for them to send me the missing items, but I've decided to use this opportunity to simply await the release of the new Fujinon XF 23mm (35mm equiv.) lens.

I've decided to take a pass on any telephoto or zoom lenses for this camera, because IMO those lenses negate the attraction of a small, lightweight, discreet travel camera. If my shooting situation requires the use of such lenses, I'll just pull out the D700 big gun.

I considered the X-Pro 1 assist grip, but I think I'll instead purchase the X-Pro 1 leather case for the protection it offers when using a standard or WA prime lens, but also because the lower case less the lid allows full access to all camera functions while providing a larger form factor when holding the camera while decreasing the likelihood of inadvertently pressing the Q button with one's thumb.

*I am amazed and disappointed that such a technically advanced, near-perfect camera does not have a OVF diopter adjustment. I suspect that many potential users of this camera are going to be older enthusiasts who recall and appreciate the film rangefinder cameras of our youth, and who will not hesitate at paying a premium price for quality. Most people who fall into that category would not only benefit from a diopter adjustment, but require it. I can't imagine how Fujifilm could neglect to include such an essential feature.

BOTTOM LINE: For a total price of $1780.00 I have a new, factory-warranted Fujifilm X-Pro 1 camera with a new, factory-warranted Fujinon XF 35mm prime lens. What's not to like?

I am not going to go into detail here about just what each compartment in this bag can hold, one can find that on the Lowepro website and elsewhere. Suffice it is to say that it will easily hold a camera body and 2-3 lenses, the small gadgets necessary for a shoot, your keys, cell phone, extra batteries, filters, memory cards, that sort of stuff. The quality of the construction is very good, it is comfortable to wear as a sling and will turn to provide easy access to a camera. One final benefit of this bag which amuses me a bit, it seems to give me more \\"creds\\" as a photographer while I am out on the street...people actually do things like stand clear of me while I am taking a photo or say \\"yes\\" when I ask permission to take their picture. product_title: Nikon D800 36.3 MP CMOS FX-Format Digital SLR Camera
review_body:
I am in the probably unusual situation of jumping from a Nikon D300 to a D800. These cameras are a good five years apart, so I may have a slightly different perspective from some.

Pros:

- The resolution is killer (but yes, be prepared to deal with your computer chugging with all of that data!)
- The sensor really does record an amazing amount of data (take a look at DXOmark giving this and the D800E its highest scores). This means I can recover more in raw, but it also just means nicer color in general.
- The color in high-ISO and incandescent situations is SO BALANCED, compared to my D300 which basically just gave red, this is worlds better. For D700/etc. users, this may not pop out as a big change.

Cons:

- In five years, the features haven't changed all that much. Which is fine, I guess!
- The video is hard to control and get used to. Hard to pull a focus without looking through the viewfinder, but it's set up so you can't (unless I'm missing something).
- The LCD screen still isn't bright enough, if you want to use LiveView at the beach you will be laughing at your overexposed results when you get home.
- \\"Quiet\\" shutter mode isn't quiet, it's basically worthless.

Neutral:

- The \\"green tint\\" thing is true, though I'm sure they'll fix that soon with firmware.
- The shutter is fairly loud, it sounds like a guillotine slicing through a neck. Some may like this, it's pretty badass-sounding.

Overall I'm very happy with the purchase. I think DSLR video still has a ways to go, the alternate focusing method during LiveView is pretty worthless and so unless I buy a $1k screen to mount on top, I'll never be able to shoot proper handheld video and see what I'm doing. I think I was too optimistic about what I would be able to do on that front.

When you buy a camera body, you're mostly buying the chip. This is the best chip there is, so you can't really go wrong here. If you have the money, go for it!

I'm still getting used to the camera and intend to read some of the manual, so I will try to update this if I've found I'm spreading misinformation.

product_title: Panasonic HDC-TM41H HD Camcorder with 16GB Internal Flash Memory
review_headline: Great Home Camera -- NEW EDIT: CAMERA BROKEN, AND NO SUPPORT
review_body:
This is a great camera for home movies or Youtube videos etc. I got it last Christmas, and have been using it constantly. I recommend storing everything on an SD card so that you can easily move it over to your computer (assuming your computer has an SD port). Picture quality is great, however it gets slightly blurry in low light, but that's to be expected. Great interface, and easy to use.

My only complaint is the video editing software it comes with. It's very basic and limited, and while useful to convert the AVCHD clips into more manageable movies, that's about it. You'll need to buy a better editing software if you want to do anything with your videos.

Overall, a great camera. I definitely recommend it.
**********************************************************************************************************************************************

EDIT: After seven months of owning this camera, it stopped recording to anything, SD cards and internal memory. It wouldn't recognize any SD cards inserted into it, and so wouldn't play anything I had recorded before this happened. When I tried to record directly to internal memory, I received an error message, and since then have not been able get anything other than a white screen on the display.

I called Panasonic to see about getting the camera repaired. They told me it was still under warranty, so I could ship it to them for repairs. Once the center received my camera, we received a call saying that while the camera was under warranty for parts, it was not for labor. Sure enough, in the fine print of the warranty, you only have a 90 day warranty. Panasonic said they would have to charge us $111 just to open the box and examine my camera.

Of course, after that, there would be more charges for the actual repairs. Needless to say, we had them send it back without repairs.

Bottom line, it's a nice camera until it breaks and Panasonic won'tfix it due to lack of confidence in their product.

product_title: Adorama Dedicated Lens Hood for Nikon 70-210mm f/4 & 75-300mm f/4.5-5.6 Lens (Hn-24)
review_headline: As good as any real Nikon product
review_body:
I bought this for a Nikon 75-300mm f/4.5-5.6 lens that I purchased used without a hood.

The quality of the hood is excellent. It's made of metal, with a nice matte black finish on the inside and the lettering printed onto a satin finish on the outside. The threads fit smoothly and without any play on my lens.

This is a screw-in lens hood that screws into the filter threads at the end of the lens. There are no internal threads on the hood to accept a filter, so if you want to use it with a filter your only option is to screw the hood into the threads on a filter that's already mounted on the lens. No big deal.

However, for this same reason, you can't put the 62mm lens cap on while the hood is mounted. I usually walk around without a lens cap on anyway, but to someone who likes to put the cap on after each shot, this could be an issue. It's not a huge hassle to unscrew the hood at the end of the day to put the lens cap back on, but it would quickly become annoying doing it over and over again. You'd have the same problem with the Nikon brand hood as well. The large end of the hood measures just under 78mm internal diameter, so a 77mm lens cap might fit in the end, but I don't have one to try.

Overall, this is a quality product at a great price, especially since the real HN-24 is getting harder and harder to find. When bought from Adorama the service is excellent, as always, and I would definitely buy this again.

product_title: Fujifilm X-Pro 1 16MP Digital Camera with APS-C X-Trans CMOS Sensor
review_body:
I am not a professional photographer or even a great one, but I love photography and that one is true. Before this, I used a Nikon D90 which I still keep, great camera btw, and an Olympus Ep-l2. Ever since I used the Oly, I never want to bring another SLR with their huge lens again for family photo or what I call daily pics. That is why I went for the Fuji X Pro1; Had to sell the Oly to fund the Fuji, damn expensive for me.

Enough background talk. The reason I gave it 5 stars despite all the quirks that sometimes made me want to throw the camera is...the pictures. Again, I am not a professional Photographer that goes into all those technical details and pixel peeps, hence I don't know much or care about distortion and fringing and stuffs. I care about the results as a whole and that beauty is in the eye of the beholder.

The main reason why I fell in love with the fuji, aside from its sexy design, is the emotions that I got from the pictures of X Pro1. It led me to believe that this camera is more intimate than any other camera I've used; It's not just an item, it's personal. It's the process of getting the pictures that made me love the Fuji.

I am not blowing things up or simply a fanboy, but all the portraits that I got from this camera is different. Especially the eyes. If I look closely, Fuji captures the reflection in the eyes beautifully. Maybe it's my lack of skills when using all my previous cameras, but for me it is different. You have to really try and see it for yourself to really understand what I'm talking about. All the portraits that I took using the Fuji gave me emotions that speak to me.

Well that is me, you have your own opinions. But don't believe all the reviews whether it is positive or negative, heck don't believe me, just grab one, shoot something and then see it for yourself.

p.s: Get an additional battery. Battery sucks and the meter is far from accurate. Oh and I uploaded some pictures,so that you guys might better understand what I'm talking about.

product_title: Canon EOS Rebel T3i Digital SLR Camera Body & EF-S 18-55mm IS II Lens with 75-300mm Lens + 16GB Card + .45x Wide Angle & 2x Telephoto Lenses + Flash + Case + Battery + Remote + (2) Filters + Accessory Kit
review_body: The camera is great, generally, but has some strange quirks--examples: having to cover the eyepiece when self-timing, and, in most modes, having it autofocus on the nearest object (even if not the object of interest). Making the various settings are too complicated--Canon needs to have a point and shoot expert work on simplifying them--and many (most?) of the settings are unnecessary. The 18-55 mm lens needs to be sharp enough at all focal lengths that full size pictures are not degraded; the 75-300 mm lens does not seem to have this defect, but it is not an IS (shake reducing) lens. ISO 400 is as good as ISO 100, and the 3200 and 6400 ISO images are surprisingly good. The auxiliary 2.5x lens gives sharp images in the center of the field but that drops off quickly and sharply away from center. I was never able to get the auxiliary wide angle lens to screw into the front of either lens, so I doubt that I'll ever use either. Remote control works only with 10 second self-timer. Other items seem fine. Haven't used the extra flash yet but have put the filters on both lenses. Extra battery is welcome. I wish I had bought the camera with the 18-135 mm regular lens or a telephoto lens with focal length overlapping the 18-55 mm lens.
